utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Ms. Tatjana Cmeric, and Christopher Gosnell appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Zupljanin, and the Office of the Prosecutor lodged appeals against the trial judgement rendered in this case on 27 March 2013 by Trial Chamber II. Pursuant to the Scheduling Order issued on 30th October 2015, the Appeals Chamber will hear the appeals today. Before doing so, I will provide a brief summary of the case and of Mr. Stanisic's and Mr. Zupljanin's appeal and that of the Prosecution. I will then outline how we will proceed today. The case concerns the responsibility of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin for crimes committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 1st of April to the 31st of December, 1992. Throughout that time, Mr. Stanisic was the minister of interior of the newly established Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, Serb Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and an ex officio member of the National Security Council. Mr. Zupljanin was the chief of the Regional Security Service Centre of Banja Luka and for part of the relevant time, he was also a member of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The Trial Chamber found that a joint criminal enterprise existed from no longer than 24th October 1991 until at least 31st December 1992, with the objective to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territory of the planned Serb state. I will refer to it as the JCE. It also found that this purpose was implemented through the commission of the crimes of persecutions, through forcible transfer and deportation, and inhumane acts, consisting of forcible transfer as crimes against humanity. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Stanisic for crimes committed in each of the 20 municipalities listed in the indictment and Mr. Zupljanin for crimes committed in the eight municipalities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. They were both convicted through the first category of joint criminal enterprise for persecutions as a crime against humanity and through the third category of joint criminal enterprise for murder and torture as violation of the laws or customs of war. In addition, Mr. Zupljanin was convicted pursuant to the third category of joint criminal enterprise for extermination as a crime against humanity and for ordering persecutions through appropriation. On the basis of the principles relating to cumulative convictions, the Trial Chamber did not enter convictions against Mr. Stanisic and Zupljanin for murder, torture, inhumane acts, deportation, and inhumane acts (forcible transfers) as crimes against humanity or cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war. The Trial Chamber sentenced both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin to 22 years of imprisonment. Mr. Stanisic advances 16 grounds of appeal; Mr. Zupljanin, six, challenging their respective convictions and sentences. Under Mr. Stanisic's ground of appeal 1 bis and Mr. Zupljanin's sixth ground of appeal, the two appellants argue that their right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial Tribunal has been violated as a result of the participation of Judge Harhoff in the trial proceedings. Under his first ground of appeal, Mr. Stanisic alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in law by failing to provide a reasoned opinion for his convictions for persecutions, murder, and torture under the first and third categories of joint criminal enterprise. Under his second through sixth grounds of appeal, Mr. Stanisic challenges the Trial Chamber's findings concerning his responsibility pursuant to the first category of joint criminal enterprise. Under his seventh ground of appeal, Mr. Stanisic challenges the Trial Chamber's assessment of his interview with the Prosecution. In his grounds of appeal eight to 11, Mr. Stanisic raises a number of challenges related to his convictions pursuant to the third category of joint criminal enterprise. And finally, under his 12th through 15th grounds of appeal, Mr. Stanisic alleges a number of errors of law and facts in relation to his sentence. The Prosecution responds that Mr. Stanisic's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety. In his first ground of appeal, Mr. Zupljanin raises a number of challenges to the Trial Chamber's findings on his responsibility pursuant to the first category of joint criminal enterprise. Under his second ground of appeal, Mr. Zupljanin challenges his convictions pursuant to the third category of joint criminal enterprise. In his third ground of appeal, he alleges errors in the Trial Chamber's findings on extermination. Under his fourth ground of appeal, Mr. Zupljanin alleges multiple errors in relation to his sentence. And finally, under his fifth ground of appeal, Mr. Zupljanin alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in finding him responsible for persecutions through the appropriation of property. The Prosecution responds that Mr. Zupljanin's appeal should be dismissed. I will now move to the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution advances two grounds of appeal. First, it challenges the sentences imposed by the Trial Chamber of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin and requests that the Appeals Chamber substitute these sentences with sentences in the range of 30 to 40 years. In its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in its application of the law related to cumulative convictions. Mr. Stanisic and Zupljanin respond that the Appeals Chamber should dismiss the Prosecution's ground of appeal in their entirety. During this hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in any order they consider suitable for their presentation. However, I would urge counsel not to repeat or summarise arguments already presented in their briefs with which - please remember - the Appeals Chamber is already very well familiar. I recall that parties are invited to discuss in their oral submissions certain matters set out in the addendum to the Scheduling Order which was issued on 4th December 2015. For the sake of clarity, I ask that parties indicate which issues they are at the beginning of their submissions. Furthermore, the parties are invited to provide precise references to material supporting their oral submissions. I would also like to recall that this appeal is not a trial de novo and the parties must refrain from repeating their cases which were presented at trial. Arguments must be limited to alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged errors of fact which occasion a miscarriage of justice. Finally, I would like to remind the parties to be particularly careful not to reveal any information that could identify a protected witness or other protected information or material. I will now turn to today's timetable. As set out in the Appeals Chamber decision on the Prosecution urgent motion to revise the timetable for the appeal hearing of 11 December, we will proceed as follows: First, we will hear submissions from counsel for Mr. Stanisic for a total of one hour and 35 minutes. Then we will continue with the Prosecution's response for 15 minutes. After a pause of 20 minutes, we will resume for the remainder of the Prosecution's response for 45 minutes, which will be followed by Mr. Stanisic's reply for 20 minutes. We will then proceed with submissions for Mr. Zupljanin for 55 minutes and we will break for lunch at five minutes past 1.00. We will resume at ten minutes past 2.00 to hear the remainder of Mr. Zupljanin's submission for another 40 minutes and then hear the Prosecution's response for 60 minutes. After that, Mr. Zupljanin will have the opportunity to reply for 20 minutes and we will take a break for 25 minutes. We will then resume at 4.35 in the afternoon to hear the Prosecution's submissions for 40 minutes and the responses of the legal teams for Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin for 20 minutes each. After that, the Prosecution will have 15 minutes to reply to these responses. Lastly, it is customary for the Appeals Chamber to give an opportunity to appellants to make a personal address to the Appeals Chamber if they so wish. Hence, at the end of this hearing, both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin will have ten minutes each for a personal address if they wish to do so. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions and may ask questions themselves following each of their submissions or at the end of the hearing, depending on what we think is best at any given time. We will now immediately move to hear submissions by Mr. Stanisic's team. We will be checking the time based on the clock in this courtroom, so you're starting at approximately five minutes past 9.00. Thank you. And, Mr. Zecevic, please go ahead.

You have heard this one before, I am sure, but I have to say it: Mico Stanisic's case is unique. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. As I was saying, Mico Stanisic's case is unique. It is unique due to the situation involving Judge Harhoff, one of the Trial Judges, who in June 2013 displayed a reasonable apprehension of bias in favour of conviction which impacts the Trial Chamber judgement of 27 March 2013. It is also unique due to the position of Minister of Interior held by Mr. Stanisic, who was a part of the government, some members of which were involved in a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer and deport Muslims and Croats from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: All other microphones in the courtroom, please off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer and deport Muslims and Croats from territories of BiH. It is unique because Mico Stanisic was found to have contributed to the JCE, not on the basis of any specific act, but rather because he failed to take sufficient action to investigate and prosecute crimes against Muslims and Croats. In our respectful submission, this is a first. It follows, Mr. President, that the context of this case is of the utmost importance, even at the appeals stage. The manner in which this case was conducted is also important. Mico Stanisic surrendered on 11 March 2005, as soon as he was informed of the indictment; consented to a detailed interview conducted by the Prosecution before the beginning of the trial; conducted his trial in line with the information he provided to the Prosecution during his interview before trial; presented his closing argument in conformity with the information he provided to the Prosecution during his interview before the trial; has been in jeopardy for a period of more than ten years. Our submission today will be presented according to the following outline: Part 1, under A, Judge Fred Harhoff's electronic correspondence addressed to 56 "friends" raises a reasonable apprehension of bias, which invalidates Mico Stanisic's convictions entered for Counts 1, 4, and 6. B: Response to Appeals Chamber's preliminary questions under (i) and (ii). Part 2: A, response to question 1(i) posed by the Appeals Chamber; B, response to question 1(ii) posed by the Appeals Chamber; C, response to question 2 posed by the Appeals Chamber; and D, response to question 1(ii) and 3 posed by the Appeals Chamber. At the end you will hear our concluding remarks. I now turn, Your Honours, over the floor to my colleague, who will address you concerning the first part of our submission. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Honourable Judges. It is both an honour and a privilege to appear before you this morning to deliver arguments on behalf of Mico Stanisic. Part 1 of our submissions has to do with the matter involving Judge Harhoff. Mr. President, the reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of Judge Frederik Harhoff which arises from his mail, his e-mail, addressed to 56 friends is a highly sensitive issue. We take no pleasure, Mr. President, in arguing this issue before the Appeals Chamber this morning. However, in light of the potential consequences for Mico Stanisic himself in the first place but also for the ICTY, and also as a result of the impact for international criminal justice as a whole, it is in the interests of justice for us to respectfully but, at the same time, openly and thoroughly present our arguments. My submissions this morning on this issue will be presented under five headings, as follows: I will first address the letter itself or the e-mail and the effect it produces in this case, that is, in the proceedings against Mico Stanisic. This was addressed in our additional appellant's brief in section B (ii) in pages 13 to 19. I will then address the rebuttal material which has been admitted in respect of this issue. And in the third place, I will explain why the decision rendered by the Specially Convened Chamber in the Seselj proceedings - I'm referring here to the first decision as well as the decision on reconsideration - I will explain why these decisions are relevant and are probative in establishing a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of Judge Harhoff in this case. I will then answer, of course, the first question posed by the Appeals Chamber and I will answer this question - no surprise to you - in the affirmative. I will explain why the participation of Judge Frederik Harhoff in Mico Stanisic's proceedings invalidates the convictions entered against him. I will also argue in this section that the proper remedy for such a violation in the circumstances of this case is no less than a stay of proceedings or, in French, "arrêt du procédure." Lastly, I will answer the second question posed by the Appeals Chamber in respect of this issue. Before moving on to these five arguments, Mr. President, I deem important to make some preliminary observations, which I believe are of the highest importance in determining whether the e-mail addressed by Judge Harhoff to 56 friends reveals, indeed, a reasonable apprehension of bias, again in the context of this case. My first preliminary observation has to do with the importance, the fundamental importance of the right of an accused to be tried by independent and impartial Judges, of course by an independent and impartial Chamber composed of three Judges. It's an issue of trust, Mr. President. Impartiality of the Judges is the most important aspect of the justice system. If there is no trust, if there is no trust in one Judge in respect of a particular case, if it appears that the Judge was not impartial to the reasonable observer - I will come back to that - there is no justice, proceedings must be invalidated. The obligation vested in the Trial Chamber to ensure the proper administration of justice, of course it's very well-known, Mr. President, justice must be done but justice must be seen to be done. My second preliminary observation has to do with the presumption of impartiality, which attaches to Judges and also the fact that this presumption is, indeed, important and is also very strong and not easy to rebut. We fully acknowledge the strength and the importance of this presumption; however, we also submit respectfully that the Appeals Chamber must not hesitate a minute. When a reasonable appearance of bias on the part of a Judge is established, measures must be taken to re-establish the confidence of the public in the administration of justice. In respect of a single accused, measure must be taken to correct the violation of his fundamental right. My third preliminary observation of course is based on the first two because I'd like to say a quick word as to why we took the position before this hearing this morning of filing many submissions to try and get this matter adjudicated earlier. Mr. President, there is no hiding the fact that the publication of Judge Harhoff's letter in the Danish newspaper on 13 June shook the Tribunal, and a decision rendered by the Specially Convened Chamber even more so. I weigh my words here. It might have shook the Tribunal, but it certainly did not shock the Tribunal. The finding of the Specially Convened Chamber found that - that's the reading of the finding itself: "By referring to a 'set practice' of convicting accused persons without reference to an evaluation of the evidence in each individual case, the Majority, Judge Liu dissenting, considers that there are grounds for concluding that a reasonable observer, properly informed, would reasonably apprehend bias on the part of Judge Harhoff" - and here the words are important - "in favour of conviction. This includes for the purposes of the present case." The specially convened Chamber's majority went on to say: "This appearance of bias is further compounded by Judge Harhoff's statement that he is confronted by a professional and moral dilemma, which in the view of the Majority, is a clear reference to his difficulty in applying the current jurisprudence of this Tribunal. In the circumstances" of this case "the Majority considers" Judge Liu dissenting "that the Letter, when read as a whole, rebuts the presumption of impartiality." This is an unprecedented finding. We have done a lot of research into this area. We have all heard the expression "convicting judge" before. We have all heard the expression "judge shopping" before. But this is way beyond the use of such terms that sometimes we hear unfortunately in the legal profession. When a judge is found to display an appearance of bias in favour of conviction, it must produce results, not only on the cases on which he is sitting, but it must also be dealt with. The ongoing impact of this finding on the legacy of the ICTY has yet to be fully assessed. Personally, as a Defence counsel for many years, with my past that is very well-known when I used to be the Chef de Cabinet for the President and I worked closely with the Judges, everyone knows how important for me the work of the Judges is and how much I respect the function of the Judges. But to me this letter has devastating consequences on the trust of the public. Of course that's not the issue today. The issue today is what does it do for Mr. Stanisic. That's what I will address. Because of the decision that came out in the Prosecutor versus Seselj, we have insisted to have the matter adjudicated because of course the appearance of bias is based on the same letter and, as I will argue later, there are very few differences between what happened in the Seselj case and in this case. Of course the Appeals Chamber has decided to deal with this issue on appeal. We are here today and this is what I will do. Nonetheless, we insist on the fact that the Appeals Chamber must first consider this ground of appeal before moving to part 2 of our appeal. If this ground of appeal should be retained by the Appeals Chamber, in our respectful submission, there's no need to go further that we even address the other grounds. If this ground should not be retained by the Appeals Chamber, then of course we move on to part 2 of our appeal. But even in part 2 of our appeal, the words of Judge Harhoff regarding, for example, his understanding that we can convict in the framework of a joint criminal enterprise on the basis of knowledge, these words also would be relevant for the second part of the appeal. Let me begin with my arguments and by quickly going over the reasonable observer test. Pursuant to the case law of the ICTY, a judge is disqualified if there is a showing of actual bias or of an unacceptable appearance of bias. And many cases, I refer to Prosecutor versus Delalic, Prosecutor versus Milosevic, Prosecutor versus Furundzija, I think that was the first time this test was laid out, where we have the following: An unacceptable appearance of bias exists if the circumstances would lead a reasonable observer, properly informed, to reasonably apprehend bias. This is commonly known as the reasonable observer test. So what is a reasonable observer? Well, this term has been defined as: "... an informed person, with knowledge of all relevant circumstances, including" as was pointed out by Judge Liu in his dissenting opinion "knowledge of all the relevant circumstances including the traditions of integrity and impartiality that form a part of the background." For us the essential elements of this reasonable observer test are the following: We require a reasonable person, a person that is properly informed of all relevant circumstances - and I will cover that - and was aware of the traditions of integrity and impartiality, but the reasonable observer on the basis of all circumstances will conclude on the existence of an unacceptable appearance of bias. We personally have a problem with the word "unacceptable." We believe it doesn't fit in that definition at all because whether it is actual bias or appearance of bias, both are unacceptable. I think what was meant by the word "unacceptable" is what we refer to as a double objective test. The real issue is that the conclusion on the existence of appearance of bias must be a reasonable one. This is the position adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada, who has defined apprehension of bias as follows: "... must be a reasonable one held by a reasonable and right-minded person, applying themselves to the question and obtaining thereon the required information ..." The test contains a two-fold objective element: The person considering the alleged bias must be reasonable and the apprehension of bias itself must also be reasonable, albeit in the circumstances of this case. The question is whether a reasonable observer, putting his mind to the letter or to the e-mail of Judge Harhoff, fully informed of the context, would conclude on the existence of a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of Judge Harhoff in this case. In this regard we take full notice of the separate opinion of Judge Afande which was appended to the decision on reconsideration of our motion for mistrial. The issue itself, the letter, does it reveal a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of Judge Harhoff? And the question at the end of the day is: Would it be more likely than not that Judge Harhoff carried this bias when adjudicating the proceedings against Mico Stanisic? At the end of the day, this is the question, we say, the Appeals Chamber must address. Let us take a look at the context. What do we have? Well, we have a Judge of the international Tribunal, a Judge who has been a professor of law, who has a concrete and known legal background. This Judge has previously worked as a Senior Legal Officer in Chambers of the same Tribunal. This Judge has been a Judge for six years. To the point of writing the letter, he has been involved in five cases before the ICTY. We look at the cases including Prosecutor versus Milosevic, that's Dragomir; we look at the case Prosecutor versus Delic, in which he was a Trial Judge; we look at the case of Prosecutor versus Seselj; Prosecutor versus Djordjevic, in which he was a Pre-Trial Judge but then was not on the trial; and finally this case, the case of Mico Stanisic and Zupljanin. These cases deal with either command responsibility and joint criminal enterprise and aiding and abetting. These cases, at least the three cases and the cases in which decisions were rendered, the results were guilty findings. Nothing wrong with a guilty finding, but of course we still have to note that in the cases in which he was involved which referred to issues in the letter, these cases ended up with a finding of guilt. It's just a fact, nothing more. The problem, Mr. President, is not the fact that Judge Frederik Harhoff reacted to certain judgements; rather, it's the problem in the manner in which he reacted to certain judgements, because those are the cases in which he was involved. But the context of the letter is when he gains information concerning two judgements rendered by his peers. What judgements are we talking about? We're talking about, first, the Perisic judgement, then the Gotovina judgement, and finally a judgement rendered by the Trial Chamber in Stanisic and Simatovic. That's the context. He gains information concerning these judgements. He reads media articles related to these judgements. The Trial Chamber issues -- having read these media articles related to these judgements, he reacts to the situation. So the mail is a reaction to these three decisions, two by the Appeals Chamber and one by a Trial Chamber. The problem is not that he reacted. After all, I mean Judges are expected to take stock of judgements issued by their peers, if only as a matter of professional development. That's not the problem. The problem is the manner in which he reacted and what the manner in which he reacted reveals. In our submission, the manner in which he reacted reveals, beyond any doubt, at a minimum, a reasonable apprehension of bias in favour of convicting any leader or accused leader having knowledge of the crimes committed in the framework of a common goal. Those are his words and this is what the letter sends as a message. It is also our respectful submission that Mico Stanisic, as minister of the interior, accused of being a member of a joint criminal enterprise involving ethnic cleansing, which is mentioned in the letter, and having contributed to furthering this JCE - that's the finding - is specifically included in the category of persons likely to be convicted as a result of Judge Harhoff's predisposition, whether in appearance or in reality, regardless of the evidence put forward. Judge Harhoff admits in his letter, "In all the courts I have worked in here, I have always presumed that it was right ..." - I insist on the word "right" because in his memo he will use a different word, in his explaining memo - "to convict leaders for the crimes committed with their knowledge within the framework of a common goal." He's referring to joint criminal enterprise and he says it's right to convict them on the basis of their knowledge of crimes. And then he explains why, but that explanation only serves to explain that he's willing to convict on the basis of knowledge. Now, how does Judge Harhoff react? Well, we learned from the letter that first he sent the two articles, two media articles, that I will talk about later, and he sends these two articles to a group of 56 so-called friends. We don't know who these 56 people are and we do not have any content of the e-mail which covered or accompanied these two articles. But we learned from the letter that his apparent aim is to add what he calls a few personal comments to his earlier e-mail, which in and of itself does not appear to be a problem. He circulates two media articles and then he wants to give a few personal comments. Of course, it does appear odd that we say for a Judge to share with 56 friends the deep concern which he says is shared by his colleagues in Chambers. But I don't think that this raises the apprehension of bias. But then he refers to the set practice. He begins by describing what in his view was the existing situation at the Tribunal until autumn 2012. He describes the situation as a "... set practice at the court that military commanders were held responsible for war crimes that their subordinates committed during the war ...", set practice as mentioned by the Specially Convened Chamber, no reference to the evidence. This is definitely problematic. This is especially the case when you read this paragraph in conjunction with a later paragraph which reads as follows: "In all the courts I have worked in here, I have always presumed that it was right to convict leaders for the crimes committed within their knowledge within a framework of a common goal." Judge Harhoff's admission refers to JCE liability and it reveals to us a predisposition to convict leaders on the basis of their knowledge, regardless of the law applicable, which always requires that members of a JCE -- always required, sorry, that members of a JCE intended to further the common goal. He refers to a change in the practice. He highlights what he perceives to be a change in the practice. A change for the worse, according to him, was implemented by the Appeals Chamber in these two judgements: Gotovina case, three Croatian generals, trial judgement 15 April 2011, but the appeals 16 November 2012. He refers to the Perisic case and then he refers to Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic case. In the latter, of course, he uses a word that is not even used in the media article where he talks about Simatovic and his, I think -- the henchman of Jovica Stanisic. Judge Harhoff does not make any comments on the Prlic case issued immediately prior to the Jovica Stanisic case which ended up in the conviction of six Croatian generals or high-level officials. In the letter he makes clear his dissatisfaction with this perceived change. In our submission, Judges should refrain from publicly criticising judgements rendered by colleagues. Nonetheless, this has happened before and there has been no allegation of bias, as far as we know, that gave rise to allegations of apprehension of bias. The situation here is wholly different. Judge Harhoff's criticism is driven by a frustration that the set -- that as a result of these judgements, the set practice of holding commanders responsible for their crimes on the basis of knowledge is a thing of the past. Judge Harhoff specifically mentions in his letter the following: "The result is ... not only that the court has taken a significant step back from the lesson that commanding military leaders have to take responsibility for their subordinates ..." and then he says "... unless it can be proven that they knew nothing about it) - but also that the theory of responsibility" - that's where it hurts - "under the specific 'joint criminal enterprise' has now been reduced from contribution to crimes (in some way or another) to demanding a direct intention to commit crime (and so not just acceptance of the crimes being committed." And then he says, "Most of the cases will lead to commanding officers walking free from here on." I mean, the reasonable observer reading this sentence clearly understands what Judge Harhoff is referring to, and Judge Harhoff goes further by his subsequent comment: "How do we explain to the thousands of victims that the Court is no longer able to convict the participants in the joint criminal enterprise unless the Judges can justify that the participants in their common goal actively and with direct intent contributed to the crimes?" And then he refers to his -- again he goes on to say: "Until now we have convicted these participants who in one way or another showed that they agreed ..." and then of course he gives the example "to eradicate the non-Serbian population from areas the Serbians had deemed cleaned, as well as in one way or another achieved or contributed to achieving the goal." But then where it says: "Without having to prove that they had a direct intention to commit every single crime to achieve it ..." Not only is he frustrated, he says, how can we explain that we can't convict anymore? It's not true that we can't convict; it's not true that there was a set practice. But his understanding of the law and the way he applied it based on his predisposition, of course, is displayed in the letter. Taking into consideration that there has been no change in the law applicable to JCE mode of liability, that is more than troubling. More importantly, for a Judge who has admitted having always presumed that it was right to convict leaders for the crimes committed with their knowledge, of course within the framework of a common goal, this plainly reveals a predisposition to convict leaders on the basis of their knowledge, in contravention of the applicable law before the Tribunal. Such a predisposition, which in our view establishes a reasonable apprehension of bias, is compounded by his statement: "The latest judgements here have brought me a deep professional and moral dilemma, not previously faced. The worst of it is the suspicion that some of my colleagues have been behind a short-sighted political pressure that completely changes the premises of my work in my service to wisdom and the law." In our submission, Judge Harhoff makes it clear that he disagrees with the law applicable with the international tribunal, including in respect of the JCE mode of liability applicable to this case and that he is struggling with the manner in which he should react. Turning to the reasonable observer, what would he make of the manner in which Judge Harhoff reacted to the situation arising from this, the two judgements, of course, and the one trial judgement rendered during the period during 16 November 2012 until 30 May 2013? Well, first the reasonable observer would note that Mico Stanisic, in his capacity as minister of the interior, is definitely included in the category of leaders discussed specifically in Judge Harhoff's letter. Second, the reasonable observer would note that Mico Stanisic was charged pursuant to JCE. Third, the reasonable observer would note that the JCE alleged in the indictment includes crimes linked to the removal of the non-Serbian population which is referred in the letter. He would note, that is, the reasonable observer, that Mico Stanisic was convicted by a Bench of three Judges, that Mico Stanisic was convicted on the basis of the JCE mode of liability. He would know that the trial judgement against Mico Stanisic was rendered on 27 March, 71 days before Judge Harhoff's letter was made public on 13 June 2013. He would know that Judge Harhoff's letter to 56 friends, considering the context in which it was drafted and published, reveals a reasonable apprehension of bias in favour of convicting leaders on the basis of knowledge, and he would note that Judge Harhoff was labouring at the time on the professional and moral dilemma, that is, at the minimum during the period during which he was deliberating in this case. Judge Harhoff's letter reveals, in our respectful submission, a reasonable apprehension of bias, that is, that Judge Harhoff, while sitting as a Judge in the trial of Mico Stanisic at least, at the minimum, in appearance, did not decide fairly, to refer to my earlier quote. I did not address in these submissions the allegations made by Judge Harhoff against other Judges of the Tribunal, including the President, Judge Meron; including Judge Orie; the Judge from Zimbabwe; and also with Judge Guney, which in our submission strengthen Judge Harhoff's willingness to convict, in addition to hurting the legacy of the international Tribunal in an incommensurable way. Part 2, let's look at the rebuttal material. The case law makes it clear that the reasonable observer test rests on the premise that the reasonable observer is properly informed. He must be fully apprised of all relevant information that might impact his assessment, including of course the context. In relation to the context, I described the context. Today I will limit my submissions to the rebuttal material which was admitted at the request of the Prosecution, the memorandum from Judge Harhoff and the two media articles. The first article is in The Economist, published on the 1st of June. It talks mainly about two judgements, Prlic, first, and talks about JCE but very -- in passing; and then talks about Stanisic and Simatovic and focuses on the specific direction criteria for aiding and abetting. It also mentions briefly Perisic, also specific direction criteria for aiding and abetting. It mentions Haradinaj, who was acquitted on a re-trial. And it mentions Gotovina, who was acquitted on appeal. It appears, according to the article, that the population is shocked by the judgements previously mentioned. So what can we draw from this first article, that it looks at the Tribunal case law over the past two years and says: Wow, something is happening there. Okay. Second article, New York Times, published immediately on the 2nd of June. Of course we know that this article is written by Eric Corney, a professor of politics who also does sociology, and was cited in the first article. He talks about the acquittal of Stanisic and Simatovic and he calls it a dramatic reversal, and he talks about the same thing, that the population has questions about these acquittals. He mentions briefly joint criminal enterprise and the criteria of mens rea. He talks about aiding and abetting mostly and he talks about specific directive. These two articles, the Appeals Chamber has already said, would help in evaluating the context. Well, we described the context. There is criticism out there about decisions rendered by a lot of people. So the reasonable observer would look at these articles and he would say: Yeah, that might have prompted Judge Harhoff to react. But as mentioned earlier, it's not his reaction that is important; it's the manner in which he reacted. Judge Harhoff's memorandum is much more important. The timing of the memorandum is not so much important, because albeit he reacted when he was given an opportunity, pursuant to Rule 15(B), in the Seselj proceedings. That's when Judge Harhoff reacted officially, at least from what's on the record. So the timing, the fact that he waited, is important but is not so important. What is sure is that he had a lot of time to think about it before giving his opinion to Judge Antonetti, the Presiding Judge in the Seselj proceedings. That e-mail is sent to the same 56 people from the first mail with the two articles and it is leaked to the press. Now, Judge Harhoff makes a big issue of the fact that it wasn't intended to be public. We say that's beside the point. When a Judge writes to 56 persons in an e-mail in today's world, he definitely accepts the risk that his views will become public. And once they are public, that is beyond the point. What is important is the appearance displayed by this article in the public. He says: The fact that I did not say certainly does not imply that I have abandoned the requirement of the evidence. Well, it's nice to say after the fact, but what the people read is what was in the letter. He said: I did not abandon the requirement to assess all the facts. Very nice to say in defence, but that should have been in his letter if that's what he means. The change in the conditions for criminal responsibility, it's wholly significant because there has been no change. There has been no further requirements in Gotovina, unlike what he says in his memo. He explains in the part on the perceived bias - and that's the most part of his memo - he explains his remark that he has always found it just - I refer to the actual e-mail which said "right". First, he said if you convict under JCE on the basis of knowledge, clearly you have abandoned the normal mens rea requirement, contrary to what he says. On the part of a Judge with his legal background, not correct. A new practice would require more than just a degree, he says, of -- a higher degree of intent. Incorrect. Even in his memo, the way he approaches the law is incorrect. Again, he says in his memo: "It might make it very difficult to convict superior military commanders, may not only make it almost impossible to convict generals in the future," but yet there was no change. So even in his memo he does not correct his predisposition to convict. He adds a little later: "I've always rendered my judgements in confidence that superior commanders would come to realise at some point that the common plan to forcibly evict 'others' from 'own areas' contradicts a fundamental order in life ..." I'm sorry to say but this gives an impression that the man is on a mission, he's on a mission to convict. They will come to realise -- I'm going to convict them on the basis of knowledge and I'm sure they'll come to realise that what they did is wrong, once they sit in a jail. That's the impression. I'm not saying this is what Judge Harhoff believes, but that's certainly the impression we get. He says it's a moral and political statement and not a legal position. That does not match the context. The context must be read in the complete reading of his letter and his statement that he always saw it right to convict on the basis of knowledge. It's not possible that a reasonable observer would miss this. Lastly, the last comment is very important when it talks about the dilemma, and I'll just mention -- I draw your attention to that paragraph, but I want you to look at the difference in what he says in his memo and what he said in his e-mail. Clearly in the memo he is labouring under this dilemma. Suddenly in his memo, because he very well knows the appearance he gave in his letter, so he backtracks and he tries to explain, and then he said "the dilemma I would be under." So from being under a dilemma for some time, now he might or would be in a dilemma if he finds out that there is international or outside interference. His attempt just to change this paragraph in itself is revealing. The Seselj decision, part 3. The letter was published on the 13 June. Seselj reacted, the first one, on 1 June, although we never learn of it until the 9th of -- he reacted on 1 July, sorry, and it only became public on 9 July because of translation issues. Mico Stanisic immediately reacted or in the same time-frame on the 2nd of July. On the 20th of June, Delic also reacted. Zupljanin reacted soon after. The fact that four accused, either being tried or having been tried, reacted soon after publication of Judge Harhoff is a fact that the reasonable observer would not miss. The Specially Convened Chamber issued its decision, concluding by majority, that Judge Harhoff has demonstrated a bias in favour of conviction, and that would be a conclusion of a reasonable observer properly informed, and found that the presumption of impartiality, no matter how important it is, has been rebutted. On 9 September, on the basis of that decision, we immediately asked for more information to be added to our request to amend our notice of appeal, and we underscored in there, and I will simply refer to that filing of ours, because we say there, we underscored, the relevance of the decision. We also underscore in there that there is no right of appeal in such decisions. Why is this so? Very clear. Once the cat is out of the bag and there has been a finding on a predisposition to convict, an appearance of bias, an appearance of conviction, it would take a lot to reverse that finding and still be consistent in terms of decisions before this Tribunal. The majority rejected the Prosecution's application for reconsideration and then because of that decision, we thought this decision is now final, we must adjudicate as soon as possible. Because of the nature and appearance of the bias, that's the reason we acted this way. If the bias displayed by Judge Harhoff was limited to the Seselj case, if, for example, he had been involved, as in a previous case before the ICTR with an affair in the Prosecution of that case, then of course it would be limited to the case in the Seselj proceedings, even though it might still produce results, but now we're talking about of an appearance of bias in favour of conviction. The matter would not have such high probative value if it wasn't so general and so personally attached to the Judge. It impacts the overall impartiality of a Judge in favour of conviction. We've said many times, the independence and impartiality of Judges is the absolute legitimacy of any judicial system. So is there any difference between that decision and this case? Yes, there are. The first one is that this case, the judgement had already been rendered. But we explain in our submissions that it is evident that the appearance of bias displayed in the letter, it did impact on the proceedings and it did exist at the time he was adjudicating in this case. The second difference, the Specially Convened Chamber appears not to have considered Judge Harhoff's memo and did not consider the two media articles, which is the rebuttal material in this case. First, I know that that was not a legal mistake because that was what Rule 15(B) provided at the time, so it's not a mistake. But of course we have two different situations. You will consider Judge Harhoff's memo and you will consider those two media articles which the Specially Convened Chamber did not. But even when you consider this material, we respectfully submit that you will come to the conclusion, especially with the issue about the moral dilemma or the dilemma he was labouring under, that you will conclude that the rebuttal material provides a context but highlights and underscores the unacceptable character of the letter. In our submission this goes way beyond conduct unbecoming of a Judge, regardless of what that means in terms of what you do with the Judge. We're talking about an appearance of bias in favour of conviction which hurts at the heart -- strikes at the heart of the decision against Mico Stanisic. I close here saying that in our submission this must lead to invalidation of the findings entered or convictions entered against Mico Stanisic. That's my answer to the first question. Our answer to the first question is straightforward. Because of the right to be judged, to be tried before a Chamber composed of three impartial Judges, which was not the case, the conviction for Counts 1, 4, and 6 must be quashed. We have explained this in our submissions. What is more important, however, is what do we do next? We quash the conviction but what? Well, considering the seriousness of the violation which has nothing to do with Mico Stanisic, considering the importance of the right to be tried by an independent and impartial Tribunal, considering that Mico Stanisic has been in jeopardy for ten years, considering that Mico Stanisic, since he arrived, at least co-operated and at least wanted to provide information which is evidenced by accepting to be interviewed by the Prosecution, for us there's only one possibility: It's to order a stay of proceedings and to release him forthwith. Now, in our written submissions we have underscored the possibility for Mico Stanisic to be tried de novo. It's not for us to say whether he should be tried de novo, not for us to argue this way. For us, it's the violation, it's the invalidation and the stay of proceedings. If there should be a trial de novo, that's for the Prosecution to determine whether this is necessary and whether this is in the interests of justice, and we will react at that time. The second question posed by the Appeals Chamber, if the Appeals Chamber finds there's a violation but not sufficient enough to warrant invalidation of the conviction, this appears to us, Mr. President, to be a straightforward theoretical question. It would be - I can't really find the word - the reaction if we say there has been an unacceptable appearance of bias, it applies to this case, but it's not important enough for the conviction to be invalidated. But you've asked a question so we will respond. In our view, the only possible remedy in such a case is of course you maintain the conviction but you must reduce the sentence to time served and send him home. In such a case, the Tribunal maintains the conviction. I think that might be in the interests of justice, but at least the accused or the convicted person gets full credit for the violation, and it is well noted for the legacy of international criminal justice. Now, we considered of course another possibility. Maybe we say because of the violation the Appeals Chamber will simply look at the rest of the appeal without taking into consideration what the Judges did, will assess the evidence de novo. Well, under a normal appeal, certainly the Appeals Chamber can do that and it will look at all the evidence and it will make some determinations de novo. That has taken place before and that can happen. Not here. Why? Because a lot of the evidence that's on the record is the result of decisions rendered by these three Judges, which means that the Appeals Chamber would have not only to make a determination for itself on the basis of the evidence, it would have to go back all the way to the beginning and start over as if it was a Chamber of first instance. This was underscored and highlighted, how difficult an exercise it can be, by Judge Afande who, of course, talked about replacing Judge Harhoff in the Seselj proceedings. We say that the Appeals Chamber cannot do this because then they would be acting as a Trial Chamber of first instance and, as such, then Mr. Stanisic would be deprived of his right of appeal. It would be a conviction entered on appeal. Judge Pocar has underscored this issue many times, albeit in dissenting or separate opinions. This concludes my submissions on Judge Harhoff. If the Appeals Chamber does not have any questions, I'll move on to the second part that has to do with question 2 -- the first question posed by the Appeals Chamber related to the resubordination of members of the RS MUP. Regarding the first question which reads as follows: "In light of the Trial Chamber's findings in paragraphs 737 to 759 and in particular 757 whether the Trial Chamber found that Stanisic was responsible for failing to investigate crimes committed by the police resubordinated to the military." The straightforward answer to this question is yes. If we look at paragraph 757, the Trial Chamber found that Mico Stanisic failed to act in the same decisive manner with regards to the other crimes, such as unlawful detention and displacement and removal of Muslims, Croats, and other non-Serb civilians, and the ensuing crimes of killing and inhumane treatment. The crimes referred by the Trial Chamber in this paragraph are, first and foremost, the crimes committed during the take-over of municipalities, and that was referred to in paragraph 737 of the judgement. Second, in paragraph 737 where the crimes are described, the perpetrators are identified as being MUP and other Serb forces. This refers exactly to the situation or the joint action on the RS MUP and the other Serb forces. Now, although the entire section dealing with Mico Stanisic's contribution to the JCE in paragraphs 729 to 756 contains no footnotes, which makes verifying or challenging the Trial Chamber's purported findings virtually impossible. Nonetheless, in 737 it describes a situation during which RS MUP forces were resubordinated to the military. I draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to paragraphs 740, 743, 745, and 750, which makes it clear that this section applies to members of the police who were resubordinated to the military. In fact, 759 is even more clear. It attributes responsibility to Mico Stanisic for taking insufficient action to put an end to the crimes mentioned previously and permitted RS MUP forces to continue participating in joint operations in the municipalities with other Serb forces. So that's the answer to the Appeals Chamber's questions, but what then? That's much more important. This is paramount to the consequences of the findings, and I draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to paragraph 342, where the Trial Chamber confirmed that it was unable to find whether the military or the civilians which might have been responsible for the investigation and prosecution of crimes against Muslims and Croats which may have been committed by policemen resubordinated to the military. What is significant was the Trial Chamber's failure to pronounce on this responsibility to investigate and prosecute is the following: First, contrary to the Trial Chamber's assertion, this goes way beyond Article 7(3) of the Statute. Second, it's incorrect for the Trial Chamber to, on one hand, say, Well, I can't say who's responsible, A or B - B being Mico Stanisic - but then I will ascribe responsibility to Mico Stanisic for failing to prosecute and investigate. You can't do the two together. Thirdly, and more importantly, the Trial Chamber compounded its own error by using this finding in order to make Mico Stanisic a member of the joint criminal enterprise. Complete circular reasoning. This error must be addressed and must lead to invalidation of Counts 1, 4, and 6. I move to the next question posed by the Appeals Chamber. That's the second part of the first question dealing of course with mens rea, but in light of failure to provide a reasoned opinion, and of course to the third question, as of when did -- or if the Trial Chamber identified as of when Mico Stanisic formed the necessary mens rea for the joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber's findings with respect to mens rea of Mico Stanisic are found in 766 to 769, merely four or five paragraphs. As argued in our submissions - and I will not repeat our submissions - we believe the Trial Chamber erred in drawing the inference that Mico Stanisic shared a mens rea. Let me begin by talking about inference. I don't want to belabour the point. The Appeals Chamber is well aware of the applicable law. But there are a number of errors which strikes at the heart of the Trial Chamber's drawing of this inference, and it has to do with the law applicable to the drawing of inferences in the absence, of course, of direct evidence. It's clearly established, first, that in order to draw an inference, the finding must be made about consideration of the totality of the evidence on the record. Second, the inference drawn from the totality of the inference on the record must be the only reasonable and logical conclusion that can be drawn in the circumstances. I draw your attention to Prosecutor versus Vasiljevic and Prosecutor versus Oric, but this can be found in many other places in the case law. It is our respectful submission that this is not what the Trial Chamber did. It did not follow this law. Indeed, first, it rests -- the inference drawn by the Trial Chamber rests on an incomplete evaluation of the evidence available. In some cases the Trial Chamber did not even refer to relevant evidence. I just give you one example, Mr. President, a report sent to Karadzic on the 17th of July, 1992, Exhibit P427.8. Nowhere to be seen in the judgement. In our view, highly relevant. In other cases, the Chamber referred to certain exhibits, for example, some of the orders issued by Mico Stanisic, but it did not consider these orders in drawing the impugned reference. For example, an order issued on the 23rd of July. We can look at paragraph 640 of the judgement: "Stanisic ordered that legal measures be taken against all members of MUP who committed crimes since the establishment of the RS MUP." Paragraph 664: "Stanisic ordered all CSB and SJB chiefs to obtain info on the treatment of prisoners of war and the conditions of detainees." Paragraph 667: "An order of 10 August, Stanisic ordered to the chief of Sarajevo, Doboj, Trebinje, Bijeljina, Banja Luka CSBs, stressing that detention should be carried out exclusively within existing regulations." Paragraph 668, "Order of 17 August, Stanisic ordered to CSB chiefs, ordering them to abide by the laws of war and international conventions." These are but a few examples. The Trial Chamber mentions these orders but does not take them into account in the paragraphs dealing with mens rea. Had the Chamber considered the totality of the evidence on the record, in particular the numerous measures taken by Mico Stanisic that impeded the implementation of the JCE, it would, in our respectful submission, necessarily have concluded that its finding or its inference that Mico Stanisic shared the required mens rea was certainly not the only reasonable inference available on the evidence. Another possible and, in fact, much more obvious conclusion was that Mico Stanisic adhered to the political, legitimate, political goal of the Republika Srpska but did not share in any way the mens rea for the common criminal purpose and the crimes comprised therein. All of our arguments in this respect are in the appellant's brief, and today I will only review a few of the most important errors. In addition to not considering all of the evidence, the Chamber committed a number of errors of fact. I refer the Appeals Chamber to the appellant's brief. I will highlight only a few of these errors because they are relevant, but there's many more. Stanisic is a member of the SDS; wrong. The evidence in this regard can be found at appellant's brief, we give a full description at paragraph 131. Stanisic is a member of the BSA, the Bosnian Serb Assembly; wrong. The evidence can be found in the appellant's brief at paragraph 125 with all the necessary evidence. Stanisic approved of Arkan's actions; wrong. Stanisic did not approve of Arkan's actions. Reference in our brief at paragraphs 140 to 146. It is necessary in our view for the Appeals Chamber to look at the evidence of Bjelosevic, confidential; the evidence of Pejic; the evidence of Adnan; the evidence of Davidovic, in particular, to find that the Trial Chamber committed an error of fact in saying that Stanisic approved of Arkan's action. The motivation of Stanisic to arrest the Yellow Wasps was not related to the commission of crimes and Stanisic's real motivation is more linked to petty theft. Wrong. This is an error of fact. Stanisic really opposed the Yellow Wasps. Two were prosecuted and convicted for war crimes outside of Republika Srpska and the others were found guilty, albeit of lesser crimes. I refer the Appeals Chamber to the appellant's brief, paragraphs 413, 417. These four examples highlight errors of fact committed by the Trial Chamber. Had the Trial Chamber not made these numerous errors of fact, it could not have drawn the impugned inference. Now, after errors of fact, we need to address the standpoint of the Trial Chamber before it set out to address the evidence, its going-in views, its initial conclusions. There are at least three I wish to highlight this morning which tainted the appreciation of the evidence by the Trial Chamber. The first one has to do with the Bosnian Serb leadership. This issue is addressed in our brief under ground 2. The Chamber erroneously constructed an entity it identified as BSL and it defined this entity as the leading members of the SDS and those who occupied important posts in the RS. The Trial Chamber goes on to say: "They all share," that is the members of the BSL, so-called BSL, "they all shared and worked toward the same goal under the Bosnian Serb leadership." Now, by taking this view even before looking at the evidence, they arbitrarily created an entity of which Mico Stanisic was evidently and automatically a member of because he's a minister, and then they ascribe to members of this group an intent to work under the same intent under the leadership -- under the Bosnian Serb leadership. By doing so, they were inclined to find that Mico Stanisic possessed the required mens rea even before looking at the evidence. The second one, the conflation of the legitimate political goal of the RS, along with the common criminal purpose or the intent to further the common criminal purpose. Considering Mico Stanisic's position as minister, of course he worked within the government and he had to interact with members of the government. Some of them were members of the joint criminal enterprise. The problem here is that when assessing the evidence, the Trial Chamber evaluated his conduct within the framework of a legitimate political goal - he's a minister; he's working in the government - and they used this to draw conclusions that he shared the intent of the common criminal purpose. It is recognised, of course, actions committed by an accused may serve to infer the intent to contribute to a legitimate political goal, while at the same time establishing the intent of a common criminal purpose. But there is nonetheless a distinction to be made when you assess the evidence, and that's what the Trial Chamber failed to do when it assessed the evidence. Third and last in the going-in position, the issue of the minority. I'll make it short. According to the Trial Chamber, it appears that if you are a Serb, if you are in a high position, then you are BSL, then you worked towards the goal of the joint criminal enterprise. All of them. The Trial Chamber identified at some point that there was a majority within the BSL, which of course implies that there was also a minority, but they did not consider the possibility that Mico Stanisic was a member of this minority, which is what we submit the evidence reveals. But what's important is that they had these views before looking at the evidence. The next issue is the knowledge criteria. Well, we go back to Judge Harhoff but only in part. It is our submission that the Trial Chamber drew its inference that Mico Stanisic shared the intent to further the JCE, but they did so using an incorrect knowledge standard. It is well established that knowledge of an accused must not be conflated with the intent of an accused. Based on knowledge, if an accused has acted some way, of course you put the two together, you may arrive - may, not might, may - arrive at an inference, but not just knowledge. The accused must have acted some way. Now, this is of the highest importance here because the manner in which he did act is contrary to the mens rea of the JCE. That underscores the whole problem. When Mico Stanisic did obtain information about the crimes - and he did; it is in the judgement and we acknowledge that - but what did he do when he got the knowledge? Let's take one example which is a defining moment in the events: 11 July, the first collegium, the first collegium on 11 July 1992 is when Mico Stanisic gains information about large-scale crimes being committed. What does he do next? 17 July, he reports to Karadzic; 18 July, he writes to Prime Minister Djeric. The first one was 427.8; the second one is P00190. 19 July, he receives a report in relation to the matter, 1D0076. 19 July, he introduces a questionnaire to find out what's going on and he instructs all police forces to report on war crimes. 27 July, he issues the order banning the special police in the SJB and the CSB because they had created some kind of a police without the approval of the minister. 19 September, he issues rules on the disciplinary responsibility of the ministry. Now, these actions which follows his gaining knowledge shows that -- at least militates in favour that he did not share the mens rea. We don't know what consideration the Trial Chamber gave to these orders in respect of mens rea. That's also the problem. In this case the Trial Chamber made it clear that they started to look at Mico Stanisic's mens rea by looking at his knowledge of crimes committed. This is very important, as will be seen in our answer to the second question, because which crimes and when the crimes were committed is highly relevant to determine when he forms the necessary mens rea. But we don't know. He gains knowledge of crimes and we don't know what specific crimes at what specific time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that -- thank you, Mr. President. I move on to the next issue with respect to mens rea which we feel is very important, and this has to do with the actions taken to oppose the paramilitary units everywhere in Bosnia, not just in one area but everywhere. Mico Stanisic's opposition to the use of paramilitary forces cost him big time. He clashed with Biljana Plavsic and was considered as a traitor. He put his family in harm's way. This goes way beyond not being a popular man. A minister who takes such actions in these circumstances cannot be said to have the intent to further the JCE. Lastly, I look at all the orders on the record that the Trial Chamber might have referred to but did not consider in respect of mens rea. For all of these reasons, it is clear, in our submission, that the mens rea of -- the inference that he shared the mens rea is wrong because it is absolutely not the only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn on the face of the evidence. As to the timing, the question of the Appeals Chamber as of when, there is no finding. In a case against Zupljanin, there is a date upon which he would have formed the mens rea. For Stanisic, there is no such date. If we try to find such a date on the basis of the evidence, we cannot find one. It's not able to establish one, and that is critical. If you cannot identify the date upon which he formed the mens rea, then of course it has a direct bearing on his convictions for Counts 1, 4, and 6. This concludes my submissions on respect of mens rea. I will turn over to my colleague for the last question which is question 2 regarding contribution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm aware of the time. It wasn't the agreement that we had, but in any case I will try to do my best. Your Honours, I will now address the second component of the first question; namely, identifying the evidence and the Trial Chamber findings undermining the conclusions concerning Stanisic's contribution to the JCE. The Trial Chamber failed to enter an express finding that Stanisic contributed, let alone significantly contributed, to the JCE. As we don't have enough time, Your Honours, our oral arguments in support of Stanisic's sixth ground of appeal are in written brief. I will focus on only the few issues now. One is the errors of fact and these are highlighted again in our written submissions. On this occasion I would only cite four specific examples of the errors in the judgement. Error at paragraph 733, the Chamber erred in finding that from April 1st, 1992, Stanisic made the majority of key appointments in the RS MUP and had the sole authority to appoint, discipline, and dismiss chiefs of the CSB and SJB. Mico Stanisic did not have the sole authority as, first of all, all these persons had been appointed by BiH Minister Delimustafic and they would have still been appointed had Mr. Stanisic did anything or not. In addition, at the paragraph 695, the Trial Chamber accepted that the rules were amended in September 1992 by Mico Stanisic, and therefore the earliest, on the accepted evidence, the legal reasoning giving Mico Stanisic sole authority to appoint, discipline, and dismiss chiefs, came into force in September 1992. Your Honours, the reference is Witness Kovac at 27238 of transcript, also paragraphs 14 and 695 of the trial judgement, as well as 1D54. Second error at paragraph 739 is the finding that Karadzic sent a request to Mico Stanisic on 1st of July, and due to this mistake the Trial Chamber attached little weight to Stanisic's statement that the RS MUP was not consulted regarding assignments of RS MUP forces to army for combat tasks. However, the evidence confirming this error is also in the judgement in paragraph 591 which shows that Karadzic actually ordered Mr. Stanisic as a supreme commander and subsequently Stanisic requested for their return. The evidence is 1D99, 1D100, and Witness Borovcanin's testimony. Your Honours, I move now to the other issue that permeates this judgement. There is a problem with the identification of specific acts. Indeed, the Trial Chamber fails to identify any specific act attributed to Stanisic through which he contributed to furthering of the JCE. Indeed, instead of identifying specific acts, the Chamber addressed his roles in his capacity as minister of interior. The reason why this is so is that specific acts taken at face value consistently went against the furtherance of the JCE. I also refer to my colleague's earlier submission that the Trial Chamber failed to identify when Stanisic possessed the required intent for the first category of JCE. Indeed, the other roles that Stanisic studied -- which were studied by the Chamber, they have one main characteristic in common: Indeed, they deal with the action which, in and of themselves, consistently went against furthering of JCE. Nonetheless, the Chamber found that Stanisic did not do enough of these acts and that, as a result, he contributed to furthering the JCE. The Trial Chamber characterised this as an omission of -- apparently this is not omission or liability per se. Had the Chamber properly considered that omissions in this context must amount to culpable omissions and that such omissions must exert concretely influence on the perpetration of the crime, it could not have reached the finding that Stanisic contributed to purported JCE. Considering that the Chamber's finding that Stanisic contributed to JCE by, on one hand, issuing a number of orders impeding the implementation of the JCE, while at the same time not doing enough, it is a failure by the Trial Chamber to identify at which point the cumulative effect of the orders impeding the JCE becomes a significant contribution to the same JCE. This is what makes this case unique and that is why the Trial Chamber's finding is wrong in law and in fact. Even if the Appeals Chamber was to try and identify at which point the cumulative effect of Stanisic's orders reaches the threshold for contributing to the JCE, the evidence simply does not exist for such a finding. I now briefly move to the third question by the Appeals Chamber. In light of our earlier submissions, there is no doubt that the contribution has to be followed or combined with the necessary mens rea for the JCE. In other words, the first step is forming the mens rea; the second step is contributing to the JCE. Therefore, consequently, acts committed before the existence of the JCE and before formation of the necessary mens rea must be disregarded. Consequently, in this case, considering that the Chamber failed to identify as of when Mico Stanisic formed the necessary mens rea, the Appeals Chamber cannot identify as of when he began to contribute to the JCE. Necessarily, what follows is that the convictions entered pursuant to Counts 1, 4, and 6 must be quashed. Your Honours, in concluding remarks, I still have some couple of minutes because there was some technical issues at the beginning, I'm sure Your Honours remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The tape ends in four minutes' time anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. First, we ask the Appeals Chamber to consider our submission in respect of the appearance of bias in favour of conviction of accused leaders on the basis of their knowledge of the crimes in the framework of JCE, even though the applicable mens rea has not been proven. If the Appeals Chamber concludes that the presumption of impartiality which attaches to Judge Harhoff is rebutted, this is the end of the matter and the Appeals Chamber needs not to consider the other arguments. Should the Appeals Chamber find that no appearance of bias on the part of Judge Harhoff has been established in this case, only then should the Appeals Chamber consider the other grounds of appeal. As you can see with our submission today, our focus has been on the alleged error committed by the Chamber in drawing the inference that Mico Stanisic shared the mens rea for the JCE as well as in light of the question posed by the Appeals Chamber, the alleged errors committed by Trial Chamber in finding that Mico Stanisic contributed to furthering the JCE. Although we have not addressed many of our grounds of appeal during our submissions today due to limitations of time, we do maintain our argument and we respectfully refer the Appeals Chamber to our written submission in relation to these grounds. In particular, I wish to draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to our grounds addressing the sentencing error omitted by the Trial Chamber. These grounds can be divided in two categories. Firstly, technical errors, but nonetheless reversible errors which warrant a reduction in sentence; secondly, and more importantly, the manifestly unreasonable quantum of sentence imposed by Mico Stanisic. Indeed, should the Appeals Chamber deny all of our grounds of appeal dealing with the convictions, one conclusion must remain: If the Appeals Chamber affirms the Trial Chamber findings that Mico Stanisic was a member of the JCE, it is our respectful submission that it could not ignore that his contribution to furthering the JCE, in light of the totality of evidence on the record, is nowhere close to the Trial Chamber's assessment of the same and that, as a result, the sentence imposed of 22 years of imprisonment should be reduced drastically. Your Honours, this concludes our submission in support of Mico Stanisic's appeal, and unless the Appeals Chamber has additional questions, I will turn over the floor to the Prosecution for its response. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no questions from the Bench. So we are going to change a little bit the schedule. We are going to have the break now, but we reconvene at 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecution, you've got 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Todd Schneider for the Prosecution. Your Honours, today I will be addressing your questions specific to Mico Stanisic and responding to the Defence arguments they've raised. My colleague Ms. Baig will then ask your question on the Judge Harhoff e-mail issue. For the remainder of the Defence submissions today and in their appeal, we would rely on our response brief. Your Honours, as minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic deployed his police to break the law rather than to uphold it, to target non-Serbs rather than to protect them, all in furtherance of the common criminal purpose, to permanently remove non-Serbs from the RS and achieve a Serb state as ethnically pure as possible. He was not merely fulfilling his duties as a minister, as the Defence has argued today, in order to achieve a legitimate political goal. Stanisic played a central role in the ethnic cleansing campaign together with his fellow JCE members, Radovan Karadzic, Stojan Zupljanin, and others. The Trial Chamber rightly concluded that he was a member of the JCE. I'm going to focus my submissions today around your questions. I'll deviate slightly from the order and focus first on the second part of question 1 concerning the Trial Chamber's findings on his JCE intent and contribution. I will spend most of my time answering that. I will then answer your questions 2 and 3 on timing issues and then finally address the first part of question A concerning resubordination. Starting with the second part of question 1, identify the evidence and findings supporting the Trial Chamber's conclusions in Volume 2, paragraphs 729 to 769, concerning Stanisic's contribution to and shared intent to further the JCE. The Trial Chamber's conclusions were based on a wide range of evidence and -- findings and evidence detailing Stanisic's key role in the JCE. These showed, first, Stanisic's extensive and important contributions, most notably using his police to force out non-Serbs; and second, his shared intent. So let me turn first to the Trial Chamber's findings on his significant contribution. As the Trial Chamber found, Stanisic contributed to the JCE by using the police forces under his command in furtherance of the common criminal purpose. He did so across 20 municipalities over a nine-month period. I'm going to cover today four examples of his contributions that the Trial Chamber relied on. First, he played a central role in creating Bosnian Serb institutions and policies. Second, he used his police in the take-overs and ensuing campaign of violence. This included, third, ensuring that they played a major role in the mass illegal detentions. And fourth, he ensured that his police turned a blind eye to the crimes against non-Serbs. Contrary to Defence arguments today, his contribution was not based solely or only on his role as a minister. Starting with his first contribution, Stanisic played a central role in the creation of Bosnian Serb institutions and policies. The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on this as forming part of his significant contribution because, through his actions, high-level policies were set and the police were created to implement the JCE; Volume 2, paragraphs 734 and 769. Stanisic was a key member of the Bosnian Serb decision-making authorities; Volume 2, paragraph 732. The Bosnian Serb leadership repeatedly turned to him when forming its most critical Bosnian Serb institutions. He was a founding member of the SDS. He was on the RS Council of Ministers from its beginning, the same with the National Security Council, and most importantly for this case, he was the minister of interior and head of the police force; Volume 2, paragraphs 144, 542, and 549. In each position he worked, together with other JCE members, to create policies and structures to implement the common criminal purpose. Stanisic took part in the first Council of Ministers meeting on 11 January 1992, when the council set as a priority the "defining of ethnic territory." Volume 2, paragraph 551. As the Trial Chamber found, defining ethnic territory involved the "forceful assumption of control over territories." Volume 2, paragraph 310. Then on 11 February 1992 Stanisic was at the Serb collegium meeting, whose very purpose was the creation of the RS police; Volume 2, paragraph 732. In attendance was Zupljanin and others key to implementing the JCE. At this meeting Stanisic explained to everyone the position of the RS Council of Ministers in Bosnian territories "which are under Serbian control. That control must be felt." Volume 2, paragraph 555. And, in fact, Stanisic's police played a key role in ensuring Serb control was felt, but to do so he needed the right people for the job. He appointed to key positions a number of persons the Trial Chamber found to be JCE members, including Zupljanin, starting on 1 April 1992; Volume 2, paragraph 579 and 744 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Apologies to the interpreters. "Thieves and criminals," as Stanisic described them, were accepted into the reserve police in its early days; Volume 2, paragraph 600. And he purged the police force of Muslims and Croats; Volume 2, paragraphs 576 to 577 and 738. With the right people in place, Stanisic was ready to -- THE APPELLANT ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] There is a problem. We are not receiving interpretation. I repeat: We are not receiving interpretation into the Serbian language. Now I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's proceed, and if you get the problem again, Mr. Zupljanin, please draw our attention straight away. Same applies to you, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Continuing. With the right people in place, Stanisic was ready to use his police to implement the JCE, and that's exactly what he did, which brings me to his next contribution. Stanisic used his police in take-overs and in the ensuing persecutory campaign of violence against non-Serbs.
