The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on this as part of his significant contribution because the take-overs and violent aftermath resulted in the mass exodus of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraph 737. Stanisic and his police were involved from the beginning, indeed they were critical to the success of the take-overs. The police had a central vole in the Variant A and B instructions, the main purpose of which was to prepare local Bosnian Serbs to take power in municipalities. The police were also, prior to establishment of the VRS, the only armed force directly and exclusively controlled by the RS leadership, and 14 of the municipalities in this case were taken over before the VRS was formed. And for the finding I've just noted, this is at paragraphs 57, 310, 731 and 741 of Volume 2. As Stanisic wrote in a letter on 18 April 1992, just three weeks into the take-overs, the police were already controlling nearly 70 per cent of the territory of BiH; Exhibit P54, page 2. And they were doing so at the behest of Stanisic, the highest commander of the RS police forces. Stanisic continually used his powers as head of the police to devote police resources to an armed joint operation with the VRS during the take-overs and their aftermath. For example, his May 15th, 1992, order. This order declared that police would be organised into war time units and said police would participate in co-ordinated action with the armed forces. This order reflected his command and control because it specified that Stanisic or a senior official had to authorise police involvement in combat and it required that the ministry be informed of deployments; Volume 2, paragraphs 758 and 739. Stanisic followed up on this order during the rest of 1992 by consistently approving police deployments; Volume 2, paragraphs 594, 743, and examples in our response brief at paragraph 128. Stanisic did not limit the use of his police to the initial take-overs alone. Even after Serb forces had taken over municipalities, his police continued to take part in the campaign of violence designed to force non-Serbs out. Let me give you one example. The special police platoon of Dusko Malovic personally commanded by Stanisic. In December 1992, this unit killed 21 Muslims in Bijeljina as part of a plan to spread terror among the Muslim population. Nevertheless, as the Trial Chamber found, higher-ups in the police tried to cover the crimes up; Volume 2, paragraphs 601 to 603, and Volume 1, 894 to 895. So let me now turn to his next contribution: Stanisic using his police to arrest, detain, and ultimately expel non-Serbs. To be clear, this is actually an important subpart of his prior contribution, using his police in the take-overs and violent aftermath but is easier to discuss it separately. The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on Stanisic using his police in the illegal detentions because these detentions formed part of the violent means that provoked the mass exodus of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraphs 737 and 761. Stanisic's police were crucial in the widespread arrest, detentions, and abuses. Substantial police resources were directed to the arrest, detention, and interrogation of thousands of non-Serbs. Detainees were held in at least 50 detention sites across the RS. In some cases the police detained prisoners in their own SJBs or in facilities attached to police stations. In other instances the police established, managed, or guarded camps or operated them jointly with the military; Volume 2, paragraphs 745, 760 and 761, and we'd also refer you to our appeal brief at paragraph 10. Stanisic directly contributed to this criminal system of detention. He could have closed down detention centres or withdrawn his police from them; Volume 2, paragraph 761. But he chose not to do so. Instead, he waited until the international outcry was so great that he had to do something, and at that point he issued toothless orders that were never followed up. The consequences for non-Serbs were horrific. The police, together with other forces, illegally detained and brutally mistreated thousands of non-Serbs. They held them in inhumane conditions, typically in places never designed to hold prisoners. Detainees were viciously beaten, often to the point of death, or else simply executed, and prisoners were raped and sexually assaulted. See the findings collected in our appeal brief at paragraphs 10 to 24. Let me turn now to the last contribution I'll discuss: Stanisic's discriminatory police that created a climate of impunity within the police and a climate of insecurity within the non-Serb population. The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on this as part of his significant contribution because this climate of impunity and insecurity left non-Serbs no choice but to flee; Volume 2, paragraphs 745, 757, and 758. What do I mean by "discriminatory policing"? It's how Stanisic prioritised the investigation of crimes against Serbs while he turned a blind eye to crimes against non-Serbs, whether committed by members of his own police or by other perpetrators. Recall the Trial Chamber's broader findings. Throughout the RS, police and prosecutors operated in a discriminatory manner by not reporting or underreporting serious crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraphs 104 and 745. This is reflected in RS police crime registers from 1992, civilian and military log-books from the same time, both of which contain barely any records on these types of crimes; Volume 2, paragraphs 34 to 35, 96 to 98, and 101. Stanisic played a leading role in this discriminatory policing that created insecurity among the non-Serb population. He repeatedly issued orders to investigate crimes against Serbs only; Volume 2, paragraphs 723, 727, and 758. And we highlight just one example, a May 16th, 1992, order. This is Exhibit P173, discussed at Volume 2, paragraph 723. In this order Stanisic wrote: "Measures and activities conducted to document war crimes, these activities require the collection of information and documents on war crimes against Serbs," - against Serbs - because that is what Stanisic really cared about. By contrast, Stanisic failed to act decisively when the victims were non-Serb; Volume 2, paragraph 757. As the Defence have noted today, he went after the notorious paramilitary unit, the Yellow Wasps; however, contrary to the Defence arguments, he did so because they refused to submit to the army command, because of auto theft and because they assaulted an RS official. He did not go after them for their commission of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Would the counsel kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Apologies again to the interpreter. And the citations for the findings I've just discussed, Volume 2, paragraphs 713 through 715 and 756. Stanisic was tasked to gather information on Muslims and others leaving the RS; Volume 2, paragraphs 627 and 650. Despite this, he failed to take decisive measures in relation to the mass expulsions and he failed to take decisive measures against the detention crimes as well; Volume 2, paragraph 757. Furthermore, Stanisic promoted a climate of impunity within the police, at least when it concerned crimes against non-Serbs. Yes, he disciplined and dismissed members of his police, but this was for theft and professional misconduct, or in the case of Obren Petrovic for protection of Muslims. He didn't discipline or dismiss them for crimes that furthered the JCE; Volume 2, paragraphs 698 to 708 and 754. Through this discriminatory policing, he promoted a climate of impunity and insecurity. Contrary to the Defence arguments, it was not merely about Stanisic failing to do enough. To sum up this section, given how Stanisic created Bosnian Serb institutions and policies, given how he used his police in the take-overs and their violent aftermath, in particular, the widespread illegal detentions, and given how he promoted a climate of impunity and insecurity, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that Stanisic made a significant contribution to the JCE. So let me now, in the context of your question 1, the second part, turn to his shared intent for the JCE. The Trial Chamber's conclusion that Stanisic shared the intent for the JCE was supported by a wide range of findings. I'm going to discuss four points: Stanisic's adherence to SDS policies; his close relationship to Karadzic, the president of the SDS; Stanisic's deal with the violent criminal Arkan; and his continued contributions to the JCE despite his awareness of crime. Contrary to the Defence arguments today, he was not found to be an automatic member of the JCE based merely on his position as minister. The Trial Chamber's findings did not rest on his knowledge alone. I turn to the first point, the first set of findings, Stanisic's continued commitment to SDS policies. The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on this as helping to show his shared intent; Volume 2, paragraphs 767 and 769. As the Trial Chamber found, the SDS party structure shared and worked toward the goal of establishing a Serb state as ethnically pure as possible through the permanent removal of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraph 311. Stanisic's own words showed that he shared that goal and the intent for the JCE. As Stanisic admitted in a November 1992 speech, he had always followed the policies of the SDS Presidency and deputies in the former state. "Those who want to separate me from that are making a mistake." Volume 2, paragraph 570 and also 734. By the time of Stanisic's November speech, what SDS policies meant in practice was obvious to all given what had already happened by then. Over 100.000 non-Serbs forced out, thousands more killed or abused. Contrary to what the Defence have claimed today, this is not about achieving a legitimate political goal. My next point, Stanisic's close relationship with Karadzic which the Trial Chamber reasonably relied on to help show his shared intent; Volume 2, paragraph 769. Karadzic was the president of the SDS and the main decision-maker in the Bosnian Serb leadership. He became president of the Presidency; Volume 2, paragraphs 132, 136, and 137. Through his leadership position, Karadzic was the key figure in developing the persecutory policies of the Bosnian Serb leadership. For instance, Karadzic publicly threatened the Muslim people with possible extinction if BiH declared independence. In March 1992, just after the conflict, Karadzic announced a war would include the forcible and bloody transfer of minorities and the creation of ethnically homogenous regions within BiH; Volume 2, paragraphs 161 and 179. Stanisic was close to Karadzic from early 1991. They were so close that he was called Radovan's man. Stanisic also served together with Karadzic on high-level RS institutions, such as the National Security Council; Volume 2, paragraph 144. And as minister of interior, Stanisic often bypassed proper channels to communicate directly with Karadzic and the Presidency; Volume 2, paragraphs 565 to 570 and 730. Stanisic never wavered in his loyalty to Karadzic and his policies even in the wake of the massive and systemic criminality committed under Karadzic's overall leadership. This is a strong indicator of Stanisic's shared intent. My third point, Stanisic's deal with Arkan which the Trial Chamber reasonably relied on for his shared intent; Volume 2, paragraph 768. Stanisic approved of Arkan and his men, notoriously violent criminals, assisting in the take-overs in exchange for which Stanisic agreed Arkan's men could take any property they wanted; Volume 2, paragraph 710. During the take-overs Arkan's men committed horrific crimes. The Defence challenges on the underlying evidence addressed in our response brief at paragraph 51 to 53. Given the Chamber correctly found Stanisic made this deal, it also further correctly found it was another strong indicator of his shared intent. The last point I'll discuss, how Stanisic persistently contributed to the JCE over a significant period of time, despite his awareness of the widespread crimes committed against non-Serbs. The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on this for his shared intent; Volume 2, paragraphs 743, 768, and 769. I've already discussed his important and extensive contributions. I'm going to focus here on his knowledge of crimes. As the Trial Chamber reasonably found, Stanisic was informed of crimes against non-Serbs through multiple channels, including various sources within the police and RS government as well as from the international media and international organisations; Volume 2, paragraphs 757 and 759. Before discussing the specific reports the Chamber relied on, I'll first touch on Stanisic's various channels of information. As the Trial Chamber found, the police structure prepared daily, weekly, and quarterly reports to inform Stanisic of what was happening in the RS; Volume 2, paragraph 690. The police security service, the SNB, kept police officials informed of developments in the municipalities; Volume 2, paragraphs 26 and 689. Stanisic attended joint meetings of the national Security Council and RS government who met daily throughout April and early May 1992. At these meetings, decisions were made on military and security activities and reports of combat and the political situation were presented; Volume 2, paragraphs 144 and 573. Stanisic was also a member of the RS government and attended most of its sessions; Volume 2, 572. In light of these many channels of communication, let me now turn to the Trial Chamber's findings on the specific reports of crimes to Stanisic. For instance, in April 1992, Stanisic was informed of the looting of Muslim property by reserve police; Volume 2, paragraph 603. In early May he was aware of "unprincipled conduct" by his reserve police; Volume 2, paragraph 613. By early June, at the latest, he was aware of the unlawful detentions of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraph 762. This finding is based on, among others, on 10 June 1992 Stanisic was at an RS government meeting where they discussed issues relating to the treatment of detainees triggered by complaints about mistreatment of the civilian population; Volume 2, paragraphs 623 and 763. By this time, the mass arrest of thousands of Muslims and Croats had begun and the existence of the camps was known internationally; Volume 2, paragraph 763. Then on 11 July 1992, Zupljanin reported to Stanisic that the army and Crisis Staffs had requested that as many Muslims as possible be gathered, and Zupljanin also reported that the Muslims were being detained by police in undefined camps in bad conditions where international norms were not observed; Volume 2, paragraph 631 and 633. Two weeks after Zupljanin reported to Stanisic that police were holding in such camps several thousand Muslims and Croats, including minors, elderly, and disabled persons. Zupljanin proposed then lawfully detained non-Serbs be used as hostages; Volume 2, paragraphs 623, 631, 633 and 638. As the Trial Chamber found, the violent crimes against non-Serbs, including the unlawful detentions and mistreatment, led to the forcible displacement of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraph 737. In fact, the displacement of non-Serbs was so widespread that on 4 July 1992 at an RS government session that Stanisic attended, the question was raised if there were "agreed criteria regarding the moving out of the Muslim population" from the RS. Stanisic's Ministry of Interior was entrusted to collect the information on this issue; Volume 2, paragraph 627, and Exhibit P236, pages 4 to 5. One week after this Stanisic learned of the relocations of certain "citizens' villages" and attempts to assign this task to the police. Soon after he received a report from Visegrad that over 2.000 Muslims moved out in an organised manner while the police exhibited a lack of professionalism; Volume 2, paragraphs 627, 632 and 634. Despite Stanisic's knowledge the crimes which kept building over time, he chose to continue contributing to the JCE. Contrary to Defence arguments today, it is Stanisic's actions after this knowledge that further confirms his shared intent for the JCE. So for all the reasons I've just mentioned, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that Stanisic shared the intent for the JCE, and to sum up our answer, a wide range of findings and evidence supported the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Stanisic was member of the JCE. That completes our answer to the second part of question 1. Your Honours, before I move on to our remaining questions, let me just address an argument raised by the Defence regarding both his shared intent and his contribution. The Defence today have argued that Stanisic tried to halt crimes against non-Serbs through his orders. They have cited a string of orders that he issued. Contrary to their argument, the Trial Chamber considered these orders and reasonably found they did not undermine its conclusion about his shared intent and significant contribution, and to understand why you need to look at the orders themselves. Many of the orders cited today and in the Defence's appeal brief relate to other types of crimes, thefts, police misconduct, not serious crimes against non-Serb victims. Other orders show that Stanisic transferred criminals from his reserve police to the army, but as the Trial Chamber reasonably found, this was not an appropriate response because it meant that known criminals would continue to interact with civilians; Volume 2, 751. As for the orders on detention crimes which the Defence have highlighted today, the Defence ignore the relevant context. Stanisic issued these orders because of international pressure and he didn't follow up his strong words in these orders with strong actions even though he knew detention crimes continued despite the orders; Volume 2, paragraphs 752 to 753. What do I mean by "strong actions"? Like the steps he took when Serbs were the victims, for example, taking on the paramilitary group the Yellow Wasps for thefts and harassing Serbs, where the police launched a major operation to arrest them after Stanisic instructed them to do whatever was necessary; Volume 2, paragraphs 714 and 756. Another example of Stanisic's strong actions when Volkswagen Golfs were being stolen from a factory, Stanisic organised a unit to secure cars at this factory; Volume 2, paragraph 708. No such measures were ever taken for the crimes against non-Serbs, including the illegal and abusive detentions. So let me now turn to questions 2 and 3 where Your Honours have asked when the Trial Chamber found Stanisic had knowledge of the crimes, when he had the required intent for JCE I, and when he began to contribute to the JCE. I'm going to address these questions in reverse order dealing with the timing of his contributions first, then his intent, and finally his knowledge of crimes. Starting with the contribution. In setting out Stanisic's JCE contributions, the first contribution the Chamber found was his participation in the 11 February 1992 meeting with Zupljanin and others when he made preparations to establish the RS police force; Volume 2, paragraphs 732 and 544 to 555. Next, intent. As to when the Chamber found Stanisic shared the intent for the JCE, the Chamber's findings show that Stanisic shared the intent from the JCE's beginning. As the Trial Chamber found, the JCE existed from no later than 24 October 1991; Volume 2, paragraph 313. Then when it turned to assessing Stanisic's mens rea, the Chamber found that he shared the intent for the JCE with the other JCE members; Volume 2, paragraph 769. The factors I've discussed previously demonstrate Stanisic's intent from the time the JCE was formed. In particular when assessing Stanisic's intent, the Chamber relied on Stanisic's commitment to SDS policies and his close connections with the key SDS policy-maker, Karadzic; Volume 2, paragraphs 565, 570, 767, and 769. Long before the outbreak of the conflict, it was clear that these policies involved the permanent forcible removal of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraphs 311, 313, and 767. In any event, at the very least, the Chamber clearly found that Stanisic shared the intent for the JCE by 1 April 1992, when the JCE crimes began because the Chamber found Stanisic responsible for committing crimes beginning in April 1992 through his participation in the JCE, and I'd refer Your Honours to the findings in Volume 2, between 801 and 885. Last within these questions, turning to the question of when the Chamber found Stanisic had knowledge of the crimes, I've already discussed the Chamber's findings about his knowledge of crimes and the many channels of information at his disposal. To answer your specific question, Stanisic was informed from April 1992 of crimes that formed part of the violent means forcing non-Serbs out, such as lootings and beatings; Volume 2, paragraphs 603, 610 to 612. By early June at the latest, he was aware of the unlawful detentions of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraph 762. He had specific reports of the displacement of non-Serbs from at least July 1992; Volume 2, paragraphs 627, 632, and 634. These reports to Stanisic only confirmed what he intended to occur once he had joined the JCE. And that completes my the answers to questions 2 and 3. Turning to the last question I will address, the first part of question 1: Discuss whether the Trial Chamber found Stanisic responsible for failing to investigate crimes committed by police resubordinated to the military. The Trial Chamber properly analysed this issue. When discussing the Chamber's analysis, I need to distinguish between its analysis of Stanisic's failure to fulfil two distinct duties: First, his duty as a superior to prevent or punish the crimes of his subordinates; second, his duty as a police official to protect the civilian population; Volume 2, paragraph 754. In relation to the first duty, the answer to your question is no. When the Chamber considered Stanisic's failure to prevent and punish the crimes of his subordinates, the Chamber properly confined its analysis to those subordinates who were under his direct authority. This included, for example, the chiefs of CSBs and SJBs who were directly subordinated to him, such as Simo Drljaca in Prijedor who had established the Omarska camp; Volume 2, paragraphs 754 to 755. It did not consider Stanisic's failure to investigate crimes committed by police resubordinated to the military. Let me turn now to Stanisic's other duty, his duty as a police official to protect the civilian population. In relation to this duty, the answer to your question is that this was an irrelevant factor to the Trial Chamber's analysis. This is because Stanisic's duty to protect civilians was broader in scope than his duty to prevent or punish his subordinates, because unlike his superior duty, Stanisic's duty as a police official to protect civilians would require, amongst other actions, that Stanisic take steps to investigate all crimes committed against the civilian population, regardless of the affiliation of the perpetrator. Given this, whether or not the perpetrators of crimes were resubordinated is irrelevant to the Trial Chamber's proper conclusion that Stanisic failed to protect the civilian population in its findings at paragraph 751 and 754 of Volume 2. That completes our answer to the first part of question 1 and I'm going to turn the floor over to my colleague Ms. Baig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you hand over, I have one question for you, Mr. Schneider. I didn't hear anything about your position with respect to the alleged membership of Mr. Stanisic as minister of the MUP in the BSA, the Bosnian Serb Assembly, but I took it from the written submissions that you have the same position as the Defence relating to paragraph 125 of the appeals brief of the Defence. Have you any idea about a legal background, what is the legal basis for this assertion that it was not possible for a minister to be at the same time a minister of the Assembly? The same question I would like to be answered during the response by the Defence. Do you have any?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Thank you for the question. We would confirm, again rely on our answer in the response brief, that he was not a member of the BSA. As far as the particular question on the legal basis, we don't have a particular submission on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you permit me, I'm going to jump right in. A reasonable -- I'm addressing the Harhoff issue, the Harhoff e-mail issue. A reasonable observer properly informed, with knowledge of all of the relevant circumstances, would view the Stanisic and Zupljanin trial as being fairly decided by an impartial Bench, with full respect for the rights of the accused. That's because in this case the circumstances of this case do not give rise to an apprehension of bias on the part of Judge Harhoff, neither the e-mail in which he expresses a legal disagreement with jurisprudential developments, nor the subsequent majority decision in the Seselj Special Trial Chamber displaces the strong presumption of impartiality. I'll first address Judge Harhoff's e-mail in which he expresses a disagreement on the law, including the context in which this e-mail must be assessed; and then I'll turn to explain how and why the approach taken in the Seselj case is wrong, unpersuasive, and should not be followed. And finally, I will address or answer Your Honours' questions concerning possible remedies. The e-mail does not give rise to an appearance of bias in this case. A reasonable observer would have to consider the e-mail in light of its informal nature, its context, and in light of the judgement itself. The e-mail was an informal communication. In it, Judge Harhoff uses casual, non-legal language, as would be expected when communicating informally to a group of friends. It is unreasonable to expect the same level of precision in informal remarks. When discussing a technical legal topic, like modes of responsibility, with a non-legal audience, the failure to use precise and technical legal language, as would be expected in a formal legal submission, is simply unsurprising and you can see this in the e-mail in the conflation of elements of different modes, command responsibility, aiding and abetting, JCE 1 and JCE 3, that my learned colleague highlighted this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have ten minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. But the informal language does not create a suggestion that Judge Harhoff is unwilling to apply the correct law and it does not create an appearance of bias. The context of the e-mail is also critically important. In the e-mail, Judge Harhoff comments on the two recent press reports that he had circulated to the same e-mail group and he reacts to these news articles and expresses a disagreement with a perceived trend in the case law culminating in the Stanisic and Simatovic trial judgement that he perceives as elevating the legal requirements for convicting high-level military leaders. This is a disagreement about the law and a trend in the case law. He does not mention the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, nor does he comment on any of the cases in which he has served as a Judge. It is unreasonable to expect that Judges do not have personal feelings about the law and legal developments or that they always agree with every case. What the reasonable observer can expect is that professional judges can put aside their personal views when it comes to deciding the case before them. That's why, Your Honours, it is also critically important for the reasonable observer to look at the e-mail in light of the judgement in this case. The judgement in this case confirms the correct interpretation of the e-mail, one that does not raise an appearance of bias. It's in the judgement where Judge Harhoff records his professional view about the facts and law applicable to this case, where he sets out his professional views on fairness, factual findings, law, reasonable doubt, and guilt. In the unanimous trial judgement, Judge Harhoff and his two fellow Judges agreed to enter both convictions and acquittals. Both the unanimity and the fact that he concurred in acquittals confirms the correct interpretation of the e-mail. If he was biased in favour of conviction, one would not expect to see him entering such acquittals. And so too does the Chamber's reasoning. This is not a judgement based on predisposition; it's based on the evidence. Further evidence, Your Honours, against any apprehension of bias can be drawn from the trial record as we've set out in our brief. A reasonable observer, considering the e-mail in light of its nature, context, and the judgement, a reasonable observer who's properly informed, would conclude that this trial was a fair one. That conclusion would not be affected by the Seselj majority decision. That decision is not a legal precedent in any sense of that word. Its erroneous outcome impacts only the Seselj case. It's a trial decision not subject to an appeal, nor is it persuasive authority. The majority provides only the barest of reasoning, a couple of paragraphs. This is certainly not a situation where two wrongs would make a right. Let me take you to two key flaws in the Seselj majority decision. First, it's legally flawed because it presumed bias rather than relying on the long-standing presumption of impartiality. It concludes that the reference to set practice implies that Judge Harhoff would convict an accused without regard to the evidence before him, but his omission to make reference to such an obvious point in an informal e-mail to a group of friends against the backdrop of his extensive professional experience as a Judge, such an omission cannot be sufficient to overcome the presumption that professional judges decide cases based on the governing law and facts before them. That decision is also factually flawed. Instead of viewing the e-mail in its totality, the majority focused on isolated phrases, taking them out of context and giving them strained meaning. There's simply no evidentiary basis for the majority's conclusion that Judge Harhoff's reference to a professional and moral dilemma referred to a reluctance to apply the correct law. In the next sentence, Judge Harhoff plainly states that the dilemma concerned his suspicions that colleagues might be under political pressure, and this correct interpretation is confirmed by Judge Harhoff's explanation in Exhibit PA1 and the content of the media report in PA3. In addition to the inherent flaws in that decision, the factual circumstances before you in this case are different than in the Seselj case. First and foremost, you have the unanimous trial judgement which shows that the majority's interpretation of that e-mail was incorrect. The trial judgement shows that the reading of the e-mail, the suggestion that Judge Harhoff might convict without with regard to the evidence, that's refuted by the judgement. The judgement also shows that the majority's reading of the dilemma language was incorrect, since the Trial Judges, including Judge Harhoff, carefully applied the Tribunal's law to the facts in the case. Your Honours also have the additional evidence admitted on appeal which was not taken into account by the Seselj majority that gives fuller context to the words in his e-mail. You have the two newspaper articles and you have Judge Harhoff's own views on the e-mail. You have his explanation, and in this memorandum, Exhibit PA1, he explains the words he used and his motivations. This explanation was not considered by the Seselj majority. This was expressly criticised by the dissenting Judge. Instead, the Seselj majority viewed the comments to be immaterial to the issue of bias, but the recent rule change to Rule 15 specifically provides that "the report of the Presiding Judge, which shall include any comments or material provided by the Challenge Judge, shall be provided to the Panel tasked with determining a motion for disqualification." So it clearly is not immaterial. So, Your Honours, the Seselj decision cannot determine the question before you today. And now I come to your question. If you find an appearance of bias, would his participation invalidate the conviction? The Prosecution's position is that in order to ensure public confidence in the integrity of this institution, a finding of judicial bias should result in the invalidation of the conviction. But this does not and cannot mean that a not guilty verdict should follow. In a case involving a unanimous conviction for international crimes, a case based on strong evidence of guilt, it would be a grave injustice to acquit on account of this e-mail or to stay the charges as was asked today. Other remedial measures are available to address the hypothetical fair trial violation that's posited in your question. One would be to remand the matter back to the two remaining Trial Judges with a substitute Judge, similar to what was done in the Seselj case for a reevaluation. A second option would be to conduct a full re-trial as the Appeals Chamber ordered yesterday in the Stanisic and Simatovic judgement. And Zupljanin is asking for a de novo review by the Appeals Chamber, which is certainly an available remedy for a fair trial error that results in an error of law. Quickly in relation to the second part of your question, it's very difficult to contemplate a situation where a finding of bias leads to a remedy other than the invalidation of the verdict. I can only point out here, Your Honours, that if an appearance of bias is found in this case, it would be at the lowest level of possible reasons to fear a lack of impartiality. It would be an appearance of bias rather than actual bias. It would arise after the fact. It would be based on a tenuous interpretation of an informal communication without any identified impact on the case itself, in a case involving the built-in safe-guards of a three-member Bench. If the hypothetical finding of an appearance of bias is so weak that it could be compensated through an alternative remedy that does not involve the invalidation of the verdict, like a declaration or sentence reduction, then, Your Honours, the real question is whether this rises to the level of an appearance of bias at all. In the Prosecution's submission, it does not. Disqualifying Judges based on unfounded allegations of bias is as much a threat to justice as a Judge who is not impartial. I think that concludes our submissions at 12.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Bourgon, you have got 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. President, Your Honours. I will start and then my colleague Mr. Bourgon would continue. I would first like to, to the best of my ability, answer the Honourable Judges' question concerning the relationship between membership or the -- being a parliamentary in the Bosnian Serb Assembly and the function of the minister. Your Honour, according to the relevant regulation, meaning, first and foremost, the Constitution of the Republika Srpska, the Law on Government, the government is responsible to Bosnian Serb Assembly for its work. The Bosnian Serb Assembly appoints, elects, the prime minister and the ministers, and they are all -- they respond for their work to the Assembly. Therefore, at this point, I'm sorry, I cannot advise Your Honours of the specific provisions of the law because I don't know them by heart, but it is understandable that it would be impermissible, a conflict of interest, that one person sits as a parliamentary, so a member of the Assembly, and at the same time be in the function of a minister which is responsible to the same Assembly. In fact, this Assembly can dismiss the ministers, which they did in the case of Mico Stanisic in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, let me try to respond, again to the best of my ability, to sum up the issues raised by my learned friend from the Prosecution. One of the propositions was that -- the Prosecution stated today that Mico Stanisic's role was not based solely or only on his role as a minister; however, his responsibility was not based on -- solely or only on his role as a minister. And then in support of this proposition, actually the Prosecution cites all the roles -- all roles which Mico Stanisic or acts that he did as a minister. In that they used the appointments and the use of police in take-overs and other roles which, according to the judgement, were cited as ways of contribution. In respect to errors, I will read two that I have -- two examples which I can -- which I think can support our position. At paragraph 758, the Chamber erred in finding that the instruction did not include the investigation - this is the federal MUP instruction - did not include the investigation of all crimes, irrespective of the -- of the ethnicity of the victims. However, the document's opening refers to verification of war crimes, crimes of genocide, and other crimes against humanity and international law committed against the Serbs and other ethnicities. The evidence which confirms this error can be found, inter alia, at 1D634 and Defence Witness Macar at transcript 22879, as well as Witness Tusevljak at 22420. Another error at paragraph 764, the Chamber erred in finding that based on the evidence of Witness Radulovic, information gathered by the SNB was available to Stanisic. The witness confirmed that Stanisic was not informed of his reports. The evidence which confirms this error can be found, inter alia, at OTP Witness Radulovic transcript 11014, 11073, 11188, 11199, as well as Witness Skipina at transcript 8412 and 8470. Your Honours, while we're talking about the knowledge issue, this was also raised by the Prosecution. I ask Your Honours to refer to paragraph 275 of the final brief -- Defence final brief where we in detail explained the situation which prevailed at the time; namely, the situation is such that according to the finding - and this is confirmed in the judgement and the evidence of course - the overall number of dispatches over nine months has come to 4.040 received in the ministry at the seat and 4.170 dispatched. Compared to the situation before the war or immediately after that in 1993, it turned out that the number of dispatches during the first nine months of the war that happened in Bosnia are less than the average monthly number of dispatches before the war or in 1993. So to compare, there was 8.500 roughly all together received and sent dispatches, while in 1993 the number rose to 353.215. So that should illustrate the situation with the communications system and the knowledge. I think the Prosecution alleges also some things which go along the errors which were committed by the Trial Chamber in its judgement. For example, one of the allegations was that the civil law apparatus was discriminatory in that period and that Mico Stanisic was responsible for that. We already made a written submission to that, and I invite you to read it. However, the situation appears to be that -- what the suggestion is also by the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber is that Mico, in some really strange way as minister of interior, would have the right to direct the prosecutors how to -- or judiciary system how to do its job. Our submission is -- our written submission is based on -- perhaps I can give one example. It's Exhibit P1609.1, which is in opposition to what the Prosecution is saying about the discriminatory nature of the work of the police. Along these lines I must say that similarly in the Trial Chamber, the Chamber found Mico Stanisic guilty for transferring the reserve policemen to the army, but also previously found that Mico Stanisic did not have any other option or disciplinary measure except to transfer the reserve policemen in case of -- reserve policemen being not suitable to work for the police, he will be transferred to the army. Therefore, I would say, if you permit me, that the Trial Chamber as well as the Prosecution tries to imply some kind of a superman standard to Mico Stanisic, where he would be expected to do more than he is obviously and realistically able to do. I give the floor to my learned friend Mr. Bourgon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I move to my colleague's arguments regarding the mens rea or defining on mens rea. My colleague's arguments focuses on the fact that Mico Stanisic would have adhered to SDS policies; number two, to a relationship with Karadzic; and number three, the fact that he would approve of Arkan's action. With respect to SDS policies, Mico Stanisic as a minister adhered to lawful policies; that was his job at the ministry, and this is outlined or laid out in arguments. The facts, we say, do not try to separate me from -- from following legitimate and lawful policies has nothing to do with mens rea. The relationship with Karadzic is addressed in our brief at ground 4. He was not close to Karadzic. There was no special relationship. And the fact that the argument that he would bypass normal channels to speak with Karadzic is also not true. It ignores all of the daily reports that are in the record which shows that there were daily reports between the Ministry of the Interior and the government. The Arkan issue is very important. We've said it before. It's completely wrong. Once the Appeals Chamber will turn its mind to the testimony of the witnesses mentioned, especially Davidovic and the way the Trial Chamber handled this testimony, it will see that Mico Stanisic did not approve of Arkan's action. I'd like to refer to what my colleague said about the Yellow Wasps. He mentioned "major operation to arrest them." This must be looked at in the context of his relationship where he got into an argument with Plavsic. When you put the two together, regardless of what these people were arrested for, it's the result that matters in order to find the mens rea of Mr. Stanisic. And when you look at the result, two of these members were prosecuted for war crimes, albeit outside of the RS; the others were relieved. The issue that my colleague says, he cared about the fact that they did not want to fall under the command of the army. It is a major issue. It is important for Stanisic to ensure that we don't have rogue criminals walking around. It is important for him. Lastly, my colleague says that there was a persistent contribution over a significant period of time despite his awareness. This fails to take into account the number of orders issued, but the content of the orders. My colleague's comment that the orders were toothless simply does not correspond to the reality. The Appeals Chamber must bear in mind Stanisic dismissed senior officials, including two assistant ministers. He disbanded the special police. With respect to the reserve police, he did everything he could do within the law. My colleague referred at page 61, lines 1 to 6, 11 July. I said previously this is a turning point. What Stanisic did after 11 July is key. The report from Visegrad mentioned at page 61, lines 21 to 24, again, is a factual error. Once the Appeals Chamber will look at this report, it will see that there's an error that this -- the link between the 2.000 displaced persons and the unprofessionalism of the police can't be matched together out of this report. Yet, it's one of the major things mentioned by the Trial Chamber in the limited paragraphs about contribution. As of when he contributed, my colleague mentions the first action, 11 February. He fails to take into account that by that time surely Mico Stanisic did not have the mens rea. Again, look at the 11 July as a date at which he did not have mens rea. As of when? My colleague mentions the JCE begins on a certain date; we say he's a member of the JCE; therefore the date must be the beginning of the JCE. Doesn't work, Mr. President. Resubordination argument. My colleague focuses on the duty to prevent and punish and the duty to protect civilians. That's not the question. The question from the Appeals Chamber is quite clear. The question was: Was he found responsible for failing to investigate and punish? Yes, he was. Did the Trial Chamber fail to say who is responsible for failing to -- for investigation and prosecuting? Yes, it did. It failed to pronounce on this issue; that closes the matter. With respect to the Harhoff issue, my colleague on the Prosecution calls it a legal disagreement based on a disagreement in the jurisprudence. It goes way further than this. And my colleague also relies on the Seselj decision. The first most important issue, whether the communication of Judge Harhoff was informal, casual, meant to be addressed to friends, that's not the question. Whether it is unreasonable or not for a Judge to write strictly or not in a memo, that's beyond the point. The issue is you read the memo and what is the appearance that comes out of the memo; this is what matters. And it is clear what comes out of this memo, that there's a clear predisposition to convict on the basis of knowledge. It's what the letter reveals. My colleague raised a very interesting issue at 69, lines 7 to 8, professional judges are able to set aside personal views. Wow. When I read this memo, this is anything but a Judge who is able to set aside his professional views. The e-mail is completely opposite. The fact that you have a unanimous decision in Stanisic has absolutely no bearing. What is at stake here is not the appearance of the trial, not whether the judgement was unanimous. What is at stake is whether that letter displays a reasonable apprehension of bias; and if so, does it impact on the trial. We have already explained why we believe it does. Whether the trial was conducted fairly or decided by three Judges unanimously, again, is beside the point. My colleague says, well, if he had an appearance of bias, you would have expected him to enter a dissenting opinion. Well, that's exactly the point we're saying. Appearance of bias, if you add the appearance of bias, then a Judge is not going put in a judgement that he disagrees with the law and that he usually convicts on the basis of knowledge, so this time he's going to say I enter a guilty finding but only on knowledge. Of course a Judge is not going to do this. So that doesn't work. In Seselj, the Specially Convened Chamber, one, did not commit any legal error - I said that before - but it did not presume bias. This is not what it says. I refer to the most important thing, I guess, in Judge Harhoff's comment, the dilemma, the way he explains the dilemma, trying to walk back because he really knows what the dilemma in his e-mail really displays and he's trying to explain it. It has become he would be under a dilemma or it was clearly "I was under a dilemma." Lastly, I just say simply about the rule change. We have a rule change. I think the rule change fits with Judge Afande's separate opinion. Yes, the report is important, but in this time, in this case, the report compounds the appearance of bias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We agree with the Prosecution that if there is an appearance of bias, and we say it is, the remedy is invalidate the conviction and send him home. If the Prosecutor wants to ask for a re-trial later, they can do so and we will respond. Thank you very much, Mr. President. This concludes our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Now, Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Gosnell - I don't know who is going to take the floor - we will go till five minutes past 1.00, and then of course we will continue after the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. For those of you who don't know me, my name is Christopher Gosnell and I appear on behalf of Mr. Zupljanin. I take the floor first to address you on three issues, the first being the violation of Mr. Zupljanin's right to be tried by a fair and impartial Tribunal; the second issue being the Trial Chamber's improper reliance on Mr. Zupljanin's alleged presence at the Holiday Inn in February 1992; and the Trial Chamber's lack of reason in imputing omissions to Mr. Zupljanin for the purpose of making findings of actus reus and mens rea for commission by JCE. My learned friend Mr. Krgovic will extend the discussion of resubordination and explain how dominant, how central, that issue was during the trial, even to the extent that the Judges themselves took the initiative to call Chamber witnesses on the issue. My learned friend Ms. Cmeric will then address Your Honours on extermination and sentencing. Your Honours, Judge Harhoff's e-mail to 56 friends and acquaintances was sent 71 days after he had signed the judgement convicting Mr. Zupljanin and sentencing him to 22 years. On that basis and that basis alone with one minor exception, and in our respectful view, that e-mail gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias through a deep-seeded reluctance to apply the standards that are well established, well known, well understood, long applied at this Tribunal in case after case. Before we embark on a discussion of the e-mail itself, it's perhaps useful to just look at what those positions -- what that doctrine is. I do have the assistance of a PowerPoint presentation. The unique aspect of JCE, joint criminal enterprise, is that this is a form of commission which permits the actus reus to be performed by a plurality of persons. This means that no single person, as in the case of physical commission, needs to commit the actus reus; it can be spread across different people. And that leads to a lowering of the actus reus threshold relative to physical commission to merely acts that in some way are directed to the furthering of the common plan. At the same time, however, the mens rea standard is the same as for physical commission and that standard is that the accused intended the crime. Now, it's not so much that JCE at this stage of the Tribunal's history is legally debatable, complex, or fraught; the issue is that it creates complexities of adjudication. Mens rea, after all, is not just an attitude or a mind-set; mens rea is the animating intent with which an act is performed. And reducing that actus reus threshold means that Judges, as Your Honours know from having sat on trials at this Tribunal, have less direct information to rely upon in inferring that animating purpose behind an act. And that analysis becomes even more complex, as is the case in this case, where there are even lawful acts of violence being committed in the course of an armed conflict and is made even more fraught by the fact that there may be those who wish to achieve their aims by lawful means, whereas there are other individuals who want to achieve the same ends by unlawful criminal means. So given that fraught background, that context in which fact-finding is so difficult, especially in respect of this reduced actus reus, how do the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal ensure that that standard of direct intent for mens rea is maintained? Well, the first step is that common purpose has to be strictly defined. It may not include a purpose that is not criminal, and if it did, that would risk analysing mens rea in respect of a purpose that is much too broad. It would permit an imputation of mens rea to something that is not entirely criminal. Now, of course, the case law of the Tribunal has long stated that the criminal purpose may amount to or involve a criminal purpose, but that must be understood, we submit, as an amounting or involving that is intrinsic to the criminal purpose rather than merely being a possible or a foreseeable means by which that purpose is achieved, because if you introduced those concepts of foreseeability or possibility, of course the standard for direct intent would be indirectly lowered below what is permitted. So what is the relationship - and it's an issue that was raised repeatedly in the trial judgement - between knowledge and intent? And this is from Your Honours' -- the Appeals Chamber's recent judgement in Sainovic, stating that the accused must share the intent for the commission of the crimes and not merely foresee their occurrence. Foreseeability cannot be mechanically or automatically applied to infer direct intent, nor can direct intent be automatically or mechanically inferred on the basis even of contemporaneous knowledge that crimes are being committed. And the particularly salient part of the passage that is now in front of you from the Krajisnik's appeals judgement is underlined and bolded there at the end which describes the proper type of fact-finding that must be engaged in before findings of mens rea and actus reus can be arrived at. And I quote: "In those instances where the Trial Chamber referred to a particular month in which leading JCE members became aware of the commission of expanded crimes, it did not specify the date when this happened or whether Krajisnik was among the leading JCE members who gained such awareness, let alone when leading JCE members went from being merely aware of the crime to intending it." This is, I suggest, the proper level of rigour that is required by Your Honours, by the Appeals Chamber, in fact-finding in respect of mens rea. So this is the jurisprudential context, and I suggest it's not complicated. It's clear, the standard that's required for JCE. It's settled. And this is the context in which we must analyse what Judge Harhoff wrote 71 days after he signed the Zupljanin trial judgement. Now, what he says -- and I propose to try to add some value to what has already been said by my colleagues about this e-mail by trying to read the e-mail wholistically, in its entirety, to ensure that there can be no misunderstanding about what Judge Harhoff, we say, must have meant, what he must have been expressing in this e-mail. And the e-mail starts in terms of the discussion of JCE with the phrase or the expression: "We had also developed an extended criminal responsibility for people (ministers, politicians, military leaders, officers and others), who had supported an overall goal to eradicate ethnic groups from certain areas through criminal violence, and which in one way or another contributed to the achievement of such a goal; it is this responsibility that goes by the name of 'joint criminal enterprise.'" Now, I pause here to say that if the words "supported an overall goal" is understood as meaning direct intent, that there would be nothing in that words to arouse in the mind of an reasonable observer that Judge Harhoff was proposing an improperly low mens rea threshold. As it stands this could be interpreted as indeed conveying the notion of direct intent. But as we'll see from the rest of the e-mail, that's not how he understands agreement or support. After this passage, there is the discussion of the three cases that have already been mentioned by my learned colleagues, and Judge Harhoff continues: "What can we learn from this? "You would think that the military establishment in leading states (such as USA and Israel) felt that the courts in practice were getting too close to the military commanders' responsibilities. One hoped that the commanders would not be held responsible unless they had actively encouraged their subordinate forces to commit crimes. In other words: "The court was heading too far in the direction of commanding officers being held responsible for every crime their subordinates committed. Thus their intention to commit crime had to be specifically proven. "But that is exactly" -- and then Judge Harhoff defends this position, the previous state of the law as he understood it: "That is exactly what the commanders get paid for: They must ensure that in their area of responsibility no crimes are committed, and if they are they must do what they can to prosecute the guilty parties. And no one who supports the idea of ethnic eradication can deny the responsibility of, in one way or another, contributing to the achievement of such a goal. "However, this is no longer the case. Now apparently the commanders must have had a direct intention to commit crimes - and not just knowledge or suspicion that the crimes were or would be committed." Now, at this point, Your Honours, a reasonable observer, I suggest, would not be able to avoid harbouring the impression or having the impression that Judge Harhoff is distinguishing between two concepts: a JCE standard on the one hand that involves support and a JCE standard that involves direct intention to commit crimes. That's a distinction that Judge Harhoff is creating between direct intent and support. We don't know precisely what Judge Harhoff might mean by "support," but we do know that it is in his view lower than direct intent and significant -- lower to a degree that is sufficient to provoke in him very, very strong expressions in this e-mail. Now, what he is also doing is repudiating, quite clearly, the standard which is well established in the law of the Tribunal and which did not change as a result of any of the decisions that he refers to. That's the law as it's been since Tadic. And the fact that Judge Harhoff is mistaken about the meaning of these recent cases that he's referring to is irrelevant. What's important is the reflection in this e-mail that Judge Harhoff is expressing disagreement with the standard of direct intent for JCE. And is such disagreement allowed in line with the Judge's oath? Certainly, Your Honours, it's allowed. Judge Schomburg expressed sharp disagreement with the doctrine of JCE and he put it in his judgement clearly and expressly. And the position as expressed in the judgement is what allowed the Appeals Chamber to look closely at what standard was being applied and to determine whether a conviction was correct on a basis of the standard expressed by the Judges. Now, it's possible that someone could attempt to argue that what Judge Harhoff was referring to was merely the actus reus not needing to be criminal, and indeed in Sainovic it's true; the actus reus does not need to involve a crime. There's no dispute about that. But even if that act, whatever that may be, is not a crime, that mens rea standard is always direct intent. Now, Your Honours, I don't propose to read what's on this slide. It's well-known what's in the content of this particular passage and I don't think it could have been put better than by Judge Liu in his dissenting opinion in the Seselj disqualification decision, who said that they constitute, and I quote, "unsubstantiated speculations and insinuations of improper conduct by other colleagues in a fashion that is unbefitting of a Judge," and that's at paragraph 2 of his dissent. What's significant without getting into the details is the stridency of the details, the level of hostility, the sense of usurpation of the law as a result of these decisions. Judge Harhoff goes on to explain that the theory -- and this is coming back to the distinction that I was drawing earlier between agreement/support on the one hand, and intent, direct intent, at least as in the mind -- expressed by the mind of -- in the e-mail of Judge Harhoff. And he says: "The theory of responsibility under the specific joint criminal enterprise has now been reduced from contribution to crimes in some way or another to demanding a direct intention to commit crime and not just acceptance of the crimes being committed." Again, we see here this juxtaposition, as we saw before, between direct intention to commit crime on the one hand and acceptance - acceptance - of the crimes being committed. Now, albeit imperfectly, the origin of this distinction might be similar to the distinction between dolus directus and dolus eventualis, between direct intent and acceptance of the risk of a possibility that crimes will occur, the same distinction, as Your Honours will know, in the mens rea between JCE 1 and JCE 3. And here we see Judge Harhoff saying the standard for JCE 3 is perfectly acceptable for imposing liability pursuant to JCE 1. And the distinction comes up again: "I have always presumed that it was right to convict leaders for the crimes committed within their knowledge within a framework of a common goal. It all boils down to the difference between knowing on the one hand that the crimes actually were committed or that they were going to be committed, and on the other hand planning to commit them. That's the bottom line!" As Your Honours know, planning requires direct intent. So again we see this dichotomy, this juxtaposition, between a standard of direct intent and mere awareness that crimes might or would be committed. And a reasonable observer could not help but infer from this passage, in conjunction with the earlier passages, that this is precisely the standard of JCE that he was applying in the Zupljanin case. And why do I say that? Because in this very passage on the page in front of you he says: "In all the courts I have worked in here, I have always presumed that it was right to convict leaders ..." Surely this applies to the case that he had just worked on, the last case he had worked on, the case whose judgement he had signed just two months before. It's an indirect implicit reference to what he had just been involved in as a Judge. So even if there's no express reference in the e-mail to any of the cases on which he was working, there's certainly an implied reference. And there's not only an implied reference but an indication of the standard that he applied in those cases. Now, the three foregoing passages, I suggest, especially, not in spite of, especially to an observer who is impeccably informed about the law of this Tribunal, that reasonable observer would understand the dichotomy, the juxtaposition being drawn repeatedly by Judge Harhoff in this e-mail, with support or agreement as something less than direct intent. Now, here we see a slight variation of the terminology being used by Judge Harhoff. He says: "How do we now explain to the thousands of victims that the court is no longer able to convict the participants of the joint criminal enterprise, unless the Judges can justify that the participants in their common goal actively and with direct intent contributed to the crimes? Until now, we have convicted these participants who in one way or another showed that they agreed with the common goal ... as well as in one way or another, had contributed to achieving the common goal - without having to specifically prove that they had a direct intention to commit every single crime to achieve it. It is almost impossible to prove." Again, Your Honours, the same distinction, the same dichotomy, the same contrast being drawn between agreement and direct intent, with agreement being something lower. Now, what does Judge Harhoff say after he's had time to reflect on the content of his e-mail in order to explain what he said? Well, what he says is: "The point was, and this is clear from the context, that the new practice would require more than just the degree of intent associated with knowledge, i.e., that the supreme commanders could only be convicted in the future if a stronger degree of intent could be proven at trial." Your Honours, we just saw the passage from Krajisnik, indicating the importance of proceeding through the steps of the analysis of the facts, of determining whether or not intent could be inferred from knowledge, whether or not there is sufficient acts that indicate that mens rea exists, that special and high threshold of mens rea that is the same for direct commission, the same for swinging an axe and killing someone, that same level of intent requires rigour, reasons, and an analysis. In relation to knowledge, yes, but certainly not comprised by knowledge as we see reflected in this passage which is written by Judge Harhoff with the benefit of hindsight. Now, the fact that before this passage there's a pro forma reference to the framework of JCE or the regular framework of mens rea and actus reus has to be read in light of this, it has to be read in light of the passages, the repeated passages in the e-mail, which shows quite distinctly, Your Honours, that Judge Harhoff's understanding of that framework, his understanding of mens rea within JCE, involves a standard that is less than direct intent. Now, the Prosecution, while it was speaking, indicated that there's no difficulty because the trial judgement shows that Judge Harhoff applied the correct standard. He set aside his deeply felt, his deep-seeded views about JCE and properly participated in the judgement that sets out the standard correctly. Well, is that really true? Are there indications in the judgement that something less than direct intent has been applied? Your Honours are a court of appeal over a range of matters with very limited jurisdiction. Yes, of course, you owe deference to Trial Chambers' reasoning and assessments, but on the other hand at this stage of the Tribunal's history, it's not likely for Trial Judges to make overt mistakes about the applicable law, nor are Your Honours expected to merely sit back and not look for indications, clues, suggestions that an improper standard was applied. And you do that, of course, by looking to see if there are omissions, failures to state reasons, or if indeed there are statements, maybe not throughout the judgement but here and there that suggest to Your Honours that, boy, there's something wrong here, something that's happened that causes difficulty for Your Honours in assessing whether or not indeed the standard that is set out in the applicable law section is what was actually applied to the facts that was before the Trial Chamber. And, Your Honours, there are indications of that absence of reasoning and incongruities in the judgement that suggest there was a problem with the mens rea being applied. Here we see at paragraph 313, in Volume 2 of the judgement, an indication that the common plan did exist, the objective of which was "to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims ... through the commission of the crimes of forcible transfer ... the Chamber finds that there is insufficient evidence to find that other crimes alleged in the indictment were part of this joint criminal enterprise." So in the Trial Chamber's view, there is only a common criminal purpose involving deportation and forcible transfer. How is forcible transfer carried out, Your Honours? Forcible transfer is carried out through coercion. It's carried out through unlawful coercion. Typically, the lowest level of coercion in the cast of crimes under the ICTY Statute is persecution, i.e., discriminating against an individual by various means to make them feel unwelcome, to put it in simplistic terms. That's normally the basic way of encouraging people to leave an area. But what does the Trial Chamber say about persecution? At paragraph 528: "The Trial Chamber recalls its findings that Serb forces carried out the forcible removal ... by committing crimes against them and by enforcing living conditions following the take-over of towns and villages. Zupljanin was also a member of both the ARK and Banja Luka Crisis Staffs, which issued orders restricting the rights of Muslims and Croats to perform certain jobs or impacting on their property rights. On this basis, the Trial Chamber finds that the possibility that Serb forces could impose and maintain restrictive and discriminatory measures against non-Serbs in the ARK municipalities in the execution of the common criminal plan was sufficiently substantial so as to be foreseeable to Stojan Zupljanin and that he willingly took that risk." And this is the same finding, Your Honours, also in respect of unlawful detention, and indeed all of the other crimes that are alleged in the indictment. Now, is that reconcilable? Are those two findings fully incompatible? Well, they may be. I would say, Your Honours, that they're probably not compatible. But even if they're possibly compatible, the fact that these incongruous findings can appear in the judgement without an explanation, without a discussion, without an attempt to say: Here is why we find that Mr. Zupljanin had direct intent in respect of coercion to encourage people to leave the area of the ARK, while on the other hand we find that we cannot convict him, we cannot find that he has direct intent in respect of persecution or unlawful confinement or imprisonment or murder or any of the other crimes charged in the indictment, here is why, here is the explanation as to why those are reconcilable. Another inference Your Honours could draw from these two passages is to see them as in fact completely compatible if you apply the standard that we see in Judge Harhoff's e-mail; namely, knowledge, foresight, some kind of acquiescence, which leads to an assumption that he has something less than direct intent but is sort of going along in a way that can nourish a foreseeability finding on the part of the Judges. Now, His Honour Judge Liu raised some important and very salient concerns about the sufficiency of the reasoning by the majority that -- of the Special Chamber that disqualified Judge Harhoff from the Seselj case, which doesn't necessarily mean that their conclusions are wrong, but on the other hand Judge Liu's observations certainly warrant further discussion. Judge Liu pointed out two particular factors that he considered important in dissenting, and the first point that he made was that the entire context should be considered, including Judge Harhoff's explanatory memorandum. Now, as the previous slide of that memorandum shows when we look at it, Judge Harhoff actually reinforces, not dispels, the impression that he believes that the state of the law is that direct intent is not required for a finding of JCE liability. The other important aspect of the 8th of July explanatory memorandum, which I believe could have been taken account and I would suggest Your Honours should take into account in your analysis here, is that notwithstanding the very striking remarks by Judge Liu about the nature of Judge Harhoff's conduct, that Judge Harhoff in his explanatory memorandum doesn't acknowledge any deviation from accepted standards of judicial conduct. He doesn't say that he's done anything wrong and that he feels any regret for having indicated some of the things that he did in his e-mail. Second point that arises from Judge Liu's dissent which is very relevant is the question as to whether the deep professional and moral dilemma is actual or potential. Judge Harhoff's position in his explanatory memorandum is that it was potential. In the e-mail itself he says that this deep professional and moral dilemma has arisen from "the latest judgements here." He also says that this is a dilemma that he has not previously faced. Again, the unmistakable impression that would be created in the mind of a reasonable observer is that Judge Harhoff is facing this dilemma. He's not facing it because of any potential misconduct in terms of communication with Judges; he's facing this dilemma because of what he describes as the developments in Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you for that direction, and I'll just say there's nothing more to say about the issue of the e-mail, except to commend Your Honours' particular attention to the Hoekstra case, which I would suggest to Your Honours does present many of the characteristics that we have here. Your Honours have asked in the Scheduling Order if there is an appearance of bias, whether it invalidates Mr. Zupljanin's conviction. Assuredly it does, Mr. President. I command to your attention the Medicaments case, paragraph 35; the Hatchcock case, paragraph 4; the Hoekstra case, paragraph 24; as well as the cases collected by Judge Afande in his dissenting opinion in the continuation of proceedings in the Seselj case, paragraph 11. Second question, if the conviction is not set aside, what remedies for the breach of Zupljanin's fair trial rights may be appropriate. The answer, Mr. President, is none. There is no remedy that is equal to the prejudice arising from the participation of a Judge who has an appearance of bias in the judgement. The position set out in the appeal brief in respect of de novo findings was a secondary position, certainly not the primary position. And in any event, given the jurisprudence of the -- or at least the tenor of the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber would not permit de novo findings of guilt against the accused. And we suggest that in a case such as this, where all of the findings would have to be started from anew, there could not be a finding of guilt. Your Honours have also asked whether or not there was a failure to -- the Trial Chamber erred in determining that Mr. Zupljanin was present at the Holiday Inn and participated or was present at the SDS Main and Executive Board meetings there, and the answer, Your Honours, is that the Trial Chamber did err in that respect. The issue was barely mentioned at trial. The meeting is mentioned in the Prosecution pre-trial brief, paragraphs 85 to 86, with no reference to Mr. Zupljanin having been present. When there was a witness present before the Trial Chamber who was at that meeting, he was not asked whether Mr. Zupljanin was present. That witness was not even asked who was present at that meeting. And then the Trial Chamber proceeded to find that Mr. Zupljanin was present on the basis of a receipt from the Holiday Inn, indicating the name Zupljanin, and an intercept in which there is a reference by an interlocutor with Mr. Karadzic, saying that he could meet with a person named Stojan during the breaks. Even accepting that evidence, assuming it's reliable, doesn't prove that Mr. Zupljanin was there at the meeting, doesn't prove that he was there - importantly - at the time of the discussion of the Variant A and Variant B proposals, which is actually what's important in terms of drawing an inference of mens rea. In that regard, Your Honours, the scarcity of evidence is striking in comparison to the reliance placed on this event, this attendance at this meeting, which is mentioned at paragraph 519 in Volume 2 of the judgement, the crucible of the Trial Chamber's mens rea findings, and yet this alleged participation is a matter that was essentially not discussed at all at trial. All of a sudden it ends up in the -- at the core finding of mens rea for the trial judgement. And why is that, Mr. President? Why is that? Why did the Trial Chamber strain to find that he was present? Because, Mr. President, this is, if not the only, then one of the only very few indications of any mens rea at the very beginning of April which the Trial Chamber imputed to Mr. Zupljanin. And, as Your Honours know from our appeal brief, I won't repeat the arguments, the Trial Chamber relied extensively on actions of Mr. Zupljanin that occurred long after April 1992 and did not make any discussion -- there was no discussion as to why those actions as late as November 1992 nourished, substantiated its finding, that he possessed that mens rea as of April. And I recall from the Sainovic case, at paragraph 1035, by the Appeals Chamber, the statement that the Appeals Chamber was not persuaded by the Prosecution's argument that Sainovic's subsequent failure to encourage the persons in charge to prosecute or punish the physical perpetrators is indicative of his intent at the time when the crimes were committed. There must be that coincidence of mens rea and actus reus. There must be an ability to find beyond a reasonable doubt that the mens rea exists at that particular point in time, and the Trial Chamber's indiscriminate, undifferentiated findings, relying on all these events up to November 1992, leaves Your Honours in doubt as of when the Trial Chamber could have said beyond a reasonable doubt now Mr. Zupljanin does possess the mens rea beyond a reasonable doubt, and that's the problem with the Trial Chamber's findings, a lack of specificity as to the timing of his joining the JCE and the basis on which that was inferred. Your Honours have asked whether in relation to Mr. Zupljanin's first ground of appeal the Trial Chamber found Mr. Zupljanin responsible for failing to investigate crimes committed by the police resubordinated to the military. The answer is yes and abundantly and pervasively. You see, Your Honours, at paragraph 519, which I referred to as the crucible paragraph for mens rea, reference to acts and omissions, and then in the middle of the paragraph: "The Trial Chamber has also considered Zupljanin's failure to protect the non-Serb population in conjunction with his enrolment of the SOS in the detachment, his inaction in relation to the crimes committed by this unit and his statements and actions taken in response." So there we see references to omissions. But it's not just there, Your Honours. It's also paragraph 504; Mr. Zupljanin is said to have done nothing. Paragraph 505, he did not impose disciplinary sanctions. At paragraphs 441 through 455, the heading of that section is "Failing While Under a Duty Under Laws and Regulations Applicable to MUP to Protect Entire Civilian Population Within Areas in ARK Municipalities." Paragraphs 457 through 488, encouraging and facilitating commission of crimes by Serb forces by not taking adequate steps to investigate, arrest, or punish perpetrators of such crimes. Now, it's true that the Trial Chamber did not make an express finding that there were occasions when a policeman who was subordinated to the military was not subject to disciplinary measures or sanctioned by Mr. Zupljanin and that there could be an inference of intent on that basis. That's true, Your Honours, but only because the Trial Chamber expressly renounced any need or obligation to set out that there ever was any subordination at any time. And it's not just - as the Prosecution argues at paragraphs 33 and 71 of their response brief - that this issue was not addressed abstractly or that this was merely a hypothetical concern. Your Honours, the issue was not only not addressed abstractly, it was not dealt with specifically in respect of all of the individual events which led up to paragraph 519, that finding of mens rea. And given the evidential context, how much time at trial was spent on these issues, some of which will be discussed by my learned colleague Mr. Krgovic, the Trial Chamber's own active interest in the issue, including discussing for quite a number of paragraphs the implications of resubordination, that evidential context leads to the conclusion that this is not simply a hypothetical concern where the Defence comes up at the last minute in its final trial brief and says, Oh, wait a minute, we have a basis for saying that it turns out he didn't have jurisdiction. No, this was an issue throughout trial as the Judges knew and yet they renounced any need to address the issue. Under what circumstances is it appropriate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
