utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please, for the sake of the interpreters and court reporter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That a person is participating in a JCE. We have guidance on this issue from the Tolimir trial judgement, paragraph 1117. This is referring to four elements and it's referring to criminal responsibility for an omission under Article 7(1). There's no indication that JCE should be exempt from this approach. JCE is a form of commission under Article 7(1). And you can see the four conditions that are set out there: A duty to act mandated by a rule; not only a public law, a criminal law that the person had the ability to act to fulfil that duty; that the person in addition failed to act intending the criminally sanctioned consequences; and that the failure to act resulted in the commission of the crime. Now, actually the Prosecution's position isn't all that different, although it's a little bit vaguer. When a Chamber considers JCE liability based in a part on an omission, it is only required in its actus reus analysis to find that an accused was under a relevant duty, that they had the ability to act, and that their failure to act factually contributed to the implementation of the JCE. Now, we say, of course, those standards are too low, but either way at least they are standards for assessing whether or not a hypothetical action which was not performed by an accused actually constitutes an omission that can be taken into account as constituting part of the actus reus and mens rea for commission by way of JCE. Now, what was the Trial Chamber's position on this issue? Well, before I turn to that, I had a chance briefly to familiarise myself with Your Honours' pronouncement in the Stanisic and Simatovic case, and what I see in that judgement based upon a fairly superficial review is that Your Honours are very concerned to ensure that findings of JCE, this very powerful form of liability, ought to be substantiated by very specific findings, very precise indications as to how actus reus was determined, how mens rea was determined. How did the Trial Chamber assess whether a hypothetical action which was not taken should be attributed to Mr. Zupljanin? No analysis, Your Honours. No description. A series of conclusions, offhand observations that he failed to do X or Y, an omission to do X or Y, did not take action against X or Y. Not only is there no framework of analysis, but when you add in the failure to address the issue of resubordination, it constitutes a complete absence of reasons that could satisfy Your Honours that the Trial Chamber has indeed taken the correct approach to mens rea and actus reus. Now, in declining to assess resubordination, the Trial Chamber may have conflated resubordination with superior responsibility, as if the former could only be relevant to the latter. But this is not a correct equivalence; it's a equivalence. Whether the police force was suspected of committing crimes at the time resubordinated to the military was mutually exclusive of Mr. Zupljanin's authority over them, and the Trial Chamber recognised that, saying they could not determine who had authority to punish, discipline, control police who were resubordinated to the military. That's the Trial Chamber's own - if I can call it a finding - that's the Trial Chamber's own finding. It's a finding that it couldn't make a finding. And it should have triggered at that point, once the Trial Chamber made that finding, it was incumbent upon them to rigorously analyse whether particular acts by policemen were or were not undertaken in the context of resubordination, because otherwise, Your Honours, what we have is a situation where the Trial Chamber cannot say, in light of its own doubts about resubordination, its own recognition of the seriousness of the issue, how central it was to assessing Mr. Zupljanin's capacity to act, obligation to act, duty to act, in light of all that, it wasn't possible for the Trial Chamber to decide beyond a reasonable doubt that particular actions or crimes committed by persons who were resubordinated to the military should be attributed to Mr. Zupljanin. Mr. President, with your leave, I will now cede the floor to Mr. Krgovic who will address you on some of the very extensive evidence that was heard about resubordination during the trial. I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell is kindly requested to switch off the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will speak in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will speak in the Serbian language because I can explain myself better with regard to some things in my native tongue, and I have provided a transcript of my speech to the booths so that there will be no problem with following my address. Your Honours, resubordination is a central topic that was dealt with by the Defence, Prosecution, and the Trial Chamber intensively throughout the trial. The issue was raised in the courtroom for the first time on the 2nd of October, 2009, at the very beginning of the trial, some two weeks after its commencement. We spent months in the courtroom, if not an entire year, discussing the issue. Dozens of witnesses were heard. A large number of documents was introduced, including two expert reports on the part of the Defence as well as those experts' testimony. In addition, both OTP experts, the police and military one testified on that issue. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber called its own two witnesses proprio motu who dealt exclusively with the topic. Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to our PowerPoint presentation, where we have Judge Hall commenting upon General Lisica's testimony, and he said: [In English] "We require your assistance on the resubordination of police forces to the army and the responsibility for an investigation and prosecution of the serious crimes allegedly committed by resubordinated forces during time of resubordination." [Interpretation] Your Honours, we began the trial with that topic and concluded it with the topic as well. What was the outcome? Following a summary of most witness testimony and evidence on the topic, the Trial Chamber first stated that it is not in a position to establish whether the military or civilian authorities would be the ones responsible for conducting investigations and prosecution for crimes against Muslims and Croats that may have been committed by members of the police resubordinated to the army. The Trial Chamber further stated that there was no need to provide any further conclusions regarding the issue of resubordination. Your Honours, despite all that, in paragraph 518 of the second volume of the judgement, the Trial Chamber found that Zupljanin was liable because he, I quote, "failed to launch criminal investigations and discipline his subordinates who had committed crimes against non-Serbs, thus creating a climate of impunity." Also, in paragraph 519 of the second volume, the Trial Chamber found that Zupljanin failed to protect the non-Serb population, inter alia, by failing to discipline the units under his control. The basic issues to which the Trial Chamber did not provide an answer which, had they been correctly analysed in detail and had they been answered, would to a significant extent, if not completely, have changed the Trial Chamber conclusions regarding Zupljanin's failure to act. The first such issue is when and under what circumstances were members of the police resubordinated to the army. In other words, in which situations and periods were the members of the police beyond the authority and competence of Zupljanin? And secondly, to what extent were the crimes that Zupljanin was charged with committed by members of the police while they were resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska? Why is this issue important, Your Honours? And I will cite relevant examples from the judgement where the relevant police stations, including entire police stations, were completely resubordinated to the military structures. Such examples are Donji Vakuf, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, the security detail at the military camps of Manjaca and Trnopolje, as well as the participation of the police in all combat activities in the territory of the ARK. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber had before them a plethora of evidence and testimony, based on which it was easy to establish who had the authority and who was responsible to launch investigations and discipline perpetrators in these places and locations. I just wanted to cite a few examples, some exhibits and the names of certain witnesses. These are Exhibits 5160, 2D159, 1D662, 1D368, P1888, P624. Then the testimony of Witness Slavko Lisica, then Witness Aleksandar Krulj, Witness SD172, Witness General Vidosav Kovacevic, as well as Witness Nenad Krejic. All this evidence was ignored by the Trial Chamber. Why is resubordination so important? Because there is evidence in the case indicating that 80 per cent of the policemen who were members of the Banja Luka CSB were resubordinated to the army between the 4th of April, 1992, until December 1992, the 31st of December, 1992. We can also have a look at P624, report on the work of the Banja Luka CSB drafted by Mr. Zupljanin, as well as the testimony of Witness Goran Macar, transcript pages 23094 and 23095. Furthermore, Your Honours, in such situations Zupljanin did not have the authority over the forces that may have committed those crimes. Furthermore, Zupljanin had difficulty exercising his authority over such members of the police who were not resubordinated as can be seen in Exhibit P624. So even had Zupljanin tried to issue an order to such forces resubordinated to the army, such individuals or units would have been under no obligation to act on such order because at that moment in time they belonged to a different chain of command and decision-making. The issue of resubordination is also closely linked to the issue of Zupljanin's obligation and criminal liability vis-à-vis protecting civilians as a whole. The very fact, Your Honours, that over 80 per cent of regular and reserve policemen were resubordinated to the army between April and December 1992 and that Zupljanin could neither exercise authority over them nor could he count on them to perform regular police tasks explains why Zupljanin de facto was not in a position to provide adequate protection to the civilian population, of which he was found guilty. Therefore, to the extent to which Zupljanin's orders were inefficient, it was not because Zupljanin wished them to be such or because he was protecting the members of the police; it was because he had neither the ways nor means to see them through. To that effect, we have the testimony of Witness SD161, transcript pages 3527 and 3528 and 3533 to 3535, as well as the testimony of Witness SD007 who expressly stated that such orders could almost never be put into practice. Finally, Your Honours, I would like to address something that my learned friend Mr. Gosnell also mentioned and that was a question by the Appeals Chamber. You wanted to know whether the Trial Chamber found Zupljanin responsible for failing to investigate crimes committed by police resubordinated to the military. Your Honours, based on everything specified in our appeal reply by Zupljanin and what I stated today, we believe that the answer to that question is positive, i.e., that the Trial Chamber indeed pronounced Zupljanin guilty of failing to investigate and discipline the perpetrators of crimes in cases where the crimes were committed by the policemen who at the time of commission were resubordinated to the VRS. Your Honours, these are no small omissions on the part of the Trial Chamber, nor are they technicalities that would not have an impact on the liability or sentence of the accused. These issues go to the gist of the Trial Chamber's conclusions regarding Stojan Zupljanin's liability. These are serious errors on behalf of the Trial Chamber invalidating the judgement on several levels. They made the conclusions regarding facts at least uncertain and, one may also say, unreasonable. As such, they require radical intervention by the Appeals Chamber. Your Honours, this is all I wanted to say on this matter and Ms. Cmeric will take it from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Tatjana Cmeric, and today I will be addressing your question concerning the extermination charge and then I will move on to discuss sentencing. Mr. President, with your permission, I would proceed to answer Your Honours' question regarding Zupljanin's third ground of appeal; namely, and I quote, "whether the Trial Chamber made the required finding that the perpetrators of the killing of 20 detainees during their transport from Betonirka detention facility to Manjaca camp on 7 July 1992 possessed the required intent for extermination; and if not, whether the absence of such a finding would invalidate the Trial Chamber's conclusion." The mens rea of extermination requires the intention of the perpetrator to kill on a large scale or to systematically subject a large number of people to conditions of living that would lead to their deaths. Only in Volume 1, paragraph 215 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber avers, and I quote, "police officers intended to inflict serious bodily harm upon the detainees being transported and that the detainees were killed." The Chamber appears to be also accepting in the same paragraph and elsewhere in the judgement the possibility that death of about 20 detainees, as they put it, may not have even been intentional; namely, in the said paragraph, 215, of the judgement the Trial Chamber stated, and I quote, "the police officers knew or should have known that with their actions they could have caused the victims' deaths." Then in Volume 2, paragraph 524, the Chamber states, and I quote: "On 7 July 1992, 20 non-Serb detainees had died in a truck while being transported by the Sanski Most police." All the facts surrounding this incident, taken at their best or at their worst, do not show beyond a reasonable doubt that principal perpetrators possessed the required mens rea for the crime of extermination. It is certainly not the only reasonable inference a trier of fact would have found on the evidence. Your Honours, I would ask if we could now move briefly into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session, please, for a while. Are we in private session yet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Ms. Cmeric, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this witness says that police members who were heading the column were not even aware of the conditions in which the detainees were transported to Manjaca. And we have no other evidence suggesting that they had any specific knowledge about it, let alone that they intended to subject the detainees to conditions that would lead to their death. The Trial Chamber completely disregarded it. Testimony like this should not have been disregarded but instead considered in conjunction with Exhibit P486, which is a daily report from Manjaca camp operational team sent to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps security intelligence department, dated 8 July 1992. The document refers to 24 prisoners who, as the report reads, died, probably due to lack of oxygen. The report criticises the Sanski Most organs, so not specifically police or not the police alone or even not the Sanski Most police at all. A similar report that can also be looked at is P487, dated 9 July 1992. Notably, both reports were sent to a military corps and not to the Sanski Most or the Banja Luka police or not to Zupljanin for that matter. So even accepting that the police or other persons involved in transport of detainees to Manjaca were aware of the transportation conditions, the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that principal perpetrators possessed the required mens rea to either kill on a massive scale or to systematically subject these people to conditions of living that would lead to their deaths. The requirement is that the perpetrators' mental state encompasses all objective elements of the crime. The annihilation of a mass of people and those directives is the level of criminality required, rather than recklessness or gross negligence. Your Honours, to go even further, if the recklessness or dolus eventualis standard would satisfy the mens rea of extermination in respect of the Sanski Most -- I apologise, could satisfy the mens rea of extermination, the Chamber's findings still do not meet even that lower standard in respect of the Sanski Most incident. The Chamber found that the police officers, and I quote again, "knew or should have known that with their actions they could have caused the victims' deaths." The "should have known" standard is a statement of negligence and carelessness, not a voluntary undertaking of a risk as required by dolus eventualis. The Chamber's findings do not meet the mens rea threshold for extermination. As noted in paragraph 234 of the Zupljanin appeal brief, the perpetrators, therefore, did not commit extermination, and that event cannot be so characterised or imputed as such to the JCE even if it was foreseeable. This was an error of law arising from a misstatement of the Chamber's own findings that invalidates the Chamber's legal conclusion. Finally, to answer the first part of Your Honours' question, the Trial Chamber did make a finding concerning principal perpetrators' intent for extermination. The issue here, therefore, is not the absence of any finding on the Chamber's part; it is that the finding does not meet the mens rea requirement for the crime of extermination. To answer the second part of Your Honours' question, the existence of the finding as it stands does invalidate the Trial Chamber's conclusion in a way that the finding of extermination with respect to 7 July 1992 incident can no longer stand. That concludes my submissions in relation to Your Honours' question. With your permission, I would now move to discuss the sentencing. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber correctly set out the applicable allow concerning sentencing but failed to follow it and did not exercise its discretion in the way to achieve a proper balance in view of the evidence on the record between the gravity of the crimes and the individual circumstances of the accused. The Trial Chamber made several discernible errors which, viewed either separately or jointly, caused irreparable damage to the sentencing part of the judgement. Sentences imposed in previous cases are not binding on subsequent Chambers that have the obligation to individualise the penalty. As the Chamber correctly held and noted in Volume 2, paragraph 887, the discretion for determining the appropriate sentence, although broad, is not unlimited. The Trial Chamber in this case failed to give sufficient weight to relevant considerations. It made clear errors as to the facts upon which it exercised its discretion and made decisions that are so unreasonable and unjust that the Appeals Chamber is able to infer that the Trial Chamber failed to properly exercise its discretion. The Trial Chamber overestimated Mr. Zupljanin's position, responsibilities, and authority and, on the other hand, undervalued his positive deeds and efforts. The Chamber took as aggravating circumstance the fact that Zupljanin had wrongfully used his authority to assist crimes. However, when paragraph 948 in Volume 2 of the judgement is carefully read, it appears that the Chamber had, in fact, relied on Zupljanin's official capacity as the chief of the Banja Luka CSB, thereby making a discernible error of double counting. In Stakic, Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber held that the Trial Chamber must provide convincing reasons for its choice of factors; that's at paragraph 416. The Trial Chamber failed to do so when it failed to establish that Zupljanin's dispatches and orders were in itself criminal. In fact, there are no findings in the trial judgement that Zupljanin has misused his authority in that respect. By his direct actions, Zupljanin, among others, managed to save over a thousand lives. He intervened when lives of nearly 600 people of Roma and Muslim ethnicity were at stake and also was actively involved in the release of several hundred detained non-Serbs in Teslic. Your Honours will find detailed submissions in paragraphs 247 and 249 of the Zupljanin appeal brief on these matters and also in transcript 27630, 27631, and all the references contained therein. The Chamber makes no mention of any of this in the sentencing section. Instead, it assesses that Zupljanin only reacted in, and I quote, "specific and isolated instances." That's judgement Volume 2, paragraph 952. And the Prosecution stated in paragraphs 212 and 213 of its response brief and will undoubtedly reiterate that Zupljanin should not benefit in mitigation from such situations as he helped create them by participating in the JCE. Your Honours, while contesting the Prosecution's submission, I draw your attention to the Krajisnik case, where the Appeals Chamber accepted as a mitigating factor his attempts to help certain non-Serbs with their imprisonment and humanitarian aid; that's judgement paragraph 816, 817. The Chamber did so, despite finding Mr. Krajisnik to be, and I quote, "an architect of ethnic cleansing with respect to creation of conditions of imprisonment." The position of the Popovic et al. Trial Chamber that saving lives is a mitigating factor, even if such act is motivated by military considerations, and that is the position relied on in footnote 340 of the Zupljanin appeal brief and contested by the Prosecution in paragraph 213 of their response brief. So that position of the Popovic et al. Trial Chamber has now been upheld by the Popovic et al. appeal judgement, and that can be found in paragraphs 2076 and 2077. Zupljanin's positive actions had no hidden or nefarious motives, yet they were given insufficient weight or were blatantly disregarded by the Chamber. Ample evidence was heard, Your Honours, in trial on the exigent circumstances existing at the relevant time-period, on the breakdown in communications system, and lack of adequate reporting. I can refer you to Exhibits 2D52, P595, P621, P160, 2D50, and also to testimony of SD166 and SD167. Also, evidence was heard in trial on shortage of personnel Zupljanin was facing; for example, you may want to look at Exhibit P560. On the risks Zupljanin was facing, and that can be found in Exhibit 2D91 and also testimony of SD182 and SD172. And despite that, on the open criticism, Zupljanin was not afraid to communicate to certain authorities and officials concerning their conduct towards the non-Serb population and highly inadequate conditions in undefined camps in a blatant breach of international norms, as he put it, and this can be found in Exhibits P160 and 2D25. Zupljanin made pleas to his peers to do everything within their power to preserve peace. He made serious efforts to devise and implement a work-plan to tackle the crime, which is 1D198. He openly opposed crime, violence, and effort to -- put a lot of effort to protect the non-Serb population. Zupljanin repeatedly made efforts to preserve and restore law and order. For instance, you may look at Exhibits P601 and P595, and also P621 and P624, not to mention the numerous criminal complaints and reports he filed. And I refer Your Honours to Exhibits 2D57, 2D58, 2D59, and so on, to name just a few. The Trial Chamber not only failed to take into account these endeavours, it went even further to aver that Zupljanin played, and I quote, "a crucial role in the commission of the crimes for which he has been found guilty," without any reference or regard to the nature of forms of Zupljanin's participation in relation to the sentence. These arguments can be found in detail in subground 4(B) of the Zupljanin appeal brief. In case, however, the Appeals Chamber upheld the factual findings on which Zupljanin's sentence lies, the sentence itself still requires reduction. As noted in the Galic appeal judgement, paragraph 455, and I quote: "Although the Trial Chamber did not err in its factual findings and correctly noted the principles governing sentencing, it committed an error in finding that the sentence imposed adequately reflects the level of gravity of the crimes committed by Galic and his degree of participation." This is also referenced by the recent Djordjevic appeal judgement, paragraph 968. Your Honours, Mr. Zupljanin may not have always managed to react as promptly and as adequately as expected from an officer of the law. He was not always adamant in his reactions and he may not have always found the most appropriate solution to a problem he was facing. Over 20 years after the war and events in question, one can easily fall into a dangerous trap of oversimplifying the circumstances at the time. Looking from this perspective, it may appear easy to choose between different options and means at one's disposal and make the right decision, but back in the times of war it was everything but simple. Seemingly simple solutions and decisions were often burdened with obstacles and difficulties unimaginable to a present-day observer. And yes, in an ideal world, much more could have been done to prevent movement of population or mistreatments and many more lives could have been saved. But the circumstances surrounding Mr. Zupljanin's daily duties and activities were anything but ideal. They were difficult; they were chaotic, unpredictable, exigent. That is why his sentence, if any, must take into account the series of efforts Zupljanin made to suppress violence, to preclude, prevent, or discover any wrong-doers, and also all the actions taken against them and numerous lives and families he did manage to save. This deserves credit and should not have been dismissed so lightly. The sentence of 22 years imposed against Mr. Zupljanin is manifestly excessive and disproportionate. In addition to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. In addition to maintaining all the arguments from the appeal brief and reply brief, it is submitted that significant weight should have been given to the aforementioned particular factors and circumstances, which were so blatantly misconceived or disregarded in the sentencing part of the trial judgement. Your Honours are, therefore, invited to rectify the errors and omissions of the Trial Chamber and reduce Mr. Zupljanin's sentence accordingly. That concludes my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Cmeric. Prosecution, you have 60 minutes. It's five past 3.00 now, according to the courtroom clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: My name is Aditya Menon and I will be responding to Zupljanin's appeal, together with Ms. Baig. In our submissions this afternoon, Your Honours, we will show you why Zupljanin's conviction is safe and why it should not be overturned, why Your Honours can be satisfied that Zupljanin was tried by a fair and impartial Bench, and why that Bench was right to convict him. The bottom line, Your Honours, is that the arguments the Defence makes challenging Zupljanin's conviction and sentence are a diversion from the simple, the obvious, and the very reasonable basis on which the Chamber established his criminal responsibility. Zupljanin was the police chief, after all, who created a unit out of criminals and deployed that unit again and again and again, even as its members victimised non-Serbs. You haven't heard it from the Defence but you'll hear it from me. He was the police chief who told non-Serbs he couldn't protect them and kept his word by allowing non-Serbs to be victimised in the building that he worked, in the town where he was based, and across the ARK region for which he was responsible. You haven't heard it from them but you'll hear it from me. He was the police chief who saw the horrid crimes that police forces perpetrated firsthand and heard and read about them through reports he received and yet was emboldened to shield perpetrators from criminal prosecution. You haven't heard it from them but you will hear it from me. For the Defence, Your Honours, there's simply no escaping the Chamber's reasoned findings about the choices Zupljanin made, the deliberate conduct he engaged in, the numerous crimes he knew of, and his unflinching commitment to the common criminal purpose, the common criminal purpose to create a Serb state as ethnically pure as possible through a persecutory campaign of forcible transfer and deportation. Now, in my submissions this afternoon, I'll discuss the basis for the Chamber's conclusion concerning Zupljanin's JCE contributions. I'll begin with the massive amount of active conduct, active conduct that the Chamber relied upon in establishing his significant contribution. As much as the Defence would like this to be an omission liability case, it simply is not one. After I discuss Zupljanin's active conduct, I'll discuss the climate of impunity that he created in the ARK through his acts and his deliberate inaction. I'll then discuss the Chamber's reliance on Zupljanin's duty to protect the civilian population and then proceed to the issue of resubordination. In the course of my submissions, Your Honours, I'll answer the questions you've raised in relation to Zupljanin's first and third grounds of appeal. Ms. Baig will conclude the Prosecution's submissions by responding to Zupljanin's arguments concerning his sixth ground of appeal, the Harhoff e-mail issue. Turning then to the active conduct that the Chamber relied upon in establishing Zupljanin's significant contribution. Whilst Zupljanin certainly contributed to the common criminal purpose through his inaction, the Chamber also made extensive findings concerning Zupljanin's active conduct, findings that in and of themselves establish his significant contribution. What did this active conduct entail? Notably it entailed creating and deploying the special police detachment, his special police detachment. It entailed disarming non-Serbs. It entailed playing a proactive role in the unlawful arrest and detention of non-Serbs. The Defence's arguments not only obscure this active conduct, it completely ignores the active conduct that he engaged in in furthering the common criminal purpose. Let me begin the discussion about Zupljanin's active conduct by talking about Banja Luka because that's where the story about his special police detachment begins. Having been one of the key actors who organised the blockade of Banja Luka by the SOS paramilitary group on the 3rd of April, 1992, Zupljanin fuelled the campaign of violence that followed that blockade by creating and deploying his special police detachment, a unit which he filled with seasoned criminals. What did the campaign of violence in Banja Luka into which Zupljanin introduced his special police detachment look like? Let me tell you what it looked like. After the blockade, the SOS, who had close links to the SDS, carried out attacks against non-Serbs and their property in Banja Luka by blowing up houses and businesses two or three times a week; that's Volume 1, paragraphs 157 and 209. Zupljanin's policemen didn't meaningfully address these crimes; instead, when patrolling Muslim neighbourhoods, they seized money and gathered information that was used to bring people in for interrogation at Zupljanin's headquarters, the Banja Luka CSB building; Volume 1, paragraph 157. A group of Serbs who drove a red van and included members of Zupljanin's police force were particularly notorious in Banja Luka. They beat, they harassed, they arrested, and they stole property from non-Serbs. Those whom they violently abducted were shoved into their red van which was driven around Banja Luka with its doors open so that the abuse suffered by their victims was seen by everybody. The red van group launched some of their attacks from Zupljanin's CSB building and then they returned there with their victims so that the victims could be beaten and humiliated some more; Volume 1, paragraphs 159 and 201. To make matters worse, Zupljanin granted these perpetrators impunity by publicly announcing in the first half of April 1992 that he couldn't guarantee the physical security and safety of non-Serbs and their property. That's Volume 2, paragraphs 450 and 496. The threatening atmosphere in Banja Luka following the blockade caused hundreds of non-Serbs to flee the municipality every week in buses escorted by the police; Volume 2, paragraphs 499 and 512. It was in the midst of this violence that was taking place all around him that Zupljanin created his special police detachment of about 150 to 200 men. Zupljanin provided them, his detachment members, with ID cards that authorised them to arrest people, to conduct searches without a warrant, and to carry and use fire-arms; Volume 2, paragraph 390. Zupljanin was warned about the dangers of inducting criminals from the SOS into his special police detachment, but he disregarded those warnings, praising the SOS for being Serbian knights; Volume 2, paragraphs 388 and 499; Volume 1, paragraph 193. Following its creation, Zupljanin unleashed the detachment in Banja Luka in May 1992 where unit members arbitrarily arrested and beat non-Serbs and looted their property. Just as other perpetrators had been doing since the blockade of Banja Luka in April, detachment members took non-Serbs to Zupljanin's - Zupljanin's - headquarters, the Banja Luka CSB building, and they beat them there; Volume 1, paragraphs 164 and 201. In May 1992 detachment members were also actively committing crimes outside of Banja Luka. That month Zupljanin sent detachment members to Bosanski Novi and Doboj and learned that they had committed crimes in these municipalities as well; Volume 2, paragraphs 405, 431, 440, and 502. Despite knowing that its members had victimised non-Serbs, Zupljanin allowed the detachment to operate in Banja Luka and deploy the detachment to assist in the take-over of other municipalities as well, and unsurprisingly members of the detachment continued to commit crimes against non-Serbs. For instance, on the 13th of June, 1992, Prijedor SJB Chief Simo Drljaca reports to Zupljanin that detachment members had carried out arbitrary arrests, were abusing and robbing prisoners at Omarska camp, and had looted property during mopping-up operations; Volume 2, paragraph 421. In June 1992, Zupljanin also deployed the detachment to Kotor Varos at the request of the local Crisis Staff, and by the end of that month, reports of the detachment's involvement in looting and killing and raping non-Serbs in Kotor Varos reached Zupljanin; Volume 1, paragraph 451; Volume 2, paragraph 425. As late as August 1992, detachment members were still expelling Muslims; Volume 2, paragraph 397. Now, beyond his role in deploying the detachment, as I mentioned at the outset, Zupljanin also actively contributed to the common criminal purpose by ordering ARK policemen to co-operate with other Serb forces in carrying out a disarming operation in May and June 1992 as the Chamber found was instrumental - instrumental - to the removal of the non-Serb population; Volume 2, paragraph 500. The disarming operation facilitated attacks on non-Serbs by Serb forces. For example, in Prijedor, a largely successful drive at confiscating arms from the Muslim and Croat population, including legally owned hunting rifles and pistols, resulted in an essentially unopposed take-over that Serb forces exploited by laying waste to the non-Serb areas they attacked. The attacks caused the civilian population to flee their homes and hide in nearby towns, forests, and valleys, where they were hunted down and arrested; Volume 1, paragraph 658. In Prijedor, as in other ARK municipalities, arrests of non-Serbs were mass and indiscriminate. These arrests formed part of the pattern of conduct designed to rid the RS of its non-Serb population. The Chamber's finding that Zupljanin played a proactive part - a proactive part - in the mass arrest and detention of non-Serbs is a further reflection of the active conduct he engaged in in furtherance of the common criminal purpose. How did Zupljanin play a proactive role in the mass arrest and detention operation? Well, first he closely supervised that operation. Remember, Your Honours, Zupljanin had firsthand knowledge of the brutal mistreatment being inflicted on detainees at the Banja Luka CSB building, his Banja Luka CSB building, where it was common practice to openly beat and humiliate non-Serbs; Volume 1, paragraphs 166 and 201; Volume 2, paragraphs 415 and 503. Beyond that, Zupljanin visited Omarska camp and saw non-Serb detainees who looked miserable and undernourished, were foul-smelling and showed signs of abuse to which they had been subjected; Volume 2, paragraphs 424 and 508. Zupljanin also visited Manjaca camp where he saw detainees who had been deprived of the basic facilities to clean themselves, living in stables built for animals; Volume 1, paragraph 182; Volume 2, paragraph 506. And beyond what he observed directly, Zupljanin received reports about the unlawful detention, mistreatment, and murder of non-Serbs; Volume 2, paragraphs 418 to 423, 425 to 427, and 506 to 510. But, Your Honours, Zupljanin didn't just closely follow the events on the ground, he provided Stanisic, his fellow JCE member, with information on the breadth of the detention operation in the ARK, crimes being committed, and he also made recommendations on how the detention operation should be carried out. That's Volume 2, paragraphs 434 to 435. Zupljanin was so deeply involved in the operation, the detention operation, that he even facilitated the removal of detainees from the RS. For example, on the 29th of September, 1992, Zupljanin ordered the Prijedor police to escort buses transporting more than 1.500 non-Serbs from Trnopolje camp in Prijedor to Croatia; Volume 2, paragraph 511. In addition to the proactive role that Zupljanin played in mass arrest and detention of non-Serbs, in addition to his role in disarming non-Serbs, and in addition to his role in creating and deploying the special police detachment, there was more because Zupljanin also created a climate of impunity in the ARK that perpetuated the cycle of violence that was driving non-Serbs out of the RS. How did he create that climate of impunity? He did it through action and he did it through deliberate - deliberate - inaction. Zupljanin deliberately filed misleading criminal reports concerning the massacre at Koricanske Stijene and the killings outside Manjaca camp in order to shield the perpetrators from criminal prosecution; Volume 2, paragraph 519. Zupljanin also formed a sham commission to inspect detention camps and facilities in Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Bosanski Novi. This commission produced a report that the Defence had acknowledged, at paragraph 166 of Zupljanin's appeal brief, was a self-serving white-wash. Their words. By filing misleading criminal reports and forming a sham commission, Zupljanin acted, he acted to shield perpetrators. But as I said, the climate of impunity in the ARK was a product of acts as well as deliberate inaction, Zupljanin's acts and his deliberate inaction. Ultimately, what the Chamber saw and determined from the evidence was that Zupljanin's acts and his inaction were all born of a choice, a choice that had deadly and horrific consequences for non-Serbs, a choice that the Chamber refers to at paragraph 519 of Volume 2, a choice not to protect non-Serbs, a choice coming from a police chief of Zupljanin's stature that said to perpetrators, It's okay to terrorise non-Serbs because the cycle of violence needed to continue, a choice Zupljanin knew would force non-Serbs to leave the ARK municipalities and, in fact, the RS. Zupljanin's choice was all too apparent in April 1992 when he broadcasted in Banja Luka by saying that he couldn't guarantee the physical security and safety of non-Serbs and their property. Zupljanin may have said he couldn't protect non-Serbs and their property, but what he really meant was that he didn't want to protect non-Serbs and their property and therefore he wouldn't protect them. After all, Your Honours, ask yourselves, who was it in Banja Luka that Zupljanin didn't think he could protect non-Serbs from? Was it the red van group who were launching attacks from his CSB building and taking victims there to be beaten up? Was it them? Was it the SOS who terrorised non-Serbs and yet who Zupljanin found it appropriate to laud as being Serbian knights? Or was it the special police detachment which he created and set loose against the non-Serb population just a few weeks after his announcement? This isn't a case, Your Honours, as the Defence have mentioned in their sentencing submissions, where Zupljanin simply failed to act as promptly and as adequately as expected from an officer of the law; it's a case where he made the choice not to, deliberately, a deliberate choice not to do so in order to drive non-Serbs out of the ARK and the RS. Non-Serbs were terrorised in Banja Luka throughout 1992; Volume 1, paragraph 164; Volume 2, paragraphs 415 and 496. When they complained to Zupljanin about the abuses they were suffering, as a group of Muslim representatives did in mid-August 1992, they were terrorised even more by Zupljanin's policemen; Volume 2, paragraph 451, paragraph 497, and paragraph 499. Just as in Banja Luka in the days, weeks, and months that followed his April announcement that he couldn't protect non-Serbs, Zupljanin kept his word by failing to genuinely try and halt the crime wave targeted at non-Serbs across the ARK. He made his choice and he stuck to it. That choice was apparent from his failure to investigate and discipline members of his own special police detachment for their crimes in Banja Luka and beyond; Volume 2, paragraphs 462, 484, 504, and 505. Zupljanin's choice was also apparent in the utter disregard that he showed on separate occasions when he justified the horrible detention crimes in Omarska, Keraterm and in Teslic on the basis that there was a war going on; Volume 2, paragraph 423; Volume 1, paragraph 849. The Defence have referred to Teslic, but far from an illustration of his efforts to protect non-Serbs, his conduct in relation to Teslic demonstrates the choice that he made not to protect them so that they would leave the RS and the ARK. His choice was apparent when he denied Predrag Radulovic's request for a forensic team to exhume the Mice's group's non-Serb victims in Teslic. What did he say to Predrag Radulovic? He said it wasn't the right time for forensic examinations. There was no need for forensic examinations of these victims; Volume 2, paragraph 455. It wasn't the right time to investigate crimes against non-Serbs in Teslic, just like it wasn't the right time to investigate the killings in front of Manjaca camp or the massacre of non-Serbs at Koricanske Stijene, or thousands of other horrible crimes against non-Serbs. Now, meaningfully addressing these crimes, Your Honours, risks slowing the cycle of violence that was driving the expulsion campaign. It risked discouraging perpetrators from terrorising non-Serbs. And so Zupljanin chose not to take any meaningful action. He chose to broadcast his choice so that there be no doubt where he stood, so he broadcast it in Banja Luka. He chose to shield perpetrators. He chose to form a sham commission to inspect detention facilities. By his deliberate inaction, Zupljanin chose not to fulfil the most basic and the most obvious duty of a police officer: the duty to protect the civilian population. That choice encouraged perpetrators to continue committing crimes and it discouraged victims from remaining in the RS. In Banja Luka, where hundreds of non-Serbs were fleeing the municipality by the week following the Serb blockade, the Muslim community was shattered. They were shattered by Zupljanin's announcement that he couldn't protect them. They realised their safety was in great jeopardy; Volume 2, paragraph 450; Volume 2, paragraph 496. The impact across the ARK was no different. At paragraph 518 of Volume 2, the Chamber found that Zupljanin's failure to protect non-Serbs exacerbated their feeling of insecurity and strongly contributed to their flight out of the ARK municipalities. Now, Your Honours, it makes no difference that the Chamber relied on a duty from RS law when assessing Zupljanin's inaction. The purpose of a duty is to inform an individual of the conduct that is required of them in a given situation. In this case, Zupljanin knew he was under a duty to protect the civilian population. He made - as the Chamber found at paragraph 519 of Volume 2 - a decision not to fulfil that duty in order to discriminate against non-Serbs and force them to leave the ARK municipalities, and in doing so he furthered the common criminal purpose by his inaction. In these circumstances, where Zupljanin's deliberate failure to fulfil a duty he knew he was under furthered the common criminal purpose, it makes no difference that the duty relied upon was found in national law and the recent Appeals Chamber judgement in Butare confirms this; Butare appeals judgement, paragraph 2194. Zupljanin's also argued this afternoon that the duty must be based in criminal law. The Appeals Chamber has never limited omission liability in this way and that's reflected in the Butare appeal judgement as well, paragraph 2194. In the context of JCE liability, where the duty is based in -- whether the duty is based in criminal law is irrelevant, Your Honours, because JCE contributions needn't be criminal nor form part of the actus reus of the crime. This principle applies regardless of whether the contribution is an act or an omission. Therefore, Your Honours, since a contribution by omission needn't be criminal, it would make no sense to require that the duty on which that contribution is based to be one that entails a criminal sanction. And in any event, Your Honours, a police officer's failure to fulfil their official duty was criminalised in the RS. I refer Your Honours to the Prosecution's response brief at footnote 331. I want to turn now, Your Honours, to the first question that you've asked concerning Zupljanin's first ground of appeal, whether the Trial Chamber found Zupljanin responsible for failing to investigate crimes committed by police resubordinated to the military. Your Honours, in answering your question I need to begin with Zupljanin's duty to protect the civilian population. Resubordination was irrelevant to Zupljanin's exercise of that duty. It was irrelevant because Zupljanin's duty to protect the civilian population imposed on him an obligation to repress crime against civilian victims, irrespective of the status or affiliation of the perpetrator. Furthermore, Your Honours, this duty wasn't just about investigating crimes; it was about taking measures, preventive measures, to stop crime. Now, there's been reference today to paragraph 342 of Volume 2. The Chamber's observations in that paragraph don't address Zupljanin's duty to protect the civilian population. The focus of that paragraph is on whether resubordinated policemen were within the military or police chain of command. Those observations are relevant to Zupljanin's duty to exercise his duty as a superior to punish his subordinates. The Chamber was careful to distinguish that duty, his duty as a superior, from his duty to protect the civilian population. The Chamber properly relied on Zupljanin's duty as a superior because it reasonably established that he exercised authority over the policemen whom it found he failed to investigate and discipline. These policemen included members of the special police detachment, policemen involved in the mass arrest and detention operation, and SJB chiefs, like Simo Drljaca who participated in crimes against non-Serbs. By establishing Zupljanin's authority over these policemen, the Chamber clearly resolved that they weren't resubordinated to the military. None of the arguments that the Defence have made concerning resubordination undermine the Chamber's careful findings concerning Zupljanin's authority. I just want to offer a couple of examples to illustrate the Chamber's correct approach to the issue of Zupljanin's authority. First, the special police detachment. The Chamber established that Zupljanin created the detachment, deployed it. Crimes committed by the detachment in Kotor Varos and beyond were consistently reported to him and detachment members sought his intervention when they ran afoul of the law; that's volume 438 to 439 and 501 to 503. The Chamber, therefore, correctly concluded that Zupljanin exercised complete authority over the detachment and that he had the authority to punish its members. The second example that I want to refer to, Zupljanin's authority over policemen involved in the mass arrest and detention operation. The Defence have made specific arguments concerning Manjaca, Trnopolje, Keraterm and Omarska camps. Those are addressed in our response brief. What I'm going to focus on is the broader context that the Chamber relied upon in establishing that Zupljanin had the authority to investigate and discipline policemen involved in the mass arrest and detention operation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. Zupljanin's authority over the policemen involved in the arrest and detention operation was apparent from his comments at the 11th of July MUP collegium meeting, where he told Stanisic and the other participants that the army and the Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies were requesting that as many Muslims as possible be gathered and were "leaving these undefined camps up to the internal affairs organs." That's P160 which is discussed at Volume 2, paragraph 434. Zupljanin isn't talking about the resubordination of policemen to the military in this passage from P160; he's talking about MUP police -- MUP personnel, excuse me, operating detention camps because, as he himself acknowledges, camps were left up to the internal affairs organs. Zupljanin's authority is also plainly apparent from his 20th of July report to Stanisic, Exhibit P583, discussed at Volume 2, paragraph 435. In that report Zupljanin refers to the arrest of several thousands of Muslims and Croats, and he indicates that numerous active and reserve policemen were involved in securing the facilities in which these detainees were held. Zupljanin asks Stanisic to contact the authority organs and the VRS in order to "assume decisive position regarding the further status and treatment" of the detainees. Zupljanin also recommends that unlawfully detained non-Serbs be treated as hostages to be used in prisoners exchanges and that the responsibility of securing detention facilities be assumed by the VRS. Your Honours, Zupljanin's report to Stanisic reveals the MUP's deep involvement in and authority over detention facilities and camps in the ARK. Zupljanin demonstrates how invested he is in the detention operation by making recommendations on how certain issues should be resolved. As far as the military's concerned, Zupljanin's talking about collaboration with the VRS to resolve issues relating to the treatment of detainees. He's talking about shifting responsibility for guarding detainees to the VRS. He's certainly not suggesting that policemen working within detention facilities and camps have been resubordinated to the VRS. The Chamber also had the benefit of evidence showing that Zupljanin was asked for instructions as to how policemen should treat detainees. On the 17th of June, Sanski Most SJB chief complained about the number of detainees being held at his SJB and asked Zupljanin to "issue an order giving the SJB strict orders regarding the treatment of prisoners." That's P411.21, discussed at Volume 2, paragraph 418. There is nothing exceptional about the mass arrest and detention operation in Sanski Most. The request that Zupljanin received from the Sanski Most SJB chief is indicative, therefore, of his general authority over policemen involved in the mass arrest and detention operation. I want to turn, Your Honours, to the second question that you've asked regarding Zupljanin's first ground of appeal, whether the Trial Chamber erred in relying on Zupljanin's presence at the meeting at the Holiday Inn of the SDS Main and Executive Boards in assessing his intent. In our submission, Your Honours, the Chamber reasonably established that Zupljanin participated in the 14 February SDS meeting at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo. The Holiday Inn receipt that the Chamber relied on, Exhibit P1353.17, that bore Zupljanin's name that said he stayed at the Holiday Inn on the very day that the Main and Executive Board meeting was held at the hotel and that he left the next day was enough to establish Zupljanin's presence at the meeting and, of course, the intercept that the Chamber relied on supports that finding. We say that having properly established Zupljanin's presence at the meeting, it was appropriate for the Chamber to rely on that finding when establishing his shared intent for the common criminal purpose. At the 14 February meeting, Karadzic called for the implementation of the final stage of the Variant A and B instructions; Volume 2, paragraph 237. The Chamber found that these instructions were designed to prepare local Serb communities and their leaders to take over power in municipalities; Volume 2, paragraph 310. And beginning in Banja Luka and through his deployments of the special police detachment to other municipalities, Zupljanin played a key role in the take-over of municipalities; Volume 2, paragraphs 495 and 518. Zupljanin's presence at the 14th of February meeting, considered in conjunction with his subsequent conduct, demonstrates his knowledge and agreement with the common criminal purpose. That said, Your Honours, even if you were to find that the Chamber erred in relying on Zupljanin's presence at the 14th of February meeting, there would be no impact on the judgement. Mr. Gosnell miscasts the judgement when he suggests that this was a core finding on which the Chamber based its shared intent conclusion. The Chamber's conclusion that Zupljanin shared the common criminal purpose is entirely supported by numerous other factors that it relied upon, including Zupljanin's close ties with the SDS and role in organising the Banja Luka blockade; Volume 2, paragraphs 495 and 519. Zupljanin's role in implementing discriminatory policies that purged non-Serbs from the police force in the ARK; Volume 2, paragraphs 44, 366, 377 to 382 and 519. His efforts to foster the climate of impunity that reigned in Banja Luka after the April blockade and his promotion of that climate of impunity across the ARK. Zupljanin's orders to disarm non-Serbs as they were being attacked in Banja Luka and just before they were attacked in other ARK municipalities. The proactive role that Zupljanin played in the mass arrest and detention operation across the ARK. His order on the 31st of July in the midst of the expulsion campaign, in which he referred to large numbers of Muslims and Croats leaving the ARK and ordered his subordinates to steal their money; Volume 2, paragraphs 490 and 526, and his creation of the special police detachment, his immediate and continued deployment of that unit, and his repeated failure to discipline the unit even as he learned of its members' persistent involvement in crimes against non-Serbs, all of these factors overwhelmingly support the Chamber's conclusion that Zupljanin shared the common criminal purpose at least as of the start of April 1992. Let me turn, Your Honours, to the question you've asked concerning Zupljanin's third ground of appeal, whether the Trial Chamber made the required finding that the perpetrators of the killing of 20 detainees during their transport from Betonirka detention facility in Sanski Most to Manjaca detention camp on 7 July 1992 possessed the required intent for extermination and, if not, whether the absence of such a finding would invalidate the Trial Chamber's conclusion. Your Honours, the Chamber made the required finding to establish the perpetrators' intent for extermination. Before reaching its conclusion on whether this incident amounted to extermination, the Chamber carefully considered the underlying evidence at paragraph 189 of volume 1, stressing the number of detainees that had been transported in the truck in which the victims perished. There were around 64 non-Serb prisoners in total in that truck. The Chamber also placed emphasis on the manner in which all of the prisoners had been transported. The prisoners were packed like sardines into the truck in which they were transported without enough air to breathe. The Chamber also took note of the particular vulnerability of some of the prisoners. It observed that some of those who perished were old and in poor health. Having considered all of these circumstances, the Chamber concluded that the requirements of extermination were satisfied at paragraph 219 of volume 1. It's implicit in this conclusion, we say, Your Honours, that the Chamber applied the correct mens rea test; in other words, that the Chamber satisfied itself that the perpetrators had the intention to subject a large number of people to conditions of living that would lead to their deaths. It's implicit that this is the test the Chamber applied because this is the mens rea standard that the Chamber stated at paragraph 45 of volume 1 needed to be met for extermination to be established. In any event, Your Honours, if you come to the view that the Chamber applied an incorrect mens rea standard for extermination, the only reasonable conclusion is that the perpetrators possessed the required intent. The Defence's attempt this afternoon to distance the police from this particular incident on the basis of a few selective pieces of evidence doesn't show error in the Chamber's finding that the police, in fact, played a central role in the deaths of these non-Serb prisoners. Your Honours, before I conclude my submissions, I'm going to turn to address the Defence's argument the Chamber's JCE 3 findings contradict its determination concerning Zupljanin's shared intent for forcible transfer and deportation. Defence is trying to introduce confusion, Your Honours, where there simply is none. First, the JCE 3 crimes don't exhaustively encompass the coercive acts through which non-Serbs were induced to flee. Consider, for example, Zupljanin's announcement in Banja Luka that he couldn't protect non-Serbs and the impact that this had on the Muslim community. Already spoken about that. This is an example of conduct that was not a JCE 3 crime, but yet added to the threatened atmosphere that was driving non-Serbs out of the RS. Second, the exclusion of the JCE 3 crimes from the scope of the common criminal purpose is irrelevant to the Chamber's conclusion that Zupljanin shared the intent for forcible transfer and deportation. To reach that conclusion that -- that conclusion about shared intent, all the Chamber needed to do was to establish that Zupljanin intended that displacement be forced; in other words, that the victims be given no choice in their displacement. This is exactly what the Chamber did. I've already spoken about the findings that underlie its shared intent conclusion. Those findings clearly show that Zupljanin intended forcible transfer and deportation and that he shared that intent with his fellow JCE members. Third and final point that I want to make is that according to the Appeals Chamber, even if an accused is acquitted of coercive acts through which forcible transfer and deportation is achieved, that wouldn't be a problem. That's what happened in Krajisnik when he was acquitted of the expanded crimes and yet his conviction for forcible transfer and deportation was unaffected. Your Honours, those are my submissions. I'll turn the podium over to Ms. Baig unless you have any questions for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I explained in more detail in my response to Stanisic's arguments this morning, a reasonable observer properly informed with knowledge of all the relevant circumstances would view the Stanisic and Zupljanin trial as fairly decided by an impartial Bench with full respect for the rights of the accused. The circumstances of this case do not give rise to an apprehension of bias on the part of Judge Harhoff. His e-mail must be interpreted in light of its informal nature and context. My learned colleague this morning took issue with the e-mail's discussion of intent in relation to modes of liability, but again, Your Honours, I have to emphasise that this is not a legal document. It is an informal e-mail to friends. The attempt to point fault at particular statements within that document serves no purpose. My learned colleague's entire argument rests on the assumption that Judge Harhoff was only discussing one specific mode of liability, that is, JCE 1, responsibility. He tested each and every statement against the legal standard for JCE 1. But that, with the greatest of respect, is a false premise. In his e-mail, Judge Harhoff is discussing modes of liability in a very holistic way. He indicates in the e-mail that he's discussing command responsibility, JCE 1; extended JCE 3; and aiding and abetting. The cases and media articles that he's discussing, as well as his references to these other modes, makes it clear. In any event, Your Honours, even if Judge Harhoff made errors in his presentation of the mental elements in relation to the modes, where does that take us? It wouldn't show bias. It would show a misunderstanding of the law. Judges, even in the judgements, even in their formal judicial writing, make errors of law. This is one of the main purposes of the entire appellate process. So whether it's a disagreement about the law, as I said this morning, or a misunderstanding about the law, even if that misunderstanding posits a lower mens rea standard, it still does not show bias. In any event, Your Honours, the trial judgement confirms that the correct interpretation of the e-mail is one that does not show any appearance of bias. For the reasons I've set out this morning, the fairness of the trial is not affected by the Seselj majority decision. In relation to your question, the Prosecution's position is that a finding of an appearance of bias would lead to the invalidation of the conviction, but this does not and cannot mean an acquittal. It would have to mean either a trial-level remand or reconsideration or, as Zupljanin has suggested, a curing review by the Appeals Chamber itself. Unless Your Honours have questions, that concludes the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions. So we have a break now which, with your indulgence, we have reduced from 25 minutes to 20 minutes. It's five to 4.00, so we'll reconvene at 20 minutes from now. Thank you. Quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Counsel for Mr. Zupljanin, you have 20 minutes, starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Again, good afternoon, Your Honours. I will respond very briefly to the Prosecution's submissions at pages 137 and 138 of today's hearing concerning Your Honours' question on the third ground of Zupljanin's appeal. Your Honours, in our submission, the Prosecution failed to adequately address the main focus of the question; instead, they tried to refute the Defence arguments concerning lack of mens rea on the perpetrators' part or, indeed, on the insufficient evidence on the police involvement, notably without making a single reference to evidence on the record to the contrary concerning the latter, and by that latter I mean the police involvement in the incident. And the reason for that, Your Honour, is simple: No such evidence exists and the Defence submissions provide a comprehensive and clear response to the question asked. My learned colleague Mr. Gosnell will address the remaining part of the OTP response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the Defence never suggested that the Trial Chamber did not rely on acts as well as omissions in coming to its conclusion about joint criminal enterprise, but I do think the extent to which omissions were relied on by the Trial Chamber are quite fairly set out in the appeal brief at paragraphs 61 and 62. And what you'll see, if you look at those two paragraphs where the elements that were relied on by the Trial Chamber are set out, is that about half of what the Trial Chamber relies on is omissions and the question that Your Honours are faced with in the absence of particularised reasons is: If the Trial Chamber made an error in respect of omissions, is it the case that the Trial Chamber would have reached the same conclusions in respect of mens rea and actus reus if it were relying only on the acts that it mentions. And there's nothing in the judgement that suggests that that's the case. The second point that I wish to address amongst the matters that were raised by the Prosecution is the ostensible duty under which Mr. Zupljanin was obliged, and this is set out, according to the Prosecution, at footnote 331 of their response brief, in which there is a reference to a law which indicates that -- a criminal law which indicates that a public official can be found guilty of, inter alia, failing to perform their official duties. Obviously, the tenor of the Prosecution's remarks in general was that Mr. Zupljanin could and should be deemed to have committed an omission, a significant omission, that could be taken into account in respect of any crime against any civilian in Bosnia or within his jurisdiction, geographic jurisdiction, at this particular time. Now, think about the breadth of that. In fact, the breadth of that is incorporated already in paragraph 520 of Volume 2 of the trial judgement, where the Trial Chamber says that it considered Zupljanin's failure to protect the non-Serb population. So the breadth of that duty, I suggest, is so extremely wide that it would mean that any inaction in terms of a crime being committed and not being stopped or the person being arrested could be treated as a legally significant omission. If you accept that, Your Honours, that means that you're treating any inaction, punitive inaction, in just the same way as an action. It's being attributed the same amount of significance in terms of inferring actus reus and mens rea. Now, why is that so dangerous in the particular circumstances that faced Mr. Zupljanin? Well, I draw Your Honours' attention to paragraph 29 of the reply brief, where there's the testimony of General Lisica, describing the situation as it existed at the time during periods of conflict. And what he says -- and remember, he is a military man, he is a general; he's not a police person trying to shift responsibility on to someone else. And he says: "All police forces were subordinated to the commander of the zone of responsibility that I had as commander of Tactical Group 3 or commander of Operative Group Doboj ..." and then he goes on to explain further. And there the record is replete with evidence of this kind, Your Honours. This is why it is so, I suggest, dangerous and reckless to use language like "Zupljanin's SPD committed crimes in, for example, Kotor Varos," and then assume that those crimes or the failure to stop them, the failure to them, must be the responsibility of Mr. Zupljanin. On the contrary, Your Honours, the evidence was that when the SP -- and this the Chamber did not, of course, decide this in the end. But when the SPD went into a combat-style operation, including, for example, in Kotor Varos, it was potentially -- or the evidence raised the possibility that they were resubordinated to the military with all that that entailed, Your Honours. Now, I'm not here to convince you one way or the other as to whether the resubordination existed, nor to convince you as to the implications of that resubordination. I'm only here to draw your attention to the fact that the Trial Chamber recognised this as an important issue, recognised that resubordination itself was complicated enough that it could not decide who had responsibility to prosecute and investigate crimes when that resubordination occurred, and then proceeded not to make any findings about whether or not, for example, when the SPD was sent to Donji Vakuf and crimes were committed, should those crimes be imputed to Mr. Zupljanin in one way or another? The Trial Chamber did that. They imputed that to him. They ascribed responsibility for those acts to him time and again, whether it was discussing his knowledge of those crimes, whether it was discussing his potential ability to investigate those crimes or to prosecute those crimes. And yet, no discussion, reasons, addressing the very real issue as to whether or not that formation, the SPD, was at the time of those crimes actually under his jurisdiction, because that's the issue: Was it under his jurisdiction at the time of those crimes? It's not enough to just sweep it all in and say, by establishment, as the Chamber found, the SPD was part of the police. Yes, that's what they found, that's true. But there was an additional finding required to draw a connection between Mr. Zupljanin's alleged inaction in respect of specific crimes and those crimes themselves. Your Honours, I think it's fitting to put on the screen 1D198 because a certain picture was painted of Mr. Zupljanin before Your Honours and we say that we have addressed all of the factual issues that were raised by my learned friend opposite in our appeal brief, but there's certainly not time in 20 minutes to address all those factual matters. But I think it's fitting - I'm not sure if it's on the screen - it's fitting to end, discussing Mr. Zupljanin's person and character, with a report that was written by Mr. Zupljanin. And this is the work-plan that he prepared and signed, dated the 25th of May, 1992, and it's entitled: "Operative work-plan for solving robberies, terrorism, extortion, et cetera, which have escalated in the territory of the Banja Luka SJB since the beginning of April." And what he does in this report, Your Honours, is forthrightly describe crimes that are taking place, identify the SOS as the formation to which individuals suspected of crimes are affiliated, and then he describes a series of actions that should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, we should wait until we have the English translation on the screen. We have both sides in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then he describes the actions that should be taken. I do believe there is an English translation somewhere, Your Honours, but I'll just proceed, push through this even without the English translation, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He identifies individuals by name. He says that these people should be arrested or investigated. I'm reliably informed that on page 3, in the middle of the page, there's a list of individuals, one of whom is somebody identified as AKA Gavrin, who apparently during the trial was identified as the driver of the notorious red van which did indeed commit certain acts, criminal acts, in Banja Luka. The point is that Mr. Zupljanin actually did make efforts to conduct investigations, particularly close to home where he was able to do it. If we could now just look at page 4, and I believe that this may give Your Honours just a little sense of the situation that was practically facing Mr. Zupljanin. And it may seem strange viewed from our comfortable perspective, but if we try and put ourselves into the atmosphere reflected in these paragraphs, it may be helpful. What we see here is Mr. Zupljanin saying that many of those suspects were mobilised by the JNA and their arrests should be carried out by members of the special police detachment together with the military police, et cetera. "We need to have a prior agreement with the regular and military courts in keeping all of the arrested persons in detention to prevent organised resistance. As long as the military prosecution office and the military court are in the process of being established, the plan cannot be implemented because most of the offenders are conscripts and members of the former TO which is why civilian courts and prosecutors refuse to conduct these proceedings." My learned friend opposite flippantly said: Oh, well, who was committing these crimes if not the police? Your Honours, there were thousands, tens of thousands, more than 150.000 people mobilised at this time or at various times in Bosnia. Those individuals were not subject to Mr. Zupljanin's jurisdiction, and that was certainly the position that was argued at trial and not decided - not decided - Your Honours, by the Trial Chamber. Now, I would like to just turn in my closing minutes to one issue in respect of the bias issue and that was the question of whether, well, isn't this merely an expression in the e-mail of a genuine misunderstanding of the law and that can happen. Judges can misunderstand the law, lawyers can misunderstand the law, and so there's nothing new here. Well, Your Honours, I commend to you again the Hoekstra decision from Scotland which commends that bias comes in many forms. It's not just about a financial interest or an association with a party; it can even arise merely from a judge's predisposition against applying a particular legal rule or principle that in practice in the case will be of benefit to the accused. That was position in the Hoekstra case. That is precisely the position also in respect of Mr. Zupljanin. Leaving aside, Your Honours, whether in and of itself it indicates that there was an error in the judgement, leaving that aside, nonetheless a predisposition, a tone, a hostility towards the application of that principle as strong as Your Honours see, that predisposition is too strong to believe that there would be anything but a lack of impartiality in the determination of the charges against Mr. Zupljanin. Your Honours, thank you for your patience and forebearance. Those are my remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I turn to the Prosecution. You have 40 minutes to present your case on your appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Hello again. I just want to, for the record, indicate to Your Honours that we've made a slight personnel shift. Instead of Ms. Harbour after the break, we now have Ms. Sarah Finnin, one of our colleagues from the Prosecution. Your Honours, before I turn to Ground 1 concerning the error in sentence, there's one small issue that I'd like to clarify in relation to Ground 2 of the Prosecution appeal and that concerns cumulative convictions. One of the issues that's disputed between the parties in relation to Ground 2 concerns the elements of persecution. I only wish to put on the record the Prosecution's position in relation to an issue raised in the Butare appeals judgement that was delivered on Monday. In the Butare appeals judgement, the ICTR Appeals Chamber finds that the ICTR has no jurisdiction to adjudicate persecution based on ethnic grounds. I just want to point out that the ICTY jurisdiction is not limited in this way, that the reasoning of the Butare appeals judgement is an ICTR-specific reasoning. As Your Honours know, the ICTY Appeals Chamber has consistently confirmed convictions for persecutions based on ethnic grounds. In Djordjevic, for example, the Appeals Chamber entered convictions for persecution on an ethnic basis, and the appeals judgement in Popovic, Kordic, Stakic, Krnojelac, Kvocka also accept persecution on ethnic grounds. There would be no cogent reasons to depart from the established ICTY Appeals Chamber jurisprudence in this regard, and certainly the ICTR-specific reasons in Butare concerning the chapeau of the ICTR provision for crimes against humanity are not cogent in relation to the established ICTY jurisdiction. In any event, Your Honours, in this case, as in so many other ICTY cases, the Trial Chamber is using the term "ethnic group" as being essentially synonymous with both a political and religious affiliation. Muslims, of course, are associated with a political party, the SDA; the Croats with the HDZ political party; and the JCE members. One of the ways that they were forcibly removing and otherwise targeting the non-Serb population was through destruction of religious buildings. So ethnicity in this sense is an umbrella term that encompasses both political and religious discriminatory grounds. Turning to Ground 1 concerning sentence. Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin were convicted of horrendous crimes affecting the lives of over 100.000 victims. The Trial Chamber found that they worked together with other leading Bosnian Serbs to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territory of the planned Serbian state through the commission of persecutory forcible displacement crimes. As a direct result of their sinister collaboration, more than 100.000 people were forcibly displaced from their homes and villages in the ARK and Stanisic was responsible for at least an additional 30.000 displacements from other Republika Srpska municipalities. This expulsion campaign resulted in the murder of more than 2.300 non-Serbs, over 1.600 in the ARK municipalities alone. Thousands more, as you've heard referred to today, were subjected to inhumane treatment in detention facilities, where rape, torture, other forms of sexual assault and beatings were commonplace. The appropriate sentence for this level, the scale of crimes that you see in this case, is life imprisonment. Based on previous case law, the Prosecution has asked for an increase to at least 30 to 40 years of imprisonment because anything else is grossly inadequate. The 22-year sentences imposed by the Trial Chamber demonstrate an abuse of sentencing discretion. It simply does not accord with the gravity of the offences for which they were convicted or the form and degree of their participation. I'm going to begin my submissions by demonstrating that their sentences are inconsistent with ICTY sentencing practice. I'll then draw on some key reasons why their sentences should be higher.
