And finally, I will address the effect that these overly lenient sentences have because they send the message that senior leaders, like Stanisic and Zupljanin, are less culpable than the low-level thugs used to carry out their criminal plan. Let me begin, Your Honours, by taking you to three cases decided by this Tribunal concerning individual killing incidents that form part of the convictions in this case. In doing so, Your Honours, the Prosecution, of course, accepts that each sentence must be crafted to suit the individual circumstances of the case, but where the crimes are not just similar but identical, this is a measure upon which the adequacy of a sentence can be tested. So one of the very serious killing incidents for which Stanisic and Zupljanin were both convicted was the Koricanske Stijene massacre of between 150 and 200 Muslim civilians on the 21st of August, 1992. Darko Mrdja, a member of the Prijedor civilian police intervention squad, the PIP, pled guilty to this same incident before an ICTY Trial Chamber, and he received a sentence of 17 years of imprisonment. Mrdja was a direct hierarchical subordinate of both Stanisic and Zupljanin. For one incident on one day in one municipality, a low-level subordinate participant, after a guilty plea, he received a sentence of 17 years of imprisonment. Mitar Vasiljevic, he was convicted of aiding and abetting the murder of five unarmed men at the Drina River bank in Visegrad. He was not the shooter; he was an accessory. And you'll remember that the Appeals Chamber imposed a sentence of 15 years of imprisonment. Again, these murders form part of Stanisic's conviction. One incident involving five deaths, one day, one municipality, a low-level accessory who did not share any common criminal purpose and did not personally kill anyone, he received a sentence of 15 years of imprisonment. And Sredoje Lukic, who was an active-duty officer in the Visegrad police force, he was convicted of aiding and abetting the incidents on Pionirska Street, most notably the fire in which 53 victims were murdered, and the Appeals Chamber imposed a sentence of 27 years. One day in one municipality, a subordinate police officer, a sentence of 27 years was found by the Appeals Chamber to be the appropriate punishment for aiding and abetting. So Stanisic, despite being convicted of these same murders, plus more than 2.000 additional murders, plus forcible displacement of more than 130.000 people, received five years less than this low-level subordinate police officer who was found to be aiding and abetting. These three cases show that participation in even one incident of multiple murder warrants a significant sentence of 15 to 27 years, even as a subordinate, even as an accessory, and even after a guilty plea. Sredoje's cousin, Milan Lukic, again a member of the reserve police force in Visegrad and a local paramilitary, he was also convicted of the Drina River incident and the Pionirska Street murders, as well as some other crimes in Visegrad. His sentence of life imprisonment for crimes in just one municipality was upheld on appeal. Other principal perpetrators whose multiple crimes were largely encompassed by Stanisic's conviction also received very significant sentences. For example, Goran Jelesic and Ranko Cesic received sentences of 40 and 18 years after guilty pleas for crimes in Brcko. Let me take you to three of the ICTY's camp cases. In the Kvocka case, the police officers involved in the running of the Omarska camp received sentences ranging from five to 20 years of imprisonment. Zoran Zigic, another reserve police officer who visited the camp in order to abuse and murder detainees, received a 25-year sentence, affirmed on appeal. Both Stanisic and Zupljanin were convicted of crimes perpetrated at this camp, broadly including the crimes for which their subordinates were found criminally responsible in the Kvocka case. One camp, one municipality, smaller number of specific incidents, and we see sentences approved by the Appeals Chamber of up to 25 years. Susica camp in Vlasenica municipality, Dragan Nikolic pled guilty and was sentenced to 20 years for the terrible crimes there. Stanisic's conviction specifically includes six of Nikolic's nine specific murders, and there's substantial overlap with the rest of the crimes. The Nikolic sentencing Chamber made clear that but for his guilty plea, his convictions would have warranted a life sentence. But again, this is only a tiny fraction of the convictions in this case. One camp, compared to more than 50 across Republika Srpska; one municipality compared to 20; nine murders compared to more than 2.000. And Keraterm camp, the police officer who ran that camp, Dusko Sikirica, received a 15-year sentence after a guilty plea and he was not convicted for any participation in the notorious murder incident involving 128 detainees in the Room 3 massacre, which does form part of both Stanisic and Zupljanin's conviction. Once again, one camp in one municipality, a significantly more limited criminal conviction, and still a very significant sentence. It's these cases that crystallise the error in Stanisic and Zupljanin's 22-year sentences and they explain why the Prosecution says that 22 years is manifestly inadequate, because the scope of Stanisic and Zupljanin's criminality is far greater than any of the ICTY cases that I've just mentioned. Their responsibility extends far beyond the sum of these parts, and for this reason their sentences should be much higher. So I'd like to elaborate on that to draw out five reasons why Stanisic and Zupljanin's criminal responsibility is more grave and thus more deserving of a higher sentence. The first four of these reasons are quantitative. In short, that they deserve a higher sentence because the magnitude of their crimes is so much greater than the single incident or camp cases, and the final reason is qualitative, that they deserve higher sentences because the nature of their criminal responsibility is more grave. So reason one, the most significant distinction is that Stanisic and Zupljanin were also convicted for forcibly displacing non-Serbs from the RS, from the Serb-claimed territory. Persecutory deportation and forcible transfer were not a component of the three murder cases or the three camp cases that I've just discussed. Zupljanin was found to be criminally responsible for the forcible displacement of more than 100.000 non-Serbs from the ARK municipalities, and Stanisic, who was higher up the chain of command and responsible for a larger geographic area, he was convicted of more than 130.000 forcible displacements. Across the RS, Serb-claimed municipalities were taken over often by initial shelling and infantry attacks directed at non-Serb parts of the village, followed by operations during which civilians were killed, their homes destroyed, civilians intimidated and forced to flee. Stanisic and Zupljanin worked closely with other Bosnian Serb civilian and military authorities and the police played an integral role in these expulsions. The Krajisnik Appeals Chamber has qualified persecutory deportation and forcible transfer as being among the most severe crimes known to humankind, and that's at paragraph 813 of the Krajisnik appeal judgement. Your Honours, when victims of the most severe crimes known to humankind are being measured in six figures, this must necessarily warrant a very significant sentence. Twenty-two years is simply not enough. Reason two, Stanisic and Zupljanin deserve a higher sentence because they were responsible for not one but many killing incidents. Over a period of nine months, Stanisic and Zupljanin engaged in conduct that resulted in the killing of more than 2.300 non-Serbs and over 1.600 in the ARK alone. Zupljanin was also convicted of extermination as a crime against humanity. The single killing incidents involving Mrdja, Vasiljevic, and Lukic, involving five to 150 victims, were only a small fraction of their convictions. When taking over towns, Serb forces, including the police, used overwhelming force, causing the death of many civilians. During and after take-overs, MUP forces exerted pressure on non-Serbs to leave, including through murder and mass murder. Those who were arrested or otherwise detained were at particular risk of being killed. Non-Serb detainees were frequently beaten to death, including during interrogations. Approximately 100 were murdered in Omarska through beating, execution, and asphyxiation. Twenty-six detainees were executed by Serb police, including members of Zupljanin's special police detachment, at the Kotor Varos medical centre. In Ljubija football stadium, Serb forces killed 60 non-Serbs. A policeman beheaded a detainee there. Sentences of 22 years do not and cannot properly reflect the large scale of murders in this case. Now, the fact that their convictions are pursuant to JCE 3 is, of course, relevant to their criminal responsibility for killings, but keep in mind, Your Honours, that all forms of JCE are classified as forms of commission. The accused intended and pursued a criminal goal, accepting the risk that murder - and for Zupljanin extermination - and the other JCE crimes were the natural and foreseeable consequence. The Babic appeals judgement has confirmed that guilt is not lessened by a JCE 3 conviction, paragraph 26 and 27. And I would point out here, Your Honours, that Vasiljevic and Sredoje Lukic were sentenced to 15 and 27 years for aiding and abetting the principal perpetrators of single killing incidents involving five and 53 victims. The scale of their criminal responsibility for the murder of 1.600 or more than 2.300 victims and Zupljanin's additional conviction for extermination must necessarily warrant a longer sentence. It must warrant a sentence greater than the perpetrators or accessories involved in the murders of only a tiny fraction of this number. Reason three, Your Honours, they deserve higher sentences because they were responsible for not just one but many camps and the crimes committed there. Stanisic and Zupljanin were convicted for crimes at 21 detention facilities in the ARK and Stanisic for a total of more than 50 in the RS. In Prijedor alone, the Trial Chamber found that over 11.000 non-Serbs were detained. Victims were mistreated in these centres across the region, Omarska, Keraterm, Susica, Manjaca, Luka, but also at smaller detention facilities like the police stations, including at Zupljanin's own CSB building in Banja Luka. The Trial Chamber found that the police were deeply involved in this unlawful detention, horrific conditions of confinement, murder, torture, cruel treatment, sadistic abuse, and sexual violence. Principal perpetrators in these camps received sentences of up to 25 years. Most of these facilities were established, run, or guarded by the police force under Stanisic and Zupljanin's command. They had the power to put an end to this horrific mistreatment and instead they continued to devote police resources to these camps. The fate of the detainees was in their hands, yet their sentences are similar to or lower than the principal perpetrators in these camps, sometimes their own subordinates. Their responsibility for a network of camps across the ARK and the RS demands a significantly higher sentence. Reason four, the brutal forms of sexual violence for which Stanisic and Zupljanin have been found to be criminally responsible also demand longer sentences. Omarska's female detainees were frequently called out by camp guards to be raped and sexually assaulted. The guards on Mlado Radic's shift were described as being the worst and he was sentenced by the ICTY to 20 years of imprisonment in the Kvocka case. At the Celopek Dom in Zvornik, again guarded by reserve police, prisoners were subjected to awful conditions of confinement, beatings, and murders. Paramilitaries who were let in by the police forced fathers and sons to rape each other. They cut off body parts of prisoners, a penis, an ear, and they forced other prisoners to eat them. At the SJB building in Kotor Varos, policemen forced male and female detainees to perform sexual acts on each other in front of a cheering crowd, including police and military onlookers. Members of Zupljanin's special police department forced two male detainees to perform oral sexual on each other while subjecting them to ethnic slurs. At the sawmill, Zupljanin's detachment raped detainees. Sexual violence of this cruelty - rapes, forced rapes by family members, public rapes, sexual mutilation, sexual cannibalism - deserves a very high sentence. Twenty-two years is simply too low. Before I move on, I just want to mention that I've not tried to paint an exhaustive picture of their criminal convictions. In addition to the crimes that I've mentioned, Stanisic and Zupljanin were also convicted of persecution through plunder, wanton destruction of buildings -- sorry, of towns and villages, including religious and cultural buildings, the imposition of restrictive and discriminatory measures. And Zupljanin was found guilty of ordering his police to appropriate property of non-Serbs. My point is quite a simple one: Stanisic and Zupljanin have been found guilty of so much more than a single incident or single camp perpetrators. This, in and of itself, explains why they deserve a much higher sentence. Reason five, Your Honour, the qualitative distinction. They also deserve a higher sentence because their actions enabled the low-level perpetrators. The JCE members in this case created the situation in which the crimes of the low-level perpetrators were allowed to take place on a massive scale. Stanisic and Zupljanin and the other JCE members set the stage for these crimes. They are qualitatively more responsible than the low-level thugs who took up their invitation. Stanisic and Zupljanin and their fellow JCE members used the forces under their control to commit ethnic cleansing. They shared and significantly contributed to the criminal goal of permanently removing Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territory of the planned Serbian state through the commission of discriminatory forcible displacement crimes. Instead of directing the police and the armed forces under their control to ensure the safety of the population, they turned these forces against the population on a discriminatory basis. In doing so, they created an atmosphere of impunity, where systematic crimes against non-Serbs were not only tolerated but officially pursued. This holds particularly true for Stanisic and Zupljanin who controlled the police. The civilian police operated on a discriminatory basis, spending their resources, following up on petty crimes against Serb interests, while turning a blind eye towards far more serious crimes against non-Serbs, all the while participating directly in crimes themselves. Stanisic set the priorities for the police force. He made it clear early on that crimes against Serbs were the only priority. He acted accordingly, continuing to assign police resources to pursue ethnic cleansing and take-overs and illegal detention camps, all the while ignoring the widespread and systematic crimes against non-Serbs committed by the police under his command, including crimes involving his own special police platoon. Zupljanin shared and implemented these priorities. He announced that he would not protect the Muslims of Banja Luka. He took no steps to hold perpetrators accountable, including members of his own special police detachment. He shielded perpetrators from criminal prosecution. He allowed non-Serbs to be brutally mistreated at his headquarters at the Banja Luka CSB. He ordered policemen to steal money from non-Serbs. Together, Stanisic and Zupljanin created an atmosphere of impunity. Crimes were committed by the police or people acting in co-operation with the police. Perpetrators were encouraged and protected by their superiors and the other leaders who were using them to commit crimes. They knew that the police, led by Stanisic and Zupljanin, would never arrest them. The crimes in this case would not and could not have happened without the involvement of the police leadership, that is, without Stanisic and Zupljanin. This is why the criminal responsibility of Stanisic and Zupljanin encompasses and eclipses that of the individual principal perpetrators. As members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, the JCE that set the stage for massive atrocity crimes, Stanisic and Zupljanin should have received considerably higher sentences. The sentences in this case do not properly reflect their role in creating the conditions in which so many crimes were purposefully committed or were a foreseeable possibility of their actions, not just in a single incident, not just in a single camp, not in a single day or in a single municipality. But again and again and again -- THE APPELLANT ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] I apologise, we are not receiving interpretation. I apologise, we are not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you still not receiving interpretation? Yes, it seems that he is not. THE APPELLANT ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] We are not receiving anything. We cannot hear the Prosecutor. Can you hear interpretation now? Okay. Then we can proceed. THE APPELLANT ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you had no problem? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask whether I need to go back at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would if I were you. You have the transcript in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would go back to one or two sentences because I suppose that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Okay. The sentences in this case do not properly reflect their role in creating the conditions in which so many crimes were purposefully committed or were a foreseeable possibility of their actions, not just in a single incident, not just in a single camp, not in a single day or in a single municipality, but again and again and again, across many municipalities over many months. So in addition to their crimes being quantitatively greater, they're qualitatively different role warrants sentences much higher than 22 years. In conclusion, Your Honours, the 22-year sentences are manifestly inadequate. The Trial Chamber erred in setting unreasonable sentences outside of the boundaries of their sentencing discretion. The 22-year sentences puts Stanisic and Zupljanin's criminal responsibility in the same range as the low-level perpetrators who committed one or another of the well over 100.000 crimes for which they were convicted. Their sentences are more lenient than some of their direct subordinates in relation to exactly the same crimes, that is, more lenient than the tools that they and their fellow JCE members used to commit the crimes. This is a clear error. Their sentences send the wrong message, the message that the principal perpetrators are more criminally responsible than the high-level leaders, and this is an error. It's not the message of international criminal law. International crimes, such as those for which Stanisic and Zupljanin have been convicted, cannot usually happen on such a massive scale without the involvement of the high-level governmental and military authorities. It's only when the state apparatus turns against the population that such crimes become possible. It's only by turning the police into perpetrators instead of protectors that such crimes can take place. And this is what Stanisic and Zupljanin did and this is what they must be punished for. In Celebici, the Appeals Chamber wisely warned that public confidence in the integrity of the administration of criminal justice requires consistency in punishment. It stated that in cases involving similar factual circumstances and similar convictions, there should be no substantial disparity in sentence, and that's Celebici appeals judgement of 20 February 2001, at paragraphs 756 and 758. But in this case there's no justification as to how or why Stanisic and Zupljanin's sentences are so out of proportion to or more lenient than the low-level perpetrators and accessories who committed their crimes in the execution of Stanisic and Zupljanin's criminal plan. The appropriate sentences for leadership perpetration through a JCE, which pursues and enables widespread and systematic crimes against humanity, must be higher than for the thugs responsible for individual particular criminal incidents. At trial the Prosecution asked for life sentences. At the very least, the sentences should not be less than those imposed in the related leadership cases of Brdjanin and Stakic. Anything less sends the wrong message. The Prosecution asks this Appeals Chamber to correct the Trial Chamber's error. The Prosecution asks you to raise the sentences of both Stanisic and Zupljanin to properly reflect their leadership role for the horrific crimes for which they've been found criminally responsible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baig. Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Bourgon, you have 20 minutes starting from now, and it's seven minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hope to take less than the 20 minutes allotted to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do we.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- for response. Mr. President, let me begin by addressing Ground 2 raised by the Prosecution. In respect of Ground 2, which is very technical in nature, as to whether cumulative convictions are allowed for persecution and other crimes for humanity, we simply refer the Appeals Chamber to our response brief in paragraphs 11 to 176. We maintain that in our view the jurisprudence remains unresolved or unsettled in respect of these type of cumulative convictions, and that if it is not unresolved or unsettled, then there are cogent reasons to depart based on fairness to the accused and based on consideration. Only very distinct crimes may justify multiple convictions. Moving on to the most important issue which is sentencing. The Prosecution focused on two key words: quantitative and qualitative. Basically, the Prosecution says that because the crimes are of such a large scale, they are more responsible and they deserve a larger sentence. That is, for the most part, what we hear today, and because the Prosecution basically repeating its argument in its brief, our response will be rather short. What matters in terms of a crime is not only the scale of the crimes or the size of the crimes. Gravity is, first and foremost, a matter of the contribution of the accused to the crime. What did he do and how did he contribute to the crime? And this is not necessarily proportional with the rank of the accused, if we're talking about a military; or about the position held by the accused in the case of a minister. The issue, Mr. President, is that the Prosecution insists on Stanisic being the highest authority within the RS MUP and Stanisic ensuring that his forces played an integral part of the JCE. Mr. President, we have already addressed the issue that even if all of our grounds of appeal were to be denied, we made it clear in our submissions, as well as this morning, that the contribution of Mico Stanisic to these crimes was nowhere close to what the Trial Chamber found, let alone what the Prosecution would like you to read from the Chamber's findings. The submissions of the Prosecution today fails to take into account that many of these crimes were committed while the members of the RS MUP were resubordinated to the military, and it's not possible to attribute this responsibility to Mico Stanisic due to the absence of the proper Trial Chamber finding in this regard. But what we have not heard a thing of today from the Prosecution is the measures taken by Stanisic, measures of dismissal of people involved in crimes, measures of disbandment of complete units created without his knowledge, measures of fighting against the paramilitaries, and the issuance of hundreds of orders, the multiple effect of which was to frustrate and at least to ensure that some of these crimes were certainly not committed. For us, Mr. President, it is clear that when you talk about the measures taken by Mr. Stanisic, the Prosecution will focus on the fact that all he was interested in was Golf vehicles and theft crimes. Well, one, this is incorrect. But what is more important, when the time comes to take measures, you take whatever measures you can take as quickly as you can in order to achieve a result. And it is the result that matters. And in this case, when we look at these orders, even though they might not have been implemented to the fullest extent possible - which was noted by the Trial Chamber - they did result in protecting victims and in minimising when Mr. Stanisic was aware of the crimes. Referring to the sentencing practice very quickly. Sentencing practice, even as laid out by the Prosecution today, the quantum differs not only based on the size of the crime but the responsibility. It is possible to have an individual perpetrator who committed crimes in the one area to get 40 years and it is possible to have a senior leader who is involved in crimes in many localities and yet because his role was much more limited, because his contribution to the joint criminal enterprise was more limited, then he gets a leaner sentence. We see absolutely no problem in respect of the quantum that was highlighted by my colleague. The problem we see with the sentence is to the contrary: Manifestly unreasonable and manifestly too high. Why? Because of the measures taken by Stanisic, because his role -- if you ever find, Mr. President, that his role -- that he was a member of this JCE, then his role, with everything that he did which is on the record - most of it was noted by the Trial Chamber but not all - when you look at what he did with what he could do in the circumstances, then we see that his responsibility, despite the number of victims, which is recognised as being very high -- we are not going to downplay the number of victims. We are not going to downplay that there were mass exodus. We're not going to downplay the fact that many people were displaced. But the Prosecution focuses on what is the link between Mr. Stanisic and the crimes. They say the crimes could not have happened without Mr. Stanisic. That is wholly incorrect, even if he was a member. And for these reasons, Mr. President, we say that the Prosecution ground of appeal on a manifestly unreasonable sentence must be dismissed. I only have one comment with respect to an observation made by my colleague concerning the crimes at Koricanske Stijene. I just wish to recall in this regard that Mr. Stanisic, of course, was acquitted at paragraph 798 of the judgement for command responsibility for this specific situation. We're not sure if this is or is not included in the crimes which fall under the joint criminal enterprise. In our submission, they don't, but I'm not positive about that. My submissions, rather, rest on the type of responsibility and the contribution to the crimes and what Mr. Stanisic did try to do as minister of the interior, even if you find that he was a member. For all these reasons, the ground of appeal should be dismissed. This ends our submission, Mr. President.

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The two Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I will begin the Zupljanin Defence response to Prosecution's appeal by addressing the second ground, that is cumulative convictions. Let me say at the outset that Zupljanin maintains all arguments from his response brief and those are paragraphs 17 to 25. Zupljanin is well aware of the divergent positions in the Tribunal's jurisprudence on entering convictions for crimes against humanity that are also the basis for persecution. The Prosecution has indicated in the footnote of their appeal brief, do not seek an increase in Zupljanin's sentence for the additional convictions of murder, torture, deportation, and inhumane acts, forcible transfer, as crimes against humanity. So if this appeal ground, as Zupljanin understands it, is more of a formal matter that primarily concerns harmonisation of jurisprudence that will not have any impact on sentencing, Zupljanin would refrain from making any further submissions and leave this matter in the Appeals Chamber's capable hands. If, however, on the basis of additional convictions the Appeals Chamber is, for one reason or another, inclined to consider an increase of Mr. Zupljanin's sentence, it is submitted that such approach would effectively amount to entering new charges on appeal which would be contrary to Mr. Zupljanin's right to appeal. So in case the Appeals Chamber decides to correct the Trial Chamber's reasoning and findings, Zupljanin submits that His Honour Judge Pocar's methodology from his partially dissenting opinion in Popovic et al. should be followed. In other words, Your Honours are invited to adopt the approach from the Krstic case and several other appeal judgements, i.e., to just pronounce the error but decline to enter new convictions against Mr. Zupljanin for murder, torture, deportation, and inhumane acts, forcible transfer, as crimes against humanity, and such pronunciation should not reflect on Mr. Zupljanin's sentence. In this manner, Your Honours, we submit the balance between fairness to the accused and the interests in convictions will be met while, at the same time, Zupljanin's right to appeal will not be violated. I will now turn over the floor to my learned colleague Mr. Gosnell, who will address the remainder of the Prosecution's appeal. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zupljanin requests dismissal of Prosecution's appeal Ground 1. The Prosecution has just submitted that the sentence for Mr. Zupljanin should not be any less than for other leadership cases arising from similar or the same circumstances. Yet, at trial the Prosecution submitted that Mr. Zupljanin wasn't a Brdjanin, he wasn't a Vukic, he wasn't a Kalenic, and that was a measured submission, a measured submission that is reflected on some degree presumably in the Trial Chamber's own assessment, full assessment, of the facts that it found as against Mr. Zupljanin. The Prosecution has not alleged or suggested that there has been an error of methodology on the part of the Trial Chamber in reaching its sentence. Quite the contrary, the methodology being proposed by the Prosecution would itself constitute a serious methodological error. In particular, it seems to suggest that intent should be accorded either no value or virtually no value, whereas obviously intent is of the utmost concern in assessing culpability which must be considered, surely, the primary factor in assessing and determining sentence. So, Your Honours, on the basis of those submissions and the submissions that have been made by my learned colleague for Mr. Stanisic, as well obviously the submissions that are made in the Defence's Ground 4 appeal, we request that appeal Ground 1 be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I hear no further submissions from your team. Prosecution reply. You have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have one small clarification to make in reply. The learned counsel for Stanisic queried whether Stanisic was, in fact, convicted for the Koricanske Stijene events and he certainly is. I would direct Your Honours to convictions for murder found at paragraph 858 of Volume 2, and further to 855 and 856. The paragraph that he refers to, 798, to clarify, there, the Chamber is clearly only speaking about extermination and because he was not found to be in a position to foresee extermination therefore was not convicted under JCE 3, the Chamber went on to look at other modes of responsibility and they found that he was not responsible pursuant to 7(3) for extermination. He was, however, convicted for murder, which was all that Mrdja was convicted for. Your Honour, for the remainder of our submissions, we would rely on our briefs. Sorry, Your Honours, just one moment. Your Honours, just a small clarification. The quotation about Brdjanin and Vukic that my learned colleague refers to, you can find that at transcript page 27365, and I believe it's been taken out of context. For the rest of our submissions, we will rely on our briefs. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, is your client going to address the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stanisic, you have an opportunity to address the Appeals Chamber and please restrict yourself to the ten-minute limit. Thank you. THE APPELLANT STANISIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, allow me to begin my address by expressing my gratitude to you for giving me this opportunity to address you today. As it has been a long day, I promise that I will try to be as brief as possible. During the last few months, you have heard and read much about me in the submissions of my counsel and the Prosecution. However, with the exception, of course, of the Presiding Judge, this is the first time you actually see me and have a chance to assesses and compare everything you have heard or read about me - be it good or bad - and which, as I'm convinced, you will assess in a proper and humane manner. More than ten years ago - and I can hardly believe it's been so long - I was informed that ICTY issued an indictment against me. Of course, as a law-abiding man who feels ethics to be an integral part of my being, I immediately expressed through the relevant organs of the Republic of Serbia my unconditional wish to travel to The Hague and respond to the accusations directed against me before ICTY. I came to The Hague with a clear purpose: I wanted to be enterprising and explain the following: Who I was and what position I took at the relevant time, what I did and what measures I took at the relevant time, why I took such measures, how I did that and how I acted under the hardly bearable conditions prevailing at the time. I, therefore, unconditionally accepted to be interviewed by the Prosecution so that they would understand my position. I gave an extensive interview to the Prosecution, and from then on up until today it turned to the battle of my life. I authorised the team of my counsel to prepare my defence in accordance with all the information I had given to the Prosecution, both with regard to the persons I communicated with in any way and the documents from the relevant period. From the first day of the trial to the closing arguments, by an identical and unchanging approach, my counsel followed my personal stand which I have had since my arrival to ICTY. They explained who I am, what steps I took, and how I conducted myself. It is needless to say that I was really unhappy when a conviction was issued at the end of the trial. However, I immediately started working on my appeal, adopting the same open and transparent approach once again. From my first day in The Hague to this day, I never had anything to hide and this never changed. Even though it is true that on my counsel's advice I initially refused to testify in the Karadzic case, from the moment when I was ordered to do so, I fully co-operated with the Trial Chamber in that case and answered all questions to the best of my ability. I am aware that what I stated there is not an integral part of the record pertaining to my appeal. In any case, it is important for me to stress that what I said as a witness in the Karadzic case shows my willingness to contribute to the establishment of truth, in particular as regards my conduct at the relevant time. I hope that you know that although I held the position of interior minister of Republika Srpska, I never was a politician. Let me note just a small part of what I had to face because of my principled and professional approach while attempting to make it possible for members of the MUP to discharge their duties under those difficult, or rather, impossible conditions. I opposed Ms. Plavsic, deputy president of Republika Srpska, because she invited and brought various paramilitary formations from the territory of the former Yugoslavia to Republika Srpska which committed various crimes, including the most serious ones on their arrival to Republika Srpska. Because of this, together with a part of the Republika Srpska leadership, she launched a fierce and comprehensive campaign against me, accusing me by saying that while she was bringing volunteers to defend the Serbian people from its enemies, I arrested them and persecuted them with the help of MUP members. Due to this accusation, my personal security as well as that of my family was threatened by extremists from our own people and a part of the Republika Srpska leadership became my enemies. After the first collegium meeting which we managed to hold only on the 11th of July, 1992, having assessed that my assistants in various departments were not sufficiently committed to the discharging of their tasks, I immediately did all that was necessary to remove them from their posts. I was successful in this, but consequently I now also had some enemies within my own ranks. President Karadzic twice removed me from my post of interior minister, once during the events that led to the accusations against me and once more later on. In both times I stepped down without any fuss and left, as politics was never something I aspired to. In so doing, I sacrificed my own security, which would have been unimportant had I not also sacrificed the security of my family, including my four children who were all underaged at the time. During the trial I was criticised for using the term "president" when referring to Radovan Karadzic, even though this happened in but a few instances. It is true that I used the term but for one reason only, because such etiquette stems from my education as a jurist and my personal courtesy. Your Honours, I assert with full responsibility that I have never committed any crime, including the relevant period. It was clear to me as a member of the government that the breakup of Yugoslavia would also result in a division of Bosnia between the warring parties, but I assert with full responsibility that I never wanted this to happen through the commission of any crimes. I also assert that I was not the only one who held such a position. It is true that I cannot claim before you that none of the members of our highest organs of power or someone at the lower levels may have had different, that is to say, incriminating intentions, but I can claim with full responsibility that I was not among those nor would they have accepted me in view of my position with regard to crimes. Your Honours, I wish to say something about a letter published by one of the honourable Judges before whom I stood trial. My counsel advised me to be wary if I intended to address this topic, and I shall do so; however, I feel it important to express my thoughts on this issue. When I read that letter, I was astonished. I wondered: Is it possible that my fate had already been sealed and that my conviction was a direct or indirect result of the ideas, views, and standards expressed in that letter? I will never know the answer to this question, which makes me really sad and concerned. Your Honours, I sincerely regret that this war ever took place and I sincerely wish that no war ever be fought again anywhere. I feel very sorry for all the victims who perished as a result of certain incriminating acts committed during the war by members of my people. I'm also very sad because of all the families who were torn apart as a result of those events. I equally regret that I could not contribute more in making sure that fewer crimes were committed and more perpetrators brought to justice. And finally, Your Honours, I stand here before you and I claim with full responsibility that considering the information that was available to me and the exceedingly difficult conditions in which we worked, I did my utmost to prevent and end the commission of crimes; and where crimes did happen, that the perpetrators be arrested and brought to justice regardless of their ethnicity or religion. I believe and I trust, Your Honours, that what you have heard is sufficient to convince you to overturn my conviction and send me back home. In view of the above, if you do not think that my conviction should be quashed and I be sent back home, please make it possible for me to have a new trial before a new Trial Chamber so that I would demonstrate that I never wanted any crimes to be committed and to explain the following: The position I had at the relevant time, the measures I took, why I took such measures, and how I took them under the exceedingly difficult conditions at the relevant time. This is what I wish regardless of the time necessary for a new impartial trial to which I came voluntarily ten years ago. I thank you once again for the opportunity to address you today. My fate is in your hands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Zupljanin, do you wish to address the Chamber? THE APPELLANT ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I'd like to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Thank you. THE APPELLANT ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not my intention to speak for long because many words have been uttered here; however, I do wish to take part in today 's work in order to remind you of some details. The war found me at the position of the chief of the Banja Luka CSB; before that, in the BH Ministry of the Interior I had spent full 17 years in different functions. I come from a mixed family encompassing the members of all three ethnicities. They lived together before the war, they lived together during the war, and they do so now. The situation we found ourselves in when the civil war began was a grave one. It was very difficult to get one's bearing in all that. Events began taking each other over. As the conflict grew, it could be less and less controlled and the polarised ethnicities and the exodus of people's grew. In such circumstances, for one to be a policeman was practically impossible. My colleagues in the ranks were Croats and Muslims as well. They held different positions. When Republika Srpska was established, I strove to keep them on board, but unfortunately I was unsuccessful and the CSB was decimated in the process. The police force was overwhelmed with the events and without the professional cadre. It was very difficult to stem the flow of those events. Unfortunately for all of us, the war took place. People came and went. Civil disobedience became more pronounced. Incidents grew in numbers. Arson took place, looting, murders; all that created chaos and insecurity for the entire population. The forces I had at my disposal were not capable to adequately address the situation we found ourselves in. I wrote many reports and I publicly spoke of such events, referring to them by their proper name. I established commissions and other working bodies in order to try and establish what the real situation on the ground is; sometimes I succeeded and others unfortunately I did not. I submitted numerous criminal reports for crimes against non-Serbs wherever I could. I created operational plans and carried out arrests. Sometimes I even went beyond what I was allowed to do under the allow in order to do good, but now I see it's turned against me as evidence to prove that my authority was great. In such a difficult war time situation, mistakes are possible and mistakes were made, but not with ill intent. It is certain that from today's perspective it is far easier to view them all than it was at the time when they were taking place, and that is why I sincerely regret some of the things. I am sorry for the omissions I may be responsible for. I'm sorry for all the victims from that period. Under such circumstances, in such times, whether I could have performed better or done more, that is something for this Chamber to decide. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Zupljanin. Any further comments? Okay. This concludes the hearing of the appeal in this case. Before we adjourn, I would like to take this moment to thank the parties for their work in this case. I would also like to express my gratitude to the Registry staff here in the courtroom and outside the courtroom who have been so ably facilitating our hearing today. Particularly, I would like to thank the interpreters, the recorders for their excellent assistance, and to the technicians and all other staff involved in our assistance during today's session. The Appeals Chamber will render its judgement in due course. The proceedings stand adjourned. Thank you.
